g I MEAN 'TO WAIT FOR JACK."-A. LESSON FOR LOVERS.
- -- Sweet Sate at Wyndham's Dalry,and Jack of Oldham Mill— they woo'd and fond they coo'd, a faithful Jack and

jill - Jut times were bad for lass and lad, and sadly both conPsq'd Vim not the thing to buy the ring before they'd lin(-d the nest. "Courage, lad !" said Katie. "Yes, we'll hare ta wait; But though, my dear, it's twenty year, I'll take no other mate."

Bet England wanted Jacky, for war was in the air, And arms more grim were press'd on him than Katie's bonny pair. So all through Spain, in rough campaign, he chivied bold lossoo, And fired his gun and made him run like fun at Waterloo. When the lads came round her, Katie bade them pack, "There's girls enoo for you to woo; I mean to wait for Jack."

- The gray in Katie's ringlets were mingling with tte brown, When, bump-a-thump,an eager stump came pegging through the town, "It's me, you see, come back," says he, "except a leg or so; And safe and sound here's twenty pound; so let the parson know." Jingle, jangle, jingle! set the bells a-chime, 'And health and bliss to love like this that bravely bides its time. —Fsznitnica LANGBILIDGE, in "Good Words" for Jove.

Brignoli was asked at a concert to appear before the cur- tain and apologise for a singer's sudden indisposition. The tenor, going forward, said—" Ladies and gentlemen, I regret to zay zit Madame N— eez a little horse die evening." Peals of laughter greeted this announcement, and the tenor looked puzzled, thinking the audience misunderstood him. He advanced once more, and with thundering emphasis roared out, " I zay zat Madame N— eez is a little horse die evening." Another roar of laughter, amid which a voice in the gallery cried out, "Then if she is a horse, why not trot her out ?" Then the mistake was plain to him, and Brignoli laughed as heartily as any one. Lord Coleridge is delighting his English friends with stories of his American visit, and among them with this. He was at Mount Vernon with Mr. Everts, and talking about Washington, said—" I have heard that he was a strong man physically, and that standing on the lawn here he could throw a dollar right across the river on to the other bank." Mr. Everts paused a moment to measure the breadth of the river with his eye. It seemed rather a "tall" story, but it was not for him to belittle the father of his conniry in the eyes of a foreigner. "Don't you believe it?" asked Lord Coleridge." "Yes," Mr. Evarts replied, "1 think its very likely to be true. You know a dollar would go further in those days than it does now." It is not often that an American is intentionally rude to 3 foreigner, or that that foreigner, especially when he hap- pens to be one of oar British cousins, is successful in return- ing an unanswerable and unruffled reply. These two things eaappened concurrently at a club in this city at the recent celebration of Evacuation-dav, in commemoration of the final exodus of the British garrison a century before. A young Englishman happens to be seated at breakfast as the procession passes by, and to him enters a convivial young American, who, in a somewhat husky voice, remarks, "I shay, do you know whash thish day we are shelebrating, oh?" "Yes," said the Briton, calmly, as he scanned his interlocutor through what a novelist would call his un- moved eyeglass, "this was the day when the—ah ! the gentlemen left New York." The most patriotic by-standers could not forbear to cheer."—Harper's Magazine. The most famous of Japanese statues has been measured and it is found that the image of Daihatsu at Nara is of the , following dimensions: Length of back, 38ft.; length of face, 81t.; breadth of face, 6ft. 7in.; long diameter of ear, 21t. 31u.; length of eye, 2ft. sin.; length of nose, 3ft. fin.; height of nose, 2ft. din.; diameter of nostril, 2ft.; length of mouth, 2ft. din.; length of hand, 4ft. Sin.; circumference of waist, 25ft. A CARNIVOROUS WATER PLANT.—Mr. G. E. Simms, of Oxford, has discovered that the bladder-traps of Utricularia roulgaris are capable of catching newly hatched fish and killing them. The plant catches the fish generally by the head, which is pushed into the bladder in the specimens ob- served until the snout touches the hinder wall. Mr. Simms intends shortly to publish an account of his observations. A preliminary notice by Mr. H. N. Moseley appears in this week's Ncdure. From the description it would appear as though the fish entered the trap and were then seized. Some of the fish are, however, caught by the tail, but the actual process has not yet been observed. CATTLE PLAGUE IN THE PANAMAS —Cattle and horses are said to be dying in great numbers on the savannahs and plains around Panama. The Panama Star and Herald says: —"The carcases remain where the animals die, and the pestilential odour thus caused has led several families to desert the country and return to town. What the disease is no one seems to know; but all agree in declaring that I animals apparently in the best condition suddenly fall dead, without having offered the least evidence of being attacked by any form of sickness. It is probable the great scarcity of water, the bad quality of the little which can be found, and the Poorness of the pasture combine to produce the plague which is now causing serious loss to the owners of live stock." MOUNTAINEERING IN NEW ZEALAND.—The Australian papers contain accounts of a recent very successful ascent of the celebrated Mount Earnelaw glacier, New Zealand, made by a Dunedin tourist, who reached a point 2,000 feet higher than that attained by the Rev. Mr. Green and his Swiss guides last year. Of the latter part of the journey the tourist writes :—" A thousand feet on an incline of about one in two is no joke, and were it not for the fern with which the mountain side is covered, I doubt whether we would have been able to get up at all. The mountain vegetation stood us in good stead, and clutching the silvery tussoks krown as sno wgrass, we made our way up. For about 500 feet we passed through a belt of large birch trees. Beneath oar feet lay the leaves of centuries, the uppermost stratum being composed of leaves recently blown from the trees and not yet withered, the whole forming a beautiful springy carpet, quite a treat to walk on after a couple of hours' toiling over rough surface through fern and snow- grass. Such a path was, however, too good to last long, and our shady belt of birch trees came to an abrupt f ermiration right under a high ledge of rock, which appeared more difficult to climb than the one we had previously encoun- tered. We traversed a dried up water bed for some 800 feet, avoiding the prickly speargrass—which proved a great source of annoyance—as much as possible. Here we got our first view of the beautiful mountain lily, with its saucer- shaped leaves, which made very suitable drinking vessels. The mountain at this part was thickly covered with the lilies. Higher up the snow was •plentifully covered with the red lichen." The scene at the farthest point reached is described as follows:—" Miles and miles of solid ice towered hundreds and hundreds of feet above us, while every few minutes masses of detached ice many tons in weight went thundering and crashing down the mountain slopes iato the valley below. It was indeed a grand and awful scene, and its impressiveness came home to our minds with full force. We had reached a point 6,700 feet high."

COTTAGE GARDEN IN G WEEDS. —A week of exceptional weather for the time of the year has enabled us to get the upper hand of the weeds for the present. We have no objection to seeing weeds growing rapidly, for we know that other members of the vegetable kingdom are making similar progress. The best way to keep down weeds is to take advantage of dry sunny weather and apply the hoe to every yard of ground, whether weeds are visible or not. In this way thousands of weeds are destroyed on the very threshold of their existence. When weeds attain any size they may be hoed one day and the sun may shine, but if rain falls a couple of days after the greater portion will take root and raise themselves up in a defiant attitude, challenging another attack from the hoe. So long as the weather is showery the weeds will have the best of it and the hoe will be thoroughly defeated, and there must be called in such auxiliary forces as the rake and hand weeding. Advantage should be taken of fine weather to stake Peas, as no injury can be done to the surface of the soil by the unavoidable treading upon it. Mach of the traffic may be avoided if the sticks are in the first instance put in small bundles at intervals along the side of the row. Where this is not convenient on account of the proximity of other crops, it is of considerable advantage to have an assistant to reach them from the nearest point. Our earli.st Peas which had a slight protection in the early period of their growth are now in flower. The making of Celery trenches and wheeling the manure into them can be more con- veniently executed when the surface of the soil is dry than when it is moist and sticky. Cucumbers may be planted out now if a slight protection is supplied to them at night for two or three weeks. The plants make more rapid growth It they are afforded a alight bottom heat, which is usually applied by making a trench 18in. to 241 n. deep and the same in width, and filling it up with, fermenting material, the best no doubt being short stable dung turned over two or three times previous to use. Into this the roots penetrate and find nourishment. Most of the soil thrown out of the trench is thrown back on the top of the manure, so that when it is completed it forms a ridge, which as time goes on will sink nearly level with the ground line. The Vegetable Marrow should have similar treatment as the Cucumber. Though the Marrow is not quite so tender, it well repays for the stimulating influence of bottom heat. If some fore- thought has been exercised in arranging the rubbish heap in a suitable corner it will be an excellent spot to plant Marrows. Should the heap not be of the required dimen- sions or deficient of heat, both.faults can be rectified by add- ing the desired quantity of stable manure, long and short, as it comes. On the top of this mixture should be placed a barrow load or two of soil for each plant to start in, as the contents of the heap may at first be too crude. THE FRONT GARDEN.—TWO conspicuous plants to be seen flowering in several cottage gardens are the Peony and the Iris or Flag. We saw the former in a garden the size of a table sufficiently large to accommodate half a dozen per- sons to dine at. This might be regarded as the height of incongruity. We admit the want of proportions in having a plant that grows a yard in diameter in such a small area; but, located as it was in one corner, we did not pass a vote of censure. In fact, we were inclined to admire it, and would have been very reluctant to advise its removal. Such a plant fixed in the centre of this extra small garden would have given it the appearance of being tolerably well fur- nished in the absence of any other plant. The Peony will thrive well in the shade ; so will the Iris. The varieties of this, like those of the former, are numerous; they are very

TRE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS ACT.—Early in March last, at a meeting of the Newcastle Farmers' Club, a com- mittee, composed of land-agents and farmers, was appointed for the purpose of framing a basis on which to estimate compensation as provided in the Agricultural Holdings Act, 1883, and on Saturday week the report of this committee was discussed by the members of the club. We have not ovine to give the whole of this report, bat extract the fol. lowing from it, as showing the methods suggested by the committee for-arriving at a fair and equitable rate of com- pensation is provided for in the Act that a tenant at the termination of his tenancy shall obtain from the land- lord such compensation as fairly represents the value of the Improvement to an incoming tenant.' It appears to your committee that, fixing a scale naming a hard and fast value for every 'improvement' named in the Act, whether well or ill-executed, whether in good or bad repair, and re- ducing the price by a certain percentage for each year used, would in effect and incidence be unjust, resulting in the good farmer getting too little, and the bad farmer too much.. For instance, in regard to under-drainage, it cannot be said that if badly planned and executed, and kept in bad repair, it would be of the same value to the landlord or incoming tenant as if it had been efficiently made and kept in g )od repair; or that the application of , purchased manures, or the consumption of purchased food, would leave the same manurial value in a holding full of weeds, badly cultivated and managed, as on that clean, thoroughly cultivated, and well managed. Therefore, to obviate as much as possible the unequal operation of the Act, your committee propose a basis on which" improve- menus' may be animated, having a certain degree of elasti- city; SO that arbiters may have sufficient scope to arrive at decisions which will not only tend to encourage tenants permanently to Improve their holdings, loot also prevent the danger of landlords or incoming tenants having to pay for that which has been so badly made or treated that it is ex- hausted, and little more left in the shape of an improvement than a name. Your committee suggest that, in regard to each 'improvement' (with one exception), there should be compensation of three degrees, viz., first class, second class, and third class. The first class to mean that when in re- gard to an improvement' the effects were very beneficial, from the management generally having been good and judi- cious; second class, when these conditions had not been so meritorious ; and third class, when the conditions had been bad. At present no machinery existed for their practical instruction, and the question was obviously difficult to deal with. The first suggestion is that in each county there should be situated a good farm, the tenant of which would agree under certain terms to take agricultural apprentices for a term. The teacher should be thoroughly capable, and the apprentices, who should be selected from those who distinguished themselves most in an examination held yearly in connection with that of the Science and Art Department, should be entitled to earn rewards. Scholarships should be given, tenable at these farm schools, which should have the assistance of the lead- ing agricultural societies. In a somewhat similar manner practical instruction could be given to girls in dairying and housekeeping. Mr. Jenkins recommends that the Govern- ment should put agriculture on at least an equal footing with science and art. As to instruction in the rudiments of agriculture in elementary country schools, Mr. Jenkins makes proposals with the object of combining technical with general instruction at public elementary schools in rural districts, so that the sons of farm labourers and farm bailiffs, who get all their schooling at such institutions, may have an education fitting them for an agricultural career. He approves the desirability of a piece of garden ground being attached to schools as a means of technical education. Each plot could be cultivated by a scholar holding it under the superintendence of the schoolmaster. With regard to school teaching, he recommends alterations in the standards of examination, with the object of aiding instruction on agricultural matters.—Following the report there are a number of useful appendices. Next week we shall give a summary of the report on agri- cultural education in North Germany.

Tux STORY OF " AULD Ronne Gaay."—Like many of the popular ballads of Sdotland, "Auld Robin Gray" was written to an old air, which was first associated with words of a coarse and vulgar nature. This melody, with its then accompanying words was frequently sang in the castle by a female friend of the family, and it was in order to give it a more fitting setting that Auld Robin Gray" was writ- ten. In a letter to Sir Walter Scott, Lady Anne gives the following account of the composition of the song :—" I longed to sing the air to different words, and to give to its plaintive tones some little history of virtuous distress in humble life, such as might suit it. While attempting to effect this in my closet, I called to my little sister, now Lady Hardwicke, who was the only person near me, 'I have been writing a ballad, my dear; I am oppressing illy heroine with many misfortunes—l have already sent her Jamie to sea, and broken her father's arm, and made her mother fall sick, and given her Auld Robin Gray for a lover; but I wish to load her with a fifth sorrow in the four lines, poor thing! Help me to one, I pray!' Steal the cow, sister Anne,' said the little Elizabeth. The cow was immediately lifted by me, and the ballad completed."—Cossell's Family Magazine. MEDITATIONS ON A BROOMSTICK.—Dean Swift was in the habit of visiting Lady Berkeley, his patron's consort. She was an admirer of " Boyle's Pious Meditations," and used often to request the Dean to read aloud some portion from them. Such occupation, however, was too little congenial with the Dean's humour, and soon he resolved to revenge himself upon Boyle for the irksome task thus imposed upon him. In short, he wrote a parody upon him, which he got printed and entitled," Meditations on a Broomstick." This he sewed into a copy of Boyle, from which her Lady- ship was accustomed to read. It was exactly the same paper, type, and so ingeniously Anterted that no one was likely to conjecture the deceit. Sw-the next time he opened the book at the "Meditations upon a Broomstick," which, with a very grave countenance, he read aloud. Lady: "No jesting, if you please, Mr. Dean, upon so grave a subject?' Swift: " Jesting ! I vow, my Lady, I read it as I find it; here it is, Meditations upon a Broomstick." Lady :"So it is—upon my word. What a singular subject! But Boyle is so full of ideas that I am persuaded he will make it ex- tremely edifying, though it looks so odd." With great gravity Swift proceeded to read a very original comparison between a broomstick and a man, and contrasted the destiny of mankind with that of the broomstick. "This stick," he continued, in a solemn tone, "this stick, that you see thrown Ignominiously into a corner, was once flourishing in the wOodil," &c. "Q excellent Boyle !" exclaimed her Lady- ship,'" how admirably he has drawn the moral from so trifling a subject. But whatever he touches he turns to gold.' The Dean, preserving his gravity, made signs of assent, as if he quite agreed with her ladyship, and then took his leave. In the evening her ladyship had a party, and one of the first topics started was Boyle's excellent "Meditations upon a Broomstick." Some of the company began to laugh. • You may laugh," exclaimed her Ladyship, "but I am astonished you should not have heard of it; it is quite worthy the pen of this great moralist." Others, however, ventured to question its existence; when her Ladyship, in triumph, pointed out the part, which they saw sure enough. " Have I convinced you, gentlemen ? I see you are quite confounded; but to tell you the truth, so was I at first. Indeed, I should still have been ignorant of the fact, but for Mr. Dean Swift, who was so good as to point it out to me, only to-day." "What !" cried some of the party, "was it Swift ? this is one of his tricks, then; let us have another copy of Boyle." They went and looked, and looked, but no "Meditations upon a Broomstick" were to be found; it was plain that the whole had been interpolated. The lady con- cealed her chagrin; but henceforth she never imposed upon ' the author of "Gulliver" the reading of these edifying lec- tures. TRE WINDOW.—The boxes intended for the outside of the window are improved if covered with virgin cork on the outer side, and we are inclined to believe that plants do much better in such boxes. If the plants do well, their roots are soon at the side of the box and on a hot sunny day they must be exposed to a very high temperature, and no doubt many perish. It will be obvious that the cork forms an extra barrier for the sun's rays, and as the pieces are usually slightly concave on the side that should be next the box, a current of air passes continually between them, which must preserve the roots in a more uniform tempera- ture. The soil for planting should be fresh and fairly en- riched with well-decayed manure. Few plants surpass the Geraniums for boxes, and most people are acquainted with the variety called Vesuvias, which is the best scarlet we know for the purpoSe. Star of Fire is also good. It is of a more .intense scarlet, but straggling In habit. The Pinks, or Rosy-Pink, might be represented by Christine, Rose Queen, and Oliver Carr, and if four plants form the back row the two centre ones may be Rose Queed and the outer two Yeenvias, assuming the building materials surrounding the window to be light-coloured bricks or stone, or imitation thereof. On the other hand, if of bright red brick, the posi- tion of the plants should be reversed. The Blue Lobelia and 'Yellow Pyretherum are admirably adapted to form front rows, and the beauty of the latter is enhanced if the former is mixed with it. The hardy variegated grass Dactylis Glomerata is unsurpassed for its gracefulness as a front. row plant mixed with Lobelia. The Yellow Calceolaria, in com- pany with a bright scarlet Geranium, makes a gorgeous dis- play. A plant of the Canary Creeper at each end of the box, to be trained each side the window, will complete the picture.

ON LETTING OFF THE STEAM.—There are more interest- ing cases by far in which excitable persons, knowing their own weakness, have provided themselves with some mode ot exercise, on purpose to divert their excitement from a hurt- ful to an innocent channel. An instance of this we find in the life of Oberlin, pastor of the Ban de in Roche, in the High Alps, in the South of France. Oberlin was one of the best of men, and endeared himself to his people almost beyond example. Besides being an earnest pastor, he was a maker of roads, a builder of bridges, a reformet and philan- thropist generally, who transformed his parish from a chaos of desolation into a beautiful abode of Christianity, civilisa- tion, and comfort. It was not to be wondered at, that a man with so many irons in the fire should be somewhat impatient, and have a little trouble with his temper. At such times Oberlin used to run backwards and forwards in his room, beating his hands together rapidly with a resounding noise, until his temper regained composure. Those who are fami• liar with the history of the Brontës will remember what is told of their father, the eccentric and excitable incumbent of Haworth. "Even during his wife's lifetime he formed the habit of taking his meals alone; he constantly carried loaded pistols in his pockets, and, when excited, he would fre these at the doors of outhouses, so that the villagers were quite accustomed to the sound of pistols at any hoar of the day in their pastor's house." If we are not mistaken, he had another outlet for his emotion, setting up a bolster and boxing it when he was angry; but of this we are not so sure.—Prof. Blaikie, in" Cassell's Family Dragazzne."

Councillor BROADBENT felt sure that the Sanitary Com- mitiee did not wish to do anything unfair or disadvanta- gous to the members of the Council. He wished to refer to the matter brought forward by Dr. Mackie. He quite agreed with that gentleman in the compliment that he had paid to the Medical Officer, and he was sure that they must all feel that Councillor Mackie's speech was actuated by the best feelings. He (Mr. Broadbent) had no doubt that injury arose in Warrington in connection with the sewer gas. Perhaps that was almost inevitable as the town wasl situated, or at any rate t was inevitable as the sewers were ' at present. He hoped that hy the satisfactory results of the system at Latchford, that system might be extended I over the other parts of the hoemsh. He thought that whilst they were speaking on this question they were bound to acknowledge the weat services that had been rendered to. the town by the Sanitary Committee. It was almost impos- sible to exaggerate the extent and the importance of those services. He believed that to the resolute action of that committee many years ago, and particularly of the chair- man, hundreds of lives, nay more, had been saved in War- rington, and whilst they lamented the injuries done by sewer gas he thought that they should not close their eyes. to other causes of disease and death. He believed that many improvements in sanitary arrangements had been and were being made in different towns, and that in this respect Warrington had taken a lead, so that they should not shut their eves to the cause of the great infant mortality If they visited some of the darker and closer alleys in Warrington they would be surprised—not that there was such a large mortality' but that children managed to live at all in such. pl ices ! How they had been reared in such circumstances. be was sometimes puzzled to know. Young healthy chil- dren required wholesome food, plenty of fresh air, and well ventilated rooms,, but how many, he asked, of the children ofeWarrington failed to get any of those requirements. He wished to mention other causes, some of them preventible, which bore floe this question. There was no doubt that temperance amongst the people would enable them to give additional comfort to their children—(hear, hear,),--and witn regard to fresh air it must be borne in mind that the action which the Council had taken from time to time to provide open spaces might be beneficial. It was only right that sewer gas as a cause of iafant mortality should be, brought before the Council, bet there were other causes which merited serious consideration. Councillor MACKIN pointed out that be had not referred to sewer gas as the sole cause, but probably as a came of large mortality in proportion to any other. Cenneillor FRANCOMB thought that the death rate of War- rington was one of the lowest in "elngland. If the sewere, he said, had been so dasperarsty bad, and Dr. Gornall had said so a few years ago, he. tnigut have been right, but dur- ing the last two or three 7ears the sewers had been flushed regularly, and he could not think that the thing was so bad after all. Councillor PLATT said that although Warrington was far advanced on the road to sanitary perfection, it was still a considerable distanco from the mark to which they all aimed. He felt sure that a great sickness and mortality did result from the sewers. Thero were some streets in War- rington that it was hardly safe to pass through, let alone to live in, and unfortunately they were the poorer streets, narrow and overcrowded, and where there were a great many children pleying about. Children were constantly seen playing near open grates, to get a breath from which was almost sufficient to knock them down. He could say from personal experience that there were very bad emanations from sewers in many parts of the town. He thought there would be a general desire to put that matter right, and bad no doubt that the chairman of the committee had it under consideration. FERIGIIS CHARGE AGAINST YEAST DRALERS.—A yeast dealer named Gilder, and his two sons, were charged at Liverpool on Monday, with wilfully damaging several baskets of yeast. The prisoners went into a railway station where 21 baskets of yeast were lying, 16 of which were consigned to them, and one of the prisoners was seen to pour something from a bottle over the other five baskets. They were immediately arrested, and the bottle WAS found to be labelled " Carbolic Acid. Poison." The only motive asslgned for the allezed offence was in the fact that that portion of the yeast belonged to a rival tradesman. The stipendiary remanded the prisoners, and refused to accept bail.

MOTIKEES TO THE PESCI:IE.—A tale of the time of Henry VIII. is going through the English Ill2otrated Magazine. The following scene relates to the pardoning of apprentices of the City of London who had been engaged in a riot, through the intercession of the Queen :--" The Recorder of London and several aldermen were to meet the King at his manor of Greenwich. This was the mothers' opportunity. The civic dignitaries rode in mourning robes, but the wives and mothers, sweethearts and sisters, every woman who had a youth's life at stake, came together, took boat, and went down the river, a strange fleet of barges, all containing white caps, and black gowns and hoods, for all were clad in I the most correct and humble citizen's costume. Never was such a sight,' said Jester Randall, who bad taken care to secuna a view, and who had come with his report to the Dragon court. le might have been Ash Wednesday for the look of them, when they landed and got into order. One would think every prentice lad had got at least three mo• there and four or five aunts and sisters! I trow, verily, that half of them came to look on at the other half, and get a sight of Greenwich and the three queens. However, be that as it might, not one of them but knew how to open the sluices. The Queen noted well what was coming, and she- and the Queens of Scotland and France sat in the great chamber with the doors open. And immediately there's a knock at the door, and as soon as the usher opens it in they come, three and three, every good wife of them with her napkin to her eyes, and working away with her sobs. Then Mistress Todd, the barber-surgeon's wife she spoke for all, being thought to have the more courtly tongue, having been tirewoman to Queen Mary ere she went to France. Verily, her husband must have penned the speech for her, for it began right scholarly, and flowery, with a likening of themselves to the mothers of Bethlehem (lusty innocents theirs, I trow !), but ere long the good woman faltered and forgot her part, and broke out, Oh! madam, you that are I a mother yourself, for the sake of your own sweet babe, give us back our sons.' And therewith they all fell on their knees, weeping and wringing their hands, and crying out, Mercy, mercy For our Blessed Lady's sake, have pity on our children!' till the good Queen, with the tears running down her cheeks for very math, told them that the power I was not in her hands, but the will wan for them and their poor sons, and that she would strive so to plead for them I with the Bing as to win their freedom. . . • . . In came the three queens, hand in hand, with tears in their eyes, so as they might have been the three queens that bore away King Arthur, and down they went on their knees, and cried aloud, • Dear sir, we, who are mothers ourselves, be- seech you-to set the hearts at ease of all the poor mothers who are mourning for their sons.' Whereupon, the door being opened, came in so piteous a sound of wailing and lamentation as our Harry's name must have been Herod to withstand! 'Stand up, Kate,' seith he, stand up, sisters, and hark in your ear. Not a hair of the silly lads shall be touched, but they must bide lock and key long enough to teach them and their masters to keep better ward.' And then, when the queens came back with the good tidings, such a storm of blessings was never heard, laughings and cryings, and the like, for verily some of the women seemed as distraught for joy as ever they had been for grief and I ear.' div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TRonsnsv. The House of Commons re-assembled to-d,y after the Whitsuntide holidays, the Speaker taking the chair a few 'minutes before four o'clock. NOTICES, kc.—Sir G. CAMPBELL gave notiee that in the *event of any plan being laid before Parliament for the corn- -mutation of perpetual pensions he should anoveits rejection Axonßsore gave notice that he would aek the Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs whether any representations had been made to the American Government as to the ducv. of a friendly Government in respect to dynamite conspire-, ties. (Hear, hear.)-,--Mr. Calm:Yr asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer, in the absence of the Secretary for War, if It was trae that another of the 100-ton guns had burst? The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER: I have no inform Rion on the subiect. THE SOUDAN.-41t. ASILMEAD BARTLETT asked the Under Secretary for 'Foreign Affairs whether any intelligence had been remived of Ceneral Gordon or with regard to the posi- tion of affairs at Khartoum and Berber.—Lord E. 'Frrz- IKAIIRICE Said that it would have been better if the hon member had given notice of the question. Since the House separated no news had been received in regard to General Gordon, except vague reports. - THE MERCEANT SHIPPING BILL.--Mt. INIACIVEE, rising to ask a question on a point of older, said he had revived from the Board of Trade a statement containing proposed ,1 alterations in the Merchant Shipping Bill effecting'42 of its I clauses and involving the withdrawal of almost the whole of the remaindez of the bill. He wished to know whether the , President of the Board of Trade would be in order if by such a method he introduced what was substantially a new bill as ; objectionable as the old one, and whether the right course I under the circumstances would not be to withdraw the Present CuaareEßKeilx explained that the Parlia- mentary paper which the hon. member had somewhat inacurately described was in the form of correspondence be- tween himself and certain gentlemen who had assisted him with their advica with reference to the Merchant Shipping 'Bill, and it included a copy of draft clauses drawn up partly in consequence of the discussion at the request of some members of the House who thought it wenld be convenient, to see the form which the bill would assume supposing the, amendments which they suggested were adopted.—The SPEAKER : No formal notice has been given, and there is nol irregularity in the action cf the President of the Board of Trade. SUPPLY.— he House went into Committee of Supply upon the Civil Service Estimates —On the vote of £33,003 for repairs, &c, to the 'Houses of Parliament, Mr. O'Comma complained of the want of accommodation in the House, the difficulty of intercommunication between one Part and another, and the bad system of ventilation.—Mr. 'SELAW-LEFEVRE replied that the want of intercommattica- tion was frequently brought under his notice, and every op- Portunity taken to improve it. He did not think the com- plaints in regard to the atmckephere was a just one, and the temperature was kept very equal.—Mr. JAMES LOWTHER suggested that the accommodation should be increased so as to afford places for all who wished to take part in debates, Whether they attended prayers sof not —Mr. Alderman FOWLER strongly objected to any enlargement of the House.—After some further suggestions the vote was agreed to. On the Tote of £206,500 for public buildings in Crreat Britain and Ireland and the Isle of man.—Phe vote was agreed to, as were votes to complete the sum of £75,000 for sites for the Admiralty and War Cffices, and £16,740 for furniture of public offices.—Progress was afterwards reported,

and the House resumed. The Committee stage of the Revision of Jurors' and Voters' Lists (Dublin County) Eill was resumed, and dur- ing the debate upon the Bill the Committee was counted out. The House resumed, and was then counted out at twenty minutes to two.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. REBEL ,DEFEAT AT DONGOLA.

CAIRO, SClNDAY.—tiajor Kitchener, accompanied by one Of the friendly tribes, left Korosko to-day on a reconnais- Bence in the direction of Murat, in order to ascertain whether the rumours of the presence of hostile tribes in that district are correct. An offieal telegram ,from Suakim mentions a rumour that Berber has surrendered, and that Osman Digma has collected a number of adherents, and is preparing to attack Suakim. No credence, however, is attached to the report, as the telegrams made mention of 20 guns, while it is known that there are only two at Berber. CAIRO, SIINR .—lVl&jor Turner, of the Egyptian,Army, who went up the lile to purchase camels, has been drowned while bathing at Kenett. The body has been Sound below Keneh. Canto. Mowney.—The following despatch has been re- ceived from the Governor of Dengola :—" ft ie untrue that Berber has fallen. On the •,contrary, Husseinirasha Khalifa has beaten the rebels. Neither has Khartoum sur- rendered. General Gordon continues fighting against the rebels. The prevince of Dongola is completely pacified as far as Merawe." The commanders aif the irregular troops engaged in the recent action in the Ssaigiyeh (F) district have telegraphed to the,ilhedive fully confirming the paoifi- • cation of the province. They express their belief in the Possibility of relieving Berber if the tiovernor of Dengola is reinforced. CAIRO, MONDAT.—A. telegram received today officially from the Mudir of Giongida states that he has gained terze alight advantage over the Shakeeyala tribe. The Matti'. also 8;13,s that Berber is no longer besieged. He further states that General Gordon is still holding tint. Another telegram, :tueived unofficially, via Snakim stated that the rebels have ! Zaire]] Berber. Hussein Paella Khalif& and allthe troops who oad remained faithful were, it is said, taken prisoners by the '-:ebels.—Daily Naos. THE MOVEMENTS OF THE REBELS. CAIRO, TUESDAY.—Sir Evelyn Wood Las received a tele- I cram from a.,,,ptain Eager at Korosko, stating that the fol- lowing despatch has reached that place from Major Kit- ehener, who left Korosko on the let instant on a reconnais- sance in the direction of Murad :—" Yesterday I met' Sheikh Sala at six o'clock in the morningEmidway between Mnrad and Abel flamed. I had sent Sala on May 26th to for posts along the road. When he reached Murad the rebels had been there two days before, and had left after Ordering the guard, under threats, to destroy the wells. The guard and Sala went on to a.distance of three hours this side of Abu flamed. Sala reports that the rebels are in force near Abu Limed. The Arneer ,of Sharnut is nending emis- saris& all over the country of the Bichareen to win over the inhabitants. He reports that Berber is closely invested, and that no communication with the town is possible. Haden- dowa is moving northward, and will march after Ramadan on Amami. A force from Kabbabish is reported to have gone towards Berber, intending to move on Dongola. It is rumoured that the Mandi is gone to Khartoum, the sur- render of which place is shortly expected. Captain Eager adds that,Zebehr's messengers to General Gordon have just arrived at Korosko, and that he is keeping them to see Major Kitchener." RUMOURED ESCAPE OF GENERAL GORDON. CAIRO, THURSDAY EVENING. A rumour is afloat this evening that General Gordon has escaped from Khartoum up the Nile on board an armoured steamer. No confirma- tory intelligence has, however, been received at the British Diplomatic Agency. According to official telegrams from Snakim, Osman Digna's forces are estimated at 7000 men. He threatens to attack Suakira on the 10th inst. ATTACK ON SUAKIM.

SULICIM, SUITDAY.—A spy, who arrived here this morning, reports that Osman Digna has assembled a force of 3,000 men and four guns, in the use of which he is daily exercising his troops, with the'intention of attacking Suakim shortly. A rumour has reached this place that Berber has fallen.— Standard. SUAKIN, MOKDAY.—Last night, about eleven o'clock, the rebels, about 200 strong, made a determined attack on the town at all points. The forts at once returned the fire, and Were supported by the guns of the fleet, and all available forces were lanied to support the garrison. Artillery and Musketry fire was kept up for four hours continuously, when the enemy retired. There was no loss on our side, and, so far as can be ascertained, the enemy left only two killed and one wounded on the field. TIIRSDAY.—Last night the rebels again made a vigorous attack on the town, diving in the picket and ad- vancing right up the lines. Here, however' they were driven back and pursued by cavalry. Two of the attacking force were killed. PORT SAID, WEDNESDAY.—Two hundred and fifty marines embarked at noon to-day on board the despatch vessel Iris, .under orders to proceed immediately to Suakim. OSMAN DICiNA'S NIGHT ATTACKS ON SUAKIM. SUARVI, TRIIRSDAY.—Osman Digna is becoming very •caggressive, and night attacks are now of regular occur- rence. In these attacks the Egyptian troops, who have 40-far behaved themselves well, have had the advantage. Caw, WRDNESDAY.—The reason why Osman Dipsa persistently attempts to take Suakim is the Mandi's inten- tion of crossing over to Mecca before moving northwards. Hence, he wants a seaport. We have no news about Berber •orjolartoum. The Mandi's presence at Khartoum is disbe- lieved. All news from those parts is equally untrustworthy, •owing to it being procured solely from native scouts, whose .fidelity and veracity are doubtful. There are still—includ- ing the French Consul and several Austrians, Italians, and Crreeks—eighty Europeans at Khartoum—Daily Telegraph. THE CONFERENCE. CONSTANSINOPLE, SUNDA'S( —The Ottoman Government has not yet replied to the last Note of the British Govern- ment on the aubject of the proposed Conference, but I have reason to believe that its answer will not much longer be deferred. From what I hear in Turkish official circles, I think it is not improbable that the Porte will accept Eng- land's invitation to take part in the Couferecce for the cln- sideration of the financial condition of Egypt, but with the reserve that its representatives shall be allowed at later hittings of the body to give. expression to the view of the Government on Egyptian afttirs•—aa-204ra. FRANCE. PARIS, SATURDAY.—Iii the Senate to-day, M.de G tvarclie Proposed to interpellate the G werwhent on the c 5 sire of 11;gypt. Tat. Julee Perry, however, declarad that it was inn- as thiti4a s'Aind at presear, to enter upon a di,cus- 4ien of the.atypti in question. On M. de Gty tedie persist- ing in speaking, he was celled to oiler and formally cue- hured.—A despatch from Shanghai announces the arrival of Mtisiral Lewes at Pekin, where he met with a very friendly teception from the Chinese authorites. • PAM, MONDAY.—According to telegrams from Rome,

the 'Vatican journal state that the Pops is much perturbed by a recerat vote of the French Senate in favour of divorce, and the decision of the Chamber of Deputies to hold semi- narists liable to military service. If the bills on these two subjects are finally adopted it is pretable that the Vatican willtainch a protest against them. FRANa AND 'CHINA. ?ants TGESI)AII.—A despatch received from General IZillot, dated Tuyen Quang, June 2nd, announces that two battalions of French troops, supported by five gunboats, had attached that place and occupied it after a feeble resistance. The defenders coraisted of remnants of bands from Bacninh and Honghoa. After having placed a garrison in Tuyen Quang General Minot wilt return to Hanoi. A party of Black Flags have tendered their submission. THE 'FRENCH CONSTITUTIONAL REVISION BILL. _ .

PARIS, TEurisnta:—The—e-OnTinittee et the Chamber of Deputies on the bill for the revision of the Constitution, has adovled the measure in the form proposed by the Go- vernment by 14 against 5 votes. SERIOUS FIRE IN A CHURCH. MAR/MLLES, THIIIISDAY.—The high altar in the Church of Notre Dame de la Grande has been destroyed by fire, together with a statue of the Virgin and several sacred objects. The value of articles destroyed is estimated at over 150fflOf. TERRIBLE BALLOON ACCIDENT. "

... Lrttu, SUNDAY: —A terrible accident occurred here to- day while a balloon was ascending, from which a view of Ude and neighbourhood cante obtained. The car become detached, and fell from a freight of forty metres. Twenty persons were in the car at the, time, of whom three were killed on the spot, and several others injured. The accident has caused great sensation here. The races were beiag held here, and the accident was taused by overloading 'ars car, which was occupied by L'S or 20 people, whereas it was in- tended to contain only eight or ten. LILLE. NIONDAY.—Ticere has been only one mete death 'up to the present through the balloon accident, but seven "or eight of those injured are believed to be in wia hope- less state.

div.head: GERMANY.
div.p: GERMANY.

RIMIPENNEIM, WIMN—ESDAY.—The Princess of Wales, accompanied by her daughters, has left here for Wies- baden. Batumi', WEDNES7AgY.—The Empress of Russia arrived.,l here at noon to-day from Rumpenheim, and was cordially,' welcomed at the railway station by the Emperor, the' Crown Princess, Princess -Victoria, the Hereditary Princess of Saxe-Meiningen, and all the Princes at present in Berlin. AUSTRIA.—ELECTION RIOTS. VIENNA, MONBAR.—A telegram from Klausenberg reporte that the electoral contest there has opened with some rather serious rioting. M. Ilegedues, the candidate of the Liberal party, on arriving in the town, WAS received with enthusiasm at the railway station, but on driving into the town in a carriage he was assailed, together with his supporters, with volleys of stones. About 60 people were injured. ITALY.

- ROME, MONDE?. —The anniversary of the death ef ari- baldi was commemorated to-day in Rome and in several towns in Italy. THE UNITED STATES.—THE PRESIDENCY. NEW Yoga, SUNDAY.—Mr. John C. Eno. late president of the Second National Bank, was arrested at Quebec as he was leaving for Europe. Delegates to the Republican Nomina- tion Convention continue to arrive in Chicago, and the•place is becoming very. lively. The partisans of both General Arthur and Mr. Blaine assert their confidence in the success of their candidates. Ten persons have been drowned by a waterspout in a cattle camp at Colorado. NEW YORE, MONDAY.—lntelligence received here from Chicago states that the contest between President Arthur and Mr. BlaMe for the Presidency of the United States will be close. The chances are said to be in favour of Mr. Blaine. The Republican National Committee have selected a sup- porter of Mr. Blaine as temporary chairman of the Conven- tion. Three receivers, including Mr. Keim, the president, have been appointed for the Readiv Railway Company. Messrs. Fisk and Hatch_have reamed payment.

div.head: ZULULAND.
div.p: ZULULAND.

DURBAN, SATURDAY.—The Boer leader in Zululand is reported to have arrived in Maritzburg, to confer with Sir H. Bulwe-, with a view to co-operate with the Crown in establishing peace and stable aovernment in the reserve. MURDER OF LIEUT. DUPUIS. Sratta, MWDAY.—Lientenant Dupuis, of the 2nd North Staffordshire regiment, recently left Quetta on a shooting expedition, and had not since been heard of. His body has to-day been found, and there is no doubt that he was mur- dered by Poe'Pathans. INDIA.

- CALCUTTA, WEDNESDAY. - A despatch from Quetta announces that the murderer of Lieut. Depuis has been arrested. Intelligence received here from Cabal states that the Ameer has advanced four months' pay to the Afghan army, and that the troops are making preparations to march. It is not yet known whether their destination will be Olinda- har or Turkestan. WHOLESALE POISONING IN HUNGARY.

In the village of Varanda, in South Hungary, a woman has been arrested on a charge, of poisoning her foarthlaus- band. She .confesses to having poisoned her three former husbands, and further. to have murdered in the same way hundreds of women in the last two years. She made use of a certain drugged preparation of brandy, which was made for her bra 'farmer's wife. This woman and many others have beea arrested.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The Treasurriarave appointed next Monday to hear Mr, Bradiaeurb, M.P., against the proposed commutation of tke Penn and Affarlborough pensions. The Sultan has erdered a post-mortem examination of the bodies of Midhat Fasha and his companions in banishment, whose deaths in, rapid succession have raaturally given rise 1 to suspicion. ; The bodiecof tlve other of the Biz men drowned by the I tcapsizing of & sailing boat at Blackool a fortnight age ,were washed &chore on Thursday at the north end of the '..promenade. The prisoners charged with being concerned in the outrage near Donougheaore were brought up on Thursday at Cork, but the witness Creed being unable to attend in consequence of his injuries, the accused were remanded. At the Brentwood Police Court, on Thursday, William Honry Harris, a soldier, was charged on remand with the murder of Mrs. Sarah Gilbert on the Great Eastern Rail- way en the 19th ult. The prisoner was commated for trial. The action for libel brought by Mr. French, deputy-inspec- tor of the Irish Constabulary, against Mr. William Varian,' M.P., proprietor of Theirfed Ireland, for having imput si im- moral practices to the plaintiff, was dismiesed in thei Irieh Court of Queen's Bench on Thursday for want of a i prose- cutor. Hans& FIRED BY LaGIITNING. During a violent thunderstorm which passed over Harwich on Thur aday afternoon, two houses were struck by lightning, w Vick smashed the roof, knocked down a chimney, dislodged the stoves in every room, and set on fire the basement of one of them. No personal injury was, however, sustained, and the fire was soon extinguished. ' THE VISIT OF THE Maolat Kueo.—Tawhiae, the Ma mi. King, and the chiefs who accompany him, and who land sal in London, on Saturday, had a private interview with lb 1n.,: Chesson, secretary of the Aborigines' Society, on Tuesda r„ • at which they intimated their wish to place the business their mission in the Society's hands. Tawhias appeared i a 1 the London streets on Tuesday, and attracted much atten- • tion. His Majesty must be regarded as much more advanced . in civilisation than Cetewayo, for he has promoted a news- paper to further his claims in New Zealand. LORD EGERTON OF TATTON ON AGRICULTURAL TOPICS. —The half-yearly meeting,,of the members of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture was held at Chester on Wednesday, Lord Egerton of Tatton presiding. In moving the adop- tion of the report of the council, his lordship referred to the recently enacted Agricultural Holdings Act, and said he had never thought that Act would of itself do much good, but it was valuable RS a recognition of the necessity for compensation for unexhausted improvements, a principle which had been adopted on all the large estates in Cheshire long before He also expressed a hope that the tenant far- mers of the county had now entered upon a period which should be much more favourable to them than the last seven years had been, and that a succession of good seasons might bring about a return of prosperity to the agricultural in- terest. LORD SALISRETRY AT PLYMODTR.—Speaking on Wednes- day after a luncheon at Davenport, the Marquis of Salisbury said that although Mr. Gladstone had denied the authorship of the article on foreign policy which appeared in a recent periodical, it was written by someone very near his foot- stool, and it created a very unpleasant feeling as to the future of England in the hands of the liberal party. He complained that the Government would not say what they were doing, and never did anything until threatened with a vote of censure. That policy had been most disastrous in far off Egypt, but what would it be closer home if the same thing occurred 7—ln he evening Lord Salisbury attended a great Conservative meeting in the Guildhtill, Plymouth. Sir M. Lopes, M.P., presiding. The noble Marquis said he earnestly hoped that a general election would be speedy; for, even if it did not return a majority of Con- servatives, it would certainly return a better Parlia- ment than the present. The country would not be deceived by the red herring which the Liberals drew across the path in the form of conflict with the I House ef Lords, but would judge of the Government by what it had done and left undone. The history of the Gov- ernment had been a record of failure in Ireland mad In every Part of the glebe. As Mr. Gladstapo had said the Clerken- well explocion brought on the disestablishment of the Irish Church, he (Lord Salisbury) should be gild to know what extravagant legislation was to follow the :recent explosion in London, for to be logical some legislation in Ireland ought to follow- The profession of peace which the Govern- ment made had shown the extent of their hypocrisy—not SO IDUOR of their impolicy as of imbecility. They were a double-minded Ministry, and as such could not rule. They now suggested multiple control in Egypt, which would pro- duce the same result. He repeated that under any circum- stances we must have a preponderating influence in that country. On Thursday Lord Salisbury addressed a crowded I meeting of the Conger vatives of South Devon and East and ' Weet Cornwall, at the Guildhall, Plymouth, thee bringing his visit to the west to a conclusion. He denied the charge of obstruction levelled at the Conservative party, and said that the Government were responsible for the opposition their measures had met with, alleging that their bills were not brought in to be passed, but were intended as mere e battle cries.

The Manch steer Cup was on Thursday Won by Fiorecce, Robertson being second, and Gerrie Roy third. In a letter to a Newcastle torrespondent, Mr. Gladstone says the Grevernnaent intend dealing with redistribution in Ibis Parliament. Sir Joseph Pease, Nix ,on Wednesday laid the corner stone of a new free library presented to Darlington by his late brother Edward. Mr. Rowlands, arbitrator in the South Staffordshire miners dispute, has decided in favour of a redirection of wages (rein 39 Si to 3s 41 per day, the sauce to take effect from the 14th inst. At North Shields, on Wednesday, Frederick Davis, master of the steamship Washington, of West Ilartlepool, was fined £25 and costs for neglecting to have a deck line properly affixed on the side of his veseel. At an early hour on Wednesday morning the north train for Manchester ran into a etanding goods train at Tyldesley. Several passengers were injured, but none seriously. After an hour's delay, and a fresh engine had been procured, the train proceeded to its destination ten circuitous route. FATAL Ttrin.—A. farmer named Kennedy, residing at Ballyduff, county Water! ord. WET, on Tuesday, so savagely beaten that he died almost immediately. It la believed the 1 crime wee not agrarian, but erase out of a long-established feud. Two men heve been arrested and charged with the i murder. DESt..AUCTIVE PLISES.—A ..lestrractive Ire occurred on 1 Wednesday at Messrs. Dean end Co.'s warehouse Toronto- street, Derby-road, Liverpool. Shortly before midnight on Tuesday a warehetse in Beedford-road, Batley, belonging to Mr. eter Dixon, and jointly occupied Sy various firms, was destroyed by fire. The sixty-fifth annual Conference Of The Primitive Mather- diet Coneexion was opened on Wednesday, in Jubilee Chapel, Tunstald. The following appointments were made: Rev. George Lomb, presklent; Mr. Thomas Bateman, vice-' preeident ; Rev. W. Graham, secretary; and the Bev. D. S. Prosser, assistant secretary. At the Bradford Borough Police Court, on WednnsdaY. David Smith. butcher and sausage-maker; of that town, and Dennis Whatley, farmer, of Clayton, near Bradford, were eoach fined .£2O and costs for preparing for sale the carcase te: a calf which was unfit for humaryfoed. It lerrel been intended 'to use the meet in the manufacture of sausages. A FARMER &ROT DEAD NEAR CORE.—A shocking nffelr has occurrectin the moorland a Donoughmere, near Mill- street. On teueday night a firm house was attacked, -end John Creed, the propaietor, was shot dead. TWO ethers, who were on the premises at the time, were severely wonnded. Creed, it is said, recently seined some cattle upon a farm which belonged to his sister. CLYDE Seetnummornaa—The returns of shipbailding on the Clyde during May show a serious failing off an tom- pared with the corresponding neriod of the past three years. Twenty-eight vessels, of 26)058 tons, were launched, while in May,rlBB3, the tonnage was 35,854; May, 1882,31138 ; May, /381, 37,621. On the other hand, the tonnage launched in May ten yearango was 17,106. THE SALVATION ARVE in Manchester held a "war demonetration " on Wednesday afternoon, when they marched in procession to the number of several hundreds from the barracks in Grosvenor-street to the Free Trade Hall. At the meeting which followed the procession, a number of converts related their experience. General Booth addressed a large gathering in the Free Trate Hall in the evening. RECORD BEATEN ON A TANDEM TRICYCVE —On Saturday. , M. Sinclair (Midlothian 8.C.) and D. H. Hide (Edinburgh ' University Cycling Club) succeeded in beating all records for a tricycle, doing 30 miles on the Edinburgh and Glass 1 , gow road in llar. 48min. 40sec., or an average of 3mina3Tsec. I per mile. The machine ridden was a Budge ."Coventry Rotary," tandem, &c, roadster geared to 2in. The road from Clarkstone to Batbgate, a distance of 15 miles, was Covered with loose stones and large patches of metal. There was no wind. ORANGE DEMONSTRATIONS.—The Lord-Lieutenant has caused a letter to be addressed to Lord Arthur Hill, stating that the Irish Government has reeolved not to ,ellow "counter demonstrations" by the Orangemen or other bodies to meetings to be held at the same time as and in the immediate neighbourhood of meetings to the objects .and promoters of which they are (mimed. If his Excellency sees no reason to prohibit a meeting, he will not, as a rule, , allow any counter demonstration to be held in , the -same neighbourhood on the same day. I Mn. PARNELL'S LAND SCHEME.—A Dublin correspondent telegraphed on Saturday :—Since Mr. Parnell's visit to Ire- land this week the Irish Land Purchase and Settlement Company, of which he is chairman, and which is hoped to .be a means of pacifying Irish discontent by migrating farmers in distressed districts to more productive land, has made its first purchase of land, the estate of Kilcluney, near Tuam, having been taken over by the company. The estate consists of 3,000 acres of prime land. The purchase has to be ratified by the Landed Estates Court. LIBERAL MEETING IN LIVERPOOL.—A meeting of the Liberal party of Liverpool was held on Wednesday night in Hengler's Circus to express approval of the general policy of Her Majesty's Government. Mr. R. D. Holt occupied the chair, and addresses were delivered by Mr. Samuel -Smith, M.P., Mr. J. A. Picton, and others. A resolution was passed recording the hearty approval of the Liberal party of Liverpool of the general policy of the -Govern- ' ment at home and abroad, and expressing the hope that the Franchise Bill will soon become the law of the land. 'TEE PREMlER.—Hawarden was thronged with visitore ' on Sunday and Monday. Mr. Gladstone was out thrice . on Monday, and was frequently recognised aed saluted. In the afternoon the right bon gentleman took a long drive through Sandyeroft and Queensferry, attended try a London detective. He also drove out for a short time alone. On the drive near the principal entrance to the iCastle grounds a stall had been erected, where, under the superintendence of Mrs. Gladstone, fancy articles were -sold in aid of the day schools. The explosions in St. James's-square, combined with that at 'Scotland Yard, threw the West End into a state of wild 'excitement, such as probably has not been witnessed for many a year, Immediately after the occurrence of the out- rage, thousands of pedestrians and a continuous stream of vehicular traffic began steadily to converge upon Pall Mall,, aud so great was the crush that the large bodies of police stationed et every approach had the utmost difficulty in keeping back the surging masses of an indignant populace. The consternation was universal. When, shortly after eleven o'clock, the theatres emptied, matters became worse than ever, and the efficiency and patience of the police were indeed sorely taxed. Adjoining the Junior Carlton Club stands Adair House, a spacious mansion used by the War Office for the purpose of an Intelligence Department. All the windows in this house were shattered. The only occupants were the housekeeper, Mrs. WC-inlay, and her daughter. Mr. M`Grinlay himself was standing ostside and he avers that the second explosion was caused by a bomb, which he saw lighted with a fuse a second or two before the explosion. His wife was at this ' very moment at the door taking in the letters, and she like-. ' wise beheld tate blaze of light and the dense smoke created by the explosion. The Army and Navy Club, outside of which there can be little doubt the second exelosion took place, escaped with far loss injury. Many of the massive plate-glass.windows were either broken or blown in, but be- yond that no material damage was sustained. The balance of evidence forthcoming here was that the bomb exploded 'half-way between the coffee-room, which is a most spacious xpartment, and Manchester House, used as a half-pay office by the War Office authorities. One of the morning-room waiters states that when he heard tha first explosion he rushed out of the room into the hall, and saw a vivid flash of light ,just 'outside the club. This WAS followed by a thick cloud of smoke, and a dreadful smell of gunpowder filled the premises. He asserts in the most positive man- ner that the instant after the second explosion he saw a. gang et men run past into Pall Mall. The discovery of the slabs of dynamite at the base of the Nelson Column was not the only find of unexploded matter made. In the course of the night a considerable quantlty of the deadly material was also found in Scotland Yard, lying against the stables. The first explosion caused by dynamite placed in the base- tneht compleAy demolished frames and all the large windows onefirst floor, and most of those on second floor; massive I glass and iron light let in the pavement blown up, leaoing a I gatfoft. by afe., which has been boarded over and railed off; iron staircase leading to basement damaged; eastward of the chefehouse, Nv. 27, windows of second floor smashed.; No. 28, it, course of rebuilding, scaffolding damaged; No. 28, Wllkinson'sgun manufactory, first and second floorwindows smashed f No. 29, ditto; No. 30, the limit of the explosive energy in this direction, two large windows on second floor smashed; westward of the Junior Canton Cleb, Adair House, a large corner building with bow windows, facing St: Jameessquare, basemen tbadly damaged, all the windows facing therequare demolished, and most of the side windows end conservatory smashed. 1 Second explosion caused by dynamite placed apparently on window-sill of Sir Watkin Wynn's mansion ;most of the large plate glass windows, also windows of the Army and 'Navy Clubhouse abutting on George-street and*St. James's- 'square, smashed; Sir Watkin Wynn's boase7all the windows, with the exception of those of the attic floor, smashed, many of the sashes demolished, and a hole about two and a half feet equal.° by about, four inches deep 'made in the stonework of the front, immediately below °tsp. of the win- dow ledges o,a the ground floor; Wincnester House all win- dows smashed, and a large house forming the-corner of King street many windows smashed. The -Furth( tat point reached by the concussion was the War Office in Pahl Mall, facing George-street. Here about half a dozen low e windows were broken, but otherwise the dam- age caused I tier the explosions was 'confined to the south and west sides o f St. James's-square, and in the Army and Navy Clubhouse t tnd Adair House in G eerge-street. Speaking; of the injared, a Central New,: telegram says that probal ily the most serious case of injury is that sus- tained by E'.C. William Clarke, whose special mission it was to watch lice urinal %hied Scotland Yard, in which the ex- plosive a abstance was deposited, and 'v/hen discovered amongst t he dibris he was unconscious, and was so covered with plaster, brick dust, etc., that he was scarcely recognis- able as a policeman. He was at once conveyed to West- minster 'Hospital. when it was discovered that he was suffer- ing froi n several severe scalp wounds, end contusions on various parts of the body, and slight.concussion of the brain. He remained in a complete state of collapse for SOllle tii us, and when eventually conscioesness returned it was Con eed that the explosion had produced deafness, and he was completely dazed. He was much better by mid- night, ' however, and there is little fear as to his ultimate recoye, 7. He states that he thought that he saw a man enter I he urinal shortly before the explosion, carrying a black 'bag, but he is unable at present to enter into further aietailt I, Tiv , Central News says no arrests havoleen made in con- necth no with the latest dynamite outragec, nor so far as can be ler trned by inquiries in various quarters have they even obtained anything like a definite clue, unless very shadowy descriptions of two men who were seen walking rapidly away', one from Scotland Yard and °the' other down Pall Mall, immediately after the explosion, may be so described. The suspicions entertained of the Scotland Yard stranger, how ever, have assumed more tangible form. The police, it is said, have been furnished with descriptions of the man by 1 two. persons, one of whom saw him enter the urinal with a I parcel of some kind itt his hand, and leave it very quickly I emoty-handed. 1 As regards the plot itself, the official theory now is that however many scoundrels were engaged in its inception, its , execution was carried out by not more than two men, one of whom placed the explosives at the -base of the Nelson column and afterwards at Scotland Yard, whilst the other simultaneously deposited the infernal machines in the areas 1 of the Junior Carlton Club and Sir Watkin Wynn's man- sion. The work was undoubtedly established by the evi- dence of scores of witnesses, that the explosion occurred to all intents and purposes simulteneouely between a quarter- past and twenty minutes past nine. IFortunately the fuse attached to the ,dynamite placed , against the Nelson column missed fire owing to some fault I• in its construction, but experts who have ereamined the ex- plosive, and know the strength and solidity of the great memorial, doubt whether it would have suffered much. 1 They confidently assert it certainly would not have collapsed, 1 but it is very probable that splinters and 'fragments of the I massive pedestal would have been scattered about the square, wounding and even killing many who might have been un- fortunate enough to be within range. By the exploeions in St. James's-square two men, servants of Sir Watkin Wynn, were severely hurt. Cue, whose name is William Hall, is a footman; the otberie the valet. Both ef them heard the report of the first explogiou, and came to the door of Sir Watkites house, which is atNo. 18, St. James's-square. They had no sooner done so than the second explosion occurred, injuring them both. They were removed to their own rooms, the doctor finding that there was no necessity to send them to the hospital, as • they were 'suffering only from severe shock. . It is stated that £5,000 will be offered by the Goverment for evidence that will lead to the arrest and conviction of the persons who were engaged in the explosions in St. James's Square and Scotland Yard. The police are making every effort to capture the criminals, and bare some evi- dence to go on, but it would tend to defeat the made of jus- tice to divulge it at present.
