ST. TIELENS. LIBERAL DEnuNSTRATION.
ADDRESSES HT MR. WILLIAMSON, M.P., MR. BRIGGS, M.P., AND OTHERS. _ .

rho annual demonstration in connection with the St. Helens Liberal Association was held on Tuesday evening, when a large and enthusiastic gathering was held in the Town Hall. In the absence of the president (Col. Gamble), the chair was occupied by Mr. Richard Pilkington, J.P.; and he was nupported by Mr. W. E. Briggs, M.P. for Black- burn; Mr. S. Williamson, M.P. for the St. Andrew's Boreughs,Scotland ; Alderman I'. Cook; Councillors R. G. Brook, Dr. McNicoll, Hanson, and Lacey; Dr. Jamieson, Dr. Ricketts; Messrs. A. Sinclair, J.P., J. C. Gamble, J.P., W. Gamble, H. Martin, W. S. Hadley, H. B. Shores, and other gentlemen. The CHAIRMAN, who was warmly received, remarked that his first duty was to tell them that their president, Col. Gamble, was unable to preside over that meeting. He thought if his health had been a little better he would have been unquestionably in his position as president of that Liberal Association. (Applause.) Besides that he had letters from Mr. Hall and Mr. Leach expressing their in- ability to attend. He went on to say that they owed their thanks to the two members of Parliament who had spared Home little time out of their Whitsuntide holiday to come amongst them. (Applause.) They were two excellent Liberals, faithful supporters of Mr. Gladstone's Government —(renewed applause)—and they knew very well that the Government was now being attacked on all sides by an un- scrupulous Opposition. They knew every attempt was being made to stop the passage of the Franchise Bill through Parliament, and to discredit the Government in foreign affairs; therefore it was a good time for them to rally to their duty as Liberals, and to take that opportunity of giving their assistance to the great cause that was now being fought out so well at Westminster. (Applause.) He alluded to the obstructive debates which had been raised, and Mr. Gladstone in a magnificent speech had protested against the waste of time. The Prime Minister sat with patience, firmness, and courtesy, and answered question after question, and they were again pat to him as If he had never given those answers—the same stupid ques- tions were put and the time of the country was frittered away in the most disgraceful and abominable manner. (Ap- plause.) The country was aroszKl at the patience and the firmness and the courtesy of the great statesman who sits and leads the Government in the House of Commons—(ap- plause)—and the people would at the proper time treat in the proper manner the men whom in that unscrupulous manner had wasted the time of the country. That time had not yet come, but when it did come there would be a day of reckoning for the men who had wasted the great powers of the great man, as well as wasted the time of other members of the House of Commons. (Hear, hear.) That night was their opportunity of doing what they could to help the Government, and be hoped they would send such a message as would show Mr. Gladstone that the Liberals of St. Helens at any rate were perfectly certain that his wise end just policy at borne, which was freedom. to all, and that his honest and right policy abroad, which was justice and honesty to the ottrcr nations—(bear, hear,)—was the only policy which was consistent with the welfare and with the honour of England. (Loud cheerc.) Dr. JAMIESON was then called upon to move tho following resolution :—" That this meeting expresses its 'entire confi- dence in the domestic and foreign policy of the Govern- ment,and protests in the strongest possible terms against the factions acd unscrupulous conduct of a minority in Parlia- ment, the evident object of which is to obstruct the business of :domestic legislation, and earnestly calla upon Mr. Gladstone teed Her Majesty's Government to persist in pressing forward the great measures they lieve introduced into Parliament." He said the resolution appeared to be framed in every strong language, but he thought it was framed scarcely strong enough—(Lear, hear)—because the obstruction of the Opposition had been carried on to such an extent. He was glad that the Liberal party of St. Helens had an opportunity of registering their protest against that opposition, and their approbation of Mr. Glad- stone's work. (Applause.) Notwithstanding Lord Ran- dolph Churchill's recent designation of the Liberal party, he (Dr. ;Jamieson) was still inclined to defend that party.,' as one which without any secret treaties or I:tick-handed in- fluences., tried to maintain the vigour of the empire with the greatest amount of justice and freedom to each individual member, In working out that high aim it had gone in for mime very great measures of domestic policy at home and just designs hbroad. There was still a great deal to be done in the future to make towns more pure and more healthy, to give the people better homes, and to enable those people to livetbetter lives in purer atmospheres, and be better edu- cated. Then there was looming in the distance reforms in relation to the Lend Laws, and reforms in relation to the Establiched Church, which needed its feudal shell throwing off, and required its fall expanse of freedom. Who were to do that? The pupils of the Liberal party—(applause)— and he asked them to give the resolution their heartiest sup- port. (Loud applause.) Mraj. C. GAMBLE, J.P., in seconding the resolution, said he thought they would all agree with both parts of it, the one approving of the policy of Mr. Gladstone's Govern- menteeoth at home and abroad, and the second part pro- testing against the obstruction which had been carried on by their opponents in the House of Commons. (Applause.) It seemed to him, and he thought they all must see it, that the obstruction was simply carried on with the object of preventing the Gladstone Government doing anything at all, not because they objected to the measures which were brought in, but because they objected to the present Go- vernment doing anything—they wanted to prevent them doing anything. They wanted to get them turned out of office by the country and then get in themselves. There was no doubt that they wanted tc turn the Government out upon the Franchise Bill, and then bring one in them- selves and get the credit of passing it. me had the greatest pleasure in seconding the resolution. (Loud ap- plause.) Mr. e. Wetammeme, M.P., who was warmly cheered, sup- ported the resolution, and in doing -so remarked that the Opposition in the House of Commons were opposing at all costs and hazards everything proposed by the Liberal Go- vernment, and doing this in a very factious and unscrupu- lous moaner. (Applause.) Last winter there was a little want et backbone in the Tory party, and Lord Randolph Churchill gave some sort of backbone to it. The noble lord, speaking at Edinburgh, scouted the Franchise Bill, and told the people of Scotland that the agricultural labourers were not fitted for the franchise, and that he would be the last man to yield one inch in his opposition to its extension to Ireland. What had come over Lord Randolph Churchill lately ? (Laughter.) lie put backbone into the Tory party and had taken it out again, for he had spoken and voted in favour of the extension of the franchise to Ireland, and the party were now as flabby as ever they were in all important matters of domestic legislation, and had to take refuge ie the Soudan. (Loud applause.) Lord Randolph Churchill had turned his cursing of the Govern- ment into blessing. He had become a candidate for the representation of Birmingham, and bad to play his cards with a good deal of delicacy, and he did so with an amount' of effrontery that few men possessed, and dragged a large number of Tories at his heels. The Franchise Bill was a *measure of justice and equity, and in St. Helena. of I all places in this part of the country, the inhabitants must be in favour of it, because it would raise the electorate of the town from 2,000 to 10,000. (Hear, hear.) The Tories opposed the measure because, as they said, they wanted to see the effects of it. He could tell them what the effects of the bill would he. It would be the means of clearing out Tories from many districts in the country. (Applause.) Then the Tories also said, " We want to see a redistribution scheme." Mr. Gladstone had very wisely not encumbered the bill with a redistribution scheme, as this would have I imported into the subject other considerations than that of justice. The legislation in regard to Ireland carried out by the present Government had been so successful that a feel- ing of satisfaction, security, peace, and contentment pre- vailed where the people were four years ago actually on the • verge of civil war. (Applause.) The bill recently intro- duced by Mr. Trevelyan, which would afford an opportunity -for tenants to become proprietors of the land they tilled, was in his opinion a most masterly and statesmanlike bill, and he hoped when it was carried a new era would dawn upon ,Ireland, and great pence, contentment, and prosperity be found where there had been nothing but trouble in time past. (Hear, hear.) He did not want to say anything dis- pleasing to Irishmen, but thought they must come to the 'conclusion that the Government had done a great deal for their country, and rest satisfied that the efforts made by Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues on behalf of Ireland had been successful. After comparing Liberal and Tory finance, contending that the Opposition were notoriously bad financiers, the speaker remarked that the Soudan had been a perfect godsend to the Tories. There had been an outcry in the country regarding the policy in the Soudan—not on the part of sensible Liberals, but on the part of London Jiagoes, and there never was a more shameful outcry. Neither was there a more shameful vote of eensure than that proposed by Sir Michael Hicks Beach, and he did not think it would have received the support of a dozen votes in any reasonable assembly of Englishmen outside the House of Commons. (Applause.) With regard to the future policy of the Government towards Egypt. be might say that they went there with the sanction of other Powers at first, followed by their approval of moral support, afterwards for beneficient purposes towards the Egyptian people and to guard the Suez Canal. There were a number of responsible statesmen who wished to annex Egypt. (A voice: Hear, hear.) He for one would never be a party to that. (Hear, hear.) England had given solemn professions and obligations to other Powers as to her inten- tions in Egypt, and he hoped the nation would not draw back from those obligations. (Applause.) He believed that if the conduct of the foreign policy of the country were left in the hands of Mr. Gladstone and his Govern- ment, they would by wise measures and acts so maintain the goodwill of other Powers that they would yet be able to carry out the benefieient purposes for which they went to Egypt and then retire. (Applause.) That was, he be- lieved, the bounden obligation of the country, and annexa- tion should not be undertaken in the face of this. Mr. Williamson concluded by stating that he was in favour of the proposed Conference of the Powers concerning Egypti in finance. (Cheers.) Mr. W. E. limos, M.P., also supported the retiolatien. Ile complained that the Tories made a redistribution bill se a etaiking horse to cover their designs. The question of proportional representation and women's suffrage had been introduced into the subject, but all these things should net be attempted at once. If the Franchise Bill were passed first then they would have a lever with which they could shift MOLIBIEjE4. (Applause.) The Tories, however, were beginning to find out that the franchise was going to be conferred upon the people seed they bad given up—at any rate in the Rowe

(of Commons—the last stronghold which they were main- taining against all comers, that this great boon ought not to be extended to Ireland. (Hear, hear.) If there should be grievances to he redressed, and even should veiled re- bellion exist in Ireland, it was better that the former should be redressed in the House of Commons and the latter should be brought to light where it could be discussed—on the floor of the House of Commons—than elsewhere. If Mr. Par- nell and his friends were to go back to the house twenty times stronger than at present, it was better this should be so than that a sense of injustice which the exclusion of the Irish people from this bill would occasion should rankle in their minds until it resulted in something worse. For his own part, be believed that in their hearts—and indeed they had shown it a little on one memorable occasion—those who traded upon the disaffection and discontent of thee Irish people, those to whom great tributes of money were made , and who sought the aid of foreign nations to keep Ireland in a state of ferment, would be sorry when the franchise : was given to the Irish people. (Loud applause.) It was l I plainly to be seen that the present constituencies were easy . to manage and manipulate. As against the farmers, who ' I had got pretty nearly all they wanted in Ireland, there 1 I was the great mess of labourers in that country whose 1 1 grievances would, after the franchise bad been conferred, have to be brought forward, and when these had been reme- died where would be the powers of the agitators? (Loud applause.) The Braelish nation would then show the Irish people that they were not, and never had been, actuated by motives of hostility and enmity to them. (Hear, hear.) They had much to atone for in the past, but of late had done their best to remedy this, and notwithstanding the in- sults and obstruction of their enemies, they were in the mind which would enable them to look On the Irish grievances dispassionately, and to do that justice, perhaps somewhat tardily, which if it had been shown some twenty- five years ago would have robbed the Irish question of all the bitterness that had caused so much mischief. (Cheers f In referring to the rumoured course of action to be taken by the House of Lords upon the Franchise Bill, Mr. Briggs said that he thought the bench of bishop might be better occupied in looking after all the sin, misery, and wicked- ness which existed in the land rather than be giving rise to sin and wickedness by voting against a measure like the Marriage with a Deceased Wife's Sister Bill. (Loud cheers.) Dr. Mcncott, in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. 'Williamson and Sir. Briggs for their interesting arid eloquent addresses, said that they had by statement, by facts, by history, by narrative, and by argument, in a clear, convincing, and straightferward way vindicated the Govern- ment of the country, and had repelled the false accusations which had been brought against them. (Applause.) They had showed that the good ship of the State was never in better hands, from the commodore downwards to the lowest midslaipman,than she was at the present time, and they ought to have received better treatment at the hands of the Opposi- tion. (ear, hear.) They had harrassed the Government, whereas they ought to have known that the cares and the fortunes of the country were in her hands, and they had har- reseed her as if she was an enemy rather than carrying the welfare and good of this country. (Applause.) Mr. A. SINCLAIR, J.P., heartily seconded the motion, which was unanimously passed with loud cheers. . _ . . .

Mr. War.matsorr,Ps., briefly responded, and concluded by moving a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was seconded by Mr. BRIGGS, M.P., and carried with enthusiasm. —The `CHAIIIILLN acknowledged the compliment, and de- clared the meeting at an end.—Thereupon a young man rose in the body of the hall, and calling out, " silence " went on to say that before the meeting concluded be wished to address a few remarks to the audience. Owing tolhe people having commenced to leave the room some dieorder ensued, amid which cries of" order" and "silence " were raised, and there were one or two shouts of "Goon the plctfortn." The Chairman ultimately said: I think I had better say at once that this meeting is now practically over, and the proceedings are really at an end. I cannot possibly ,prolong the meeting any further. (Applause.)—The Cpeaker : I say with all due respect to our chairman.—Mr. Pilkington : Will you please send in your name.—The Speaker: William Woken, and I think I have sent you a copy of the resonation I wish to move.—Mr. Pilkington :Is it any question you wish to ask?-111r. Wogan : No,! wish to move, a resolution.—After some further discussion, he said be wished to move a resolution expressive of disap- proval of the exclusion of Mr. Bradlaugh from the House of Commons, but he was informed that the meeting had been concluded, and it was too late.—The proceedings then concluded.

div.head: WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES.
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES.

On Whit Monday St. Helens presented a very holiday appearance , and notwithstanding the dull and threatening atmospherical surroundings pleasure-seekers generally en- joyed themselves throughout the day. From an early hour in the morning thousands of persons were observed making their way to the railway station, where they booked to the various places of interest in the country. The chief points of attraction appeared to be Windermere (to which sow. a trip was ran in connection with St. Thhmas's Sanday , School), the Belle Vue Gardens, Manchester, Southport, Blackpool, and Liverpool. About 300 persons accompanied the first-named excursion, about a thousand journeyed to Manchester, and large numbers also booked to the other places mentioned. Notwithstanding the fact that all the offices, shops, and business premises were closed for the day, the town presented an animated appearance, the streets being well-thronged with gaily dressed pedestrians until a 'late hour. There were numerous attractions in the after- noon, an account of which is given below. BAND DF HOPE UNION DEIIONSTRATION.—The four- teenth annual demonstration iie connection with the St. Helens Band of Hope Union was held early in the after- noon, and the arrangements were carried out in a Yery successful manner. Twenty branches of the Union took part in the proceedings. which were held under the patron- age of his worship the Mayor (Mr. H. Baxter, J.P.) The members of the various societies assembled at their respective schoolrooms, and after being formed in proces- sional order were marched to the front of the Town Hail, where an imposing gathering was held. Under the direc- tions of officers of the Union, the children were marshalled in stated post6ons, and from the Town Hall steps they pre- sented a very attractive appearance. There were nearly 3,000 well dressed children in attendance, while some thousands of persons gathered to witness the interesting proceedings. The hymn "Rescue the perishing" was sung by the assemblage, Mr. W. D. Stoba (treasurer of the Union) ably conducting,; the arrangements being carried out by Mr. J. B. Leach (president), Mr. W. Owen, and ' Mr. W. H. Leach (hon. secs.), assisted by a band of will- ing workers. Shortly afterwards the Mayor and Mayoress (Mr. and Mrs. Baxter) made their appearance from the Town Hall, and were very warmly received. Among the la4ies and gentlemen then present on the steps of the Town Hall were Miss Baxter, Alderman J. Cook, Mrs. Cook. Councillors Dr. McNicoll and Foster, Revs. R. J. Ward (Congregational), J. M. Wamsley (Wes. !even), and W. C: Taylor (Baptist), Messrs. Leach, Stoba, H. S. Gibson. Smith, Edmondson (Prescot). Westworth, Superintendent Johnson, Jsc. A ballot was made among a number of girls as to whom should have the honour of pre- senting a handsome basket of flowers to the Mayoress, and the task fell upon Miss Lucy Ann Wynn, or the Parr Primitive Methodist branch. After this pleasing ceremony had been performed. Mrs. Baxter pinned the flower she wore upon the breast of Miss Wynn, after which Mr. J. B. Leach (addressing the :Mayor) said the object of the Union was to train our young people of the town into habits of sobriety, cleanliness, temperance, and thrift. They had 5,000 members, who were very largely represented that day, but some were absent through sickness, and some from one cause or another. He hoped they would all be better for their meeting that day. (Cheers).—His Worship the Mayor, on coming forward to reply, was heartily applauded, He said he was quite sure since be had been the Mayor of St. Helens be had witnessed no such pleasing sight as that. He was sure it reflected great credit upon Mr. Leach and all bis co-workers in the good cause. He had mentioned one or two virtues to which they trained the children up, but he omitted to mention truthfulness, and be thought truthful- ness was a very great virtue. The next which he thought was a great point was cleanliness, personal habits of cleanli- ness. He believed they would lessen the work of the Cor- poration immensely in bringing people to proper notpns of cleanliness. They say virtue has its cwn reward, knd he was quite sure they would have their reward for what they were doing. (Cheers.)—The hymn, "Sound the battle cry," was then sung, after which three cheers for the Mayor and Mayoress were heartily given. A monstre procession , was then formed, and proceeded along the principal streets lof the town. Taking part in the procession were the follow- ing Bands of Hope in the.order indicated :—Baptist, headed by the St. Peter's (Parr) Brass Band; Bickerstaffs-street; Congregational (Brook-street), headed by the Ravenshoad Sunday School Brass Band; Ashton Congregational ; Gerard's Bridge Congregational; Peasley Cross Congrega- tional; Huyton, headed by the Fife Band of the Albert Institute (Liverpool) ; Presbyterian branch; Primitive Methodist (Kirkland-street); Park-road Primitive Metho- dist ; Parr Socks Primitive Methodist- Haydock Primitive Methodist Ragged School; United Methodist Free Church; Marshall's oross United Methodist; Haydock Wesleyan Methodist; Park-road Wesleyan Methodist; Prescot Wes- leyan -Methodist; Sutton-road Wesleyan Methodist; and Waterloo-street Wesleyan ;Tethodist.- On arriving in Denton's Green-lane a large field was entered, and here sports and amusements were held. Prizes were offered in various contests for speaking, reciting, &c , and at intervals fancy balloons were sent on aerial voyages. Refreshments were also supplied to the children in the course of the afternoon. The results of the different contests were as follows :—Best turn-out of horses and carts ;1, Thomas Foster, driver, Charles Mather ;„2, Joseph Williams, driver John Tooth; 3, the Mayor, driver John • Gallagher. A special prize was given to the Union Plato Glass Company, driver John Leatherbridge, and to the Corporation for water-cart. Fife Band contest, Albert Institute, St. Helens. Brass Band contest, Ravenhead Church Sunday School. Speaking contest; 1, John Norton, Hoyt-n; 2, W. C. Duncan, U.M.F. Church, St. Helens, who also took the first prize in the junior class for reciting; Edward Hunt, Brook-street School, taking second, and P. Dickenson, Htlyton. third. Reciting, senior class. 1, s. C. Duncan, U.M.F.C.; 2, Miss E. A. Lin- don, U.M.F.C. So'. Elsr..mrs Pearsu CHURCH SCROOLs. The annual procession and field day in connection with the Pary.,, Church Sunday Schools, was held on Whit-Monday aft. - noon, and were of a very enjoyable character. The schole., assembled at the schools and to the number of 600 formed in processional order by to .olicers and teachers of the schools. In the ranks were numerous flagt and. banner,. Headed by the brass band from the Rev. T. Major-Lestel's Industrial school, Liverpool, the scholars marched along ti- wards Duke-street where they were joined 14 over 500

•1 scholars connected with the York-street Mission, and sub- t sequently about 120 scholars from Moss Bank school. sat) I further increased the number taking part in the demonstra- • Lion. The jMnt procession afterwards marched to a field sc Denton's Green-lane, belonging to Mrs. Littler, where the usual sports were indulged in. The juvenile scholars were regaled with buns,lmilk, lemonade, &c., while the adult per- sons were kindly provided with an excellent tea by the Rev. Canon Carr. It is estimated that about 2,500 persons were present on the field, and everyone appeared to thoroughly enjoy themselves. , . • COSIGREGATIONAL SawnLs.—A pleesing ceremony took place in the Congregational School, St. Helens, on Monday afternoon. By previous arrangement the membeirs of the Band of Hope gathered at the school before taking part in , the United Band of Ilene demonstration which was subse- quently held. Mrs. Ward (wife of the Rev. R. J. Ward) welcomed the members as they made their appearance. and subsequently that lady was presented with a handsome bouquet of flowers. The presentation was made by Miss Edith Wilson on behalf of the members of the Society. The Rev. R. J. Ward acknowledged the gift in anpropriate terms, after which a procession was formed and marched to the front of the Town Hall to take their part in the demon- stration. _

WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE GATHERING AT Nums.osig. —A very enjoyable gathering was held at Nntgrove in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Sunday School Band of Hope. Early in the afternoon a procession of the members and frioads was held, and over 375 persons marched through the village, beaded by an excellent brass band. In a field near the chapel innocent sports and pas- times were indulged in until dusk; refreshments having been provided for those present during the afternoon.

RAILWAY ACCIDENTS. On the arrivit of a trait, at the Westminster Station of the District Railway, on S iturday, a porter on the platform noticed a gentleman suddenly fall between a carriage and the platform while the train was in motion. The train was stopped, and the nnfortunate person conveyed to Westmin- ster Hospital. Here be was seen by the house surgeon, but was so shockingly injured that little hope could be enter- tained of his recovery. One of his arms was so badly crushed that it had to be amputated. His name is H. E. Evans, and he resides in Thicket-road, Norwood.__

Mrs. Jackson, wife of Mr. Wm. Jackson, of Roe Green, was crossing the line at Worsley Station, on Friday evening, on her return from Manchester, when her heel caught the metals and shb was tripped on to the line. Before she contd. recover herself an express came up and killed her on the spot, her head being severed from the body. A fatal accident occurred on the Crystal Palace line of railway, between Honor Oak and the Nunhead Junction, on Monday. At the point in question there is a steep bank, where several boys had trespassed and got on to the line ; and an empty train was on its way from Sydenhain to Ho', born Viaduct. The poor little fellow who fell a victim WaB named William Fox, aged eight years, residing at Camber- well. The deceased stumbled and fell in his endeavour to ' avoid the approaching train, which passed over him, almorit severing his legs and dreadfully injuring his head. Lite was extinct before the unfortunate boy reached St. Bar- tholomew's Hospital. RAILWAY COLLISION AT BLACKBURN.

A collision, happily unattended by serious consequences,. occurred in the long tunnel on the Clitheroe side of the Blackburn Railway Station on Tuesday morning. Through a misunderstanding between the signalmen the passenger train from Gisburne to Manchester, due at Blackburn at 10-55 a.m., was sent into the tunnel while the fast goons train from HelWield to Miles Platting was standing in it. Fortunately the signals were at danger, so that the passenger train was proceeding slowly when it ran into the rear of the goods train, or the result might have been very disastrous. The guard's van and a waggon were thrown from the metals and a number of carboys of petroleum were broken, rendering it necessary to work the traffic on a single. line for a couple of hours afterwards. The engine of the passenger train was slightly damaged. Five persons were somewhat injured. The worst case was that of Mrs. Sarah Barton; an elderly resident of Copster Green, who was badly cut on the head, and also shaken. Three ocher females and one male were slightly cut and shaken, but all were able to return home by special train immediately after the accident, after havingtbeir wounds dressed by Dr.Musson, of Clitterov, who was a passenger by the train which collided. The train concerned was delayed half an hour., but the other traffic was very little affected. ACCIDENT NEAR SALISBURY.—FIVE PERSONS

div.head: KILLED.
div.p: KILLED.

A chocking railway accident occurred about five o'clock on Tuesday afternoon, about eight miles from Salisbury, where it occasioned the utmost alarm and consternation, the !leather of killed being five, while about twenty persons are injured. The catastrophe betel the train leaving the Salisbury and Dorset line at 4-33, and occurred en the bridge between Downton and Braempre. The train was the ordin- ary passenger train, and was moderately filled, but tla-re was no pressure. It was drawn by two engines, the first one being what is known as a pilot, and just as the train was proceeding at the usual careful pace over the well-known bridge it was in part precipitated over the embankment and into the river Avon. The utmost alarm and con- sternation. as may well be imagined, was created, but many of the passengers exhibited the greatest calmness and pre- sence of mind and escaped. Amongst these was Mr. Hillier, bookseller, of Salisbury, and Miss Kate Fawcett, daughter of Mr. W. Fawcett, of Church Fields, Salisbury, both of whom sustained a severe shaking and slight injuries and returned by the next train to this city. On the occurrence of the sad disaster there was a scene of wildest confusion. In- formation by telegraph was immediately sent to Salisbury and Wimborne, and a special was soon despatched with Mr. S. N. Davis, the superintendent of the London and South- Western line in the Salisbury district. lie took with him three doctors, Mr. Gowen, Mr. Wilkes, and Mr. C. W. Costes, of this city, and on the arrival of the special on the scene of the catastrophe every effort was at once made to rescue the passengers. Assistance had already been at hand, the news of the occurrence having reached the College of Agriculture at Charcord, of which Professor Wrightson is the head. To this establishment many of the injured were conveyed, while others were brought by the next train to Salisbury, and carried te the Infirmary. At Salisbury station there was a crowd of about four or five hundred persons, many of them inquiring as to whether their rela- tives or friends who had gone by the unfortunate train were amongst the injured or killed. The throng increased up to eight o'clock, when a train from Downton was due and many persons went by the last up train to Braemore, whilst others drove over by road. At eight o'clock Mr. Goering, one of the medical gentlemen, had returned to Salisbury, so that all the medical aid possible had been rendered at the scene of the catastrophe. Up to eleven o'clock the greatest excitement prevailed in the city, anxious inquirers being assembled outside the railway station and the Infirmary to glean the latest particulars of the sad event. A Salisbury correspondent says the cause of the railway accident at Downton is as yet unexplained. The state- ment that the axle of one of the engines broke is not correct, and both engines remained standing on the no ,tal.r, mt. Davies, the district superintendent, and Mr. Verrinder, the traffic agent of the South-Western line, on Wednesday morning visited the scene of the catastrophe, and have been engaged in directing the operations of about a hundred men who were engaged in clearing the line. General Custance's daughter was not among the dead, as first reported, but this does not raduce the fatal total, as Mrs. Lush, of Gods- hill, was another victim. It is impossible to give a full list of those injured, as many went to their homes unat- tended; but the station authorities have furnished the following ;Het r—Dead—Mrs. Lush, Godshill, Fording- bridge ; Mr. G. Csrbin, Ringwood; Miss Chandler, Fordingbridge ; and Mr. Waters, Soyd Farm, Fording. bridge. The injured, who were lying at the College of Agriculture, Downton, have gone to their homes. Among those admitted to Salisbury Infirmary are Rabert C. Allen, The Parade, Poole, who is injured in the head and chest, and Matthew Dent, 2, Chalfont Villas, Bournemouth, who is seriously hurt, and his condition gives some cause for anxiety. With this exception, the injured are progress- ing satisfactorily, though in more than one place somewhat slowly. Traffic was resumed on Wednesday morning at the scene of the accident, and the wrecked carriages are being raised from the river.

A telegram from Salisbury states that Mr. Dent, of Bour- nemouth, died in the infirmary on Wednesday Ldternoon, thus making the fifth fatal case. The other Cases are reported to be progressing favourably. The inquest on four of the persons killed by the accident was opened at the Agricultural College, noon, by Mr. Hannen, of Fordingbridge. The coronerWednesday airntetr; dmeantoees to admitat he only t 12e bodies that day Pr° °s ei e being a inttaekirrendg. susffiirc.leMn.t va attended for the railway company. The bodies having been identified, the coroner gave an order for interment, and the inquest was adj.urned till Friday. Tah rey message has been received at Salisbury 14.. firm directors:—" Mr. Wynd- ham Porta l and Colonel Camphlll fofrlolomwintgwo South-western desire those in the Infirmary should 'oct informed that the Queen has telegraphed from ilalmoral expressing anxiety to know how the poor sufferers aro progressing. A telegram has been sent in reply." COLLISION WITH A MANCHESTER TRAA'N. The north train for Manchester came into cellision at Tyldesley at four o'clock on Wednesday morning with a luggage train. Several passengers were slightly injured. The engine of the passenger train was disabled, and the guard's van of the goods train and several wagons were damaged. One line was blocked until ten in the Iyenoon. The plssenger train was delayed an hour and sent on round by Kenyon Junction and the old Liverpool and Manchester line. Among the injured, who were attended to by Dr. Duncan, were the following: Edward Platt, Leogeig" Manchester, cut bead; John Willams. Thistle-stree• • Levenshulme,‘ -Mane heater, shook; Nils. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JUNE 7, 1884.

Dr. GortNALL's annual report as Medical Officer of Health for the borouvh of Warring- ton, received, as it deserved to do, consider- able attention from the members of the Town Council, at their monthly meeting on Tues- day. It is an able and exhaustive document, and we commend it to the attention of our readers. Speaking of the condition of the borough as a whole, it must be said that the health of the town is fairly good; the death rate is somewhat less than the average of the kingdom, and the birth rate is so much higher as to suggest that the Malthusian philosophy has not many supporters• in this part of the country. Councillor MAcKIZ called special attention to the heavy death rate amongst children under five years of age, and considerable discussion ensued as to the principal causes of so calamitous a state of things. It is notorious that there is greater mortality amongst the offspring of the poor, although there is reason to believe that they are at birth stron7er than the children of the rich. It is suggested that the intemperance and immorality of the parents— particu- larly mothers has much to do with the mortality of ckldren, and there iS no denying that both these causes operate in some degree in this direction, 13ut the great mass of the mothers of, our working-class population are neither interperate nor immoral, and we must be careful therefore not to draw wide conclusions front narrow premises, or slander the many for the shortcomings of the few. It is contended als° that a certain class of parents, by over insuring the lives of their little ones, have a greater interest in their dying than in their living. But these cases apply only to the very worst class—the vagabonds of society--; for the rule is that the maternal and paterna' feeling is a powerful factor even amongst the poorest. The merchant who over-in3nres his ship has, maybe, no regard beyond that which is prompted by common humanity ; the sailors whose lives are at stake; but it 1 somewhat different with the mother who ifl sures her child, for, as the proverb has "blood is thicker than water." We are dis" posed therefore to conclude that neither jut; temperance, nor over-insurence, nor b°,t: combined are sufficient to account for tile high death rate amongst the children of tile poor, not merely in Warrington but in everY large manufacturing town in the king&4l" It is the result rather of the struggle for eX; istence under -destructive conditions which the ever-burdened toiler has but litt'7. control. Take the first year of existence two children—one born of rich, the other VA ,rOO. poor parents. In the one case, pure atf,b • food, uniform warmth, and skilful nursku,b_ are always at command; in the other, as ` r.sif in most cases, it is exactly the reverse. it 1 ..1. k. stock saying that—" It is one body's wori„u_ mind a child ; " but what when the jaded fed mother has to mind three or four,P e'e.! wash, cook, and, as best she can, to It, ,ft the house tidy? Can we wonder* s o'l tri, the little ones under such circumstance !lc; get all the attention they shoul °del d have' an: that they sicken and die? What in

conditions can do in the way of preserving life is shown by the fact that of the patients taken to the hospital only 13 in the roo will succumb as against 42 who, when attacked witlt infectious disease, are nursed at home It is pretty much the same with children; they are about as susceptible in their earliest Years as invalids, and they perish because the conditions preservative of life are not at the command of their unfortunate parents. But What is to be done, it may be asked, and the answer is —improve the circumstances—the social status of the masses, and just in pro- portion as that improvement is great or small Will be the reduction in infant and other mortality. Town Councils can do something towards this end, but they cannot do all. They can do what Dr. GORNALL so strongly urges—they can resort to "frequent flushing, and better ventilation" as a means of getting rid of the poisonous emanations from the sewers." Councillor MACKIE says some of the sewers are "neither more nor less than stagnant ditches," and Councillor PLATT makes the equally startling statement that there are "some streets of the town that are really dangerous to pass through; they are overcrowdbed, and many children play about the sewer grids." This is 'Rain-speaking, and, assuming that the statements are ac- curate, not a moment should be lost before setting about to provide a remedy for such a deplorable state of things. The Corporation cannot very well deal with the intemperance or immorality of the people, but it can and should do something towards saving them from "the poisonous emanations of the , sewers.''

The yolice did not wish to persecute Mr. Jackson or anybody eiee, but in Justice to other publicans they wished Wilsou'etio, el both) be the resort of people coming from Widnes on a zeileday after- noon—Mr. Fletcher simply remarked that the two barmen ought to have known that they were committing air offence :against the law in misleading a publican in the way they had done.—Mr. Rigby said the defendants knew perfectly well that to gratify their own appetites they were about to place the keeper of this hotel in a very precarious position, end the Bench agreed with the inspector that it was-abso- Intelv necessary that a stop should be put t 6 this Practice of persons from Widnes misrepresenting facts in order to drink in Runcorn, and jeopardising men who were striving and desirous of obtaining an honourable livelihood. For having been fetand on licensed premises, Gray, Caldwell, and Russell were each fined 5s and costs 10s al, or seven days' im- prisonment. Owen, Lennan, and Albert Cotton, the barman, were eached fined lOs and costs lOs 61 for the same offence, Mr. Rigby observing that it was impessible to believe that they did not know they were infringing the law. For giv ingrfalee addresses, Gray, Caldwell, and Russell were each fined 203 and coats lOs 6d; and Lerman and Cotton Ws and costs. For falsely representing; themselves to be travellers, Gray, Caldwell, and Russell were each fined 103 and costs ; I i and Lrennan and Cotton each £1 and costs lOs 6i. I
THE TERRIBLE ASSAULT BY A CAPTAIN AT RUNCORN : DEPOSITIONS OF THE INSURED MAN TAKEN.

Dr. Bagnali having expressed the opinion that William 1 Stringer, the man who was seriously injured by a ship's ! captain named Michael Murphy, was not likely to recover, 1 the depositions of the injured man were taken at his house, 29, Peed:and-street, on Thursday morning, before Mr. W. Bankex. He deposed :—I am a dock labourer and am 57 years of age. I remember Saturday the 17th of May lat. I left the place where I work about half-past two in the afternoon. On my way home I called at Joeeph Braalborn's, the Darwell Vaults beerhouse, to get a pint of ale. I got the ale and drank it in the tap room Ani sat at the first table on the left side of the room. James Kirkham sat on the same form with me and William Hardy and a man whom ! they said was Thomas Howard. Mr. Bradburn was also in fthe same room. The prisoner was there also. When I had finished my beer I ot up to go home. I got my can from the form and was about to leave. The prisoner got hold of me and I cannot say whether he put his bead or his foot into my belly and threw me over his head. It was done so quickly that I could not tell what way exactly he did it. I belteve that he took hold of my arms the first. As soon as I fell on the floor I was gasping fora long time, five minutes or more. I couldn't tell the time exactly. I tried to speak but it was some time before I could do so. When I could do so lacked them to send for my son Joe to tase me home, I was,so badly hurt. I fell on to my back, and my head came in contact with the settle or something. When the prisoner got hold of me he stood in front of Md. I couldn't say thae the !nen had any ill-feeling towards me. When I first went in the prisoner was there, bet there was a Man, James Kirkham, sat between me and the prisoner. They were talking together, but I had no conversation with the prisoner. I don't remember having seen the prisoner before that day. He did not say anything when lib got held of me. Gross-examined by Mr. Edmondson, solicitor, of Fleetwood, who appeared for the prisoner. Witness said : I had two pints of beer at the place. I had not any beer with the prisoner. I didn't hear any conversation about wrestling. I have wrestled in ray time when I was young. I cannot say that there was any ill-feeling at all. I didn't owe him anv grudge and I cannot say what he had in his heart. There was no cross words, amongst any one in the house. I don't remember the prisoner saying when he got hold of me that he would show me how they wrestled in America. Nothing of that sort was said. My memory is too good for that. I hadn't had any beer before I went in Disraeli Vaults. Ido not remem- ber being lifted up by the prisoner and put on the seat. I believe I was conscious enough, but had lost my speech for a time. I remember being brought heme on a wheelbarrow. I was placed on a sofa in the kitchen, and was there till Sunday. I didn't fall off the sofa during the night. The prisoner took hold of my arms first, and stood right in ,front of me. I never thought of being hurt, and never resisted him taking hold of my arms previous to being thrown. I never thought when he took hold of my arms that be was going to hurt me in the manner he did. To all appearances he was qeite sober. I had been conversing with James Kirk- ham. I cannot tell what we wet e talking about—all sorts of nonsense very likely—Murphy on Thursday surrendered to his bail, and was placed under arrest. He will be brought before the magistrates this (Saturday) morning. At the time of writing there was no change in the prisoner's con- dition, but Dr. Aspinall nes no hope of his recovery.

THE BONA-FIDE TRAVELLER QUESTION. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. F. Rigby and Mr. A. Thomas, Mr. H. Jackson, the landlord of the Commercial Hotel, Bridge-street, Runcorn, was sum- moned to answer a charge of having on Sunday the 18th May, at four o'clock in the afternoon opened his premises for the sale of intoxicating liquor, and persons who were not bona-fide travellers or persons lodging in the house. He was further charged with selling liquor to such persons at the same time,--Mr. A. Fletcher, of Northwich, defended.— On the application of Inspector Hollingsworth the witnesses were ordered out of court.—P.S. Walley said that at four o'clock on the day named he visited Wilson's Hotel in com- pany with Constable Smith. On going into the smoke-room he found five men each with a glass of beer before him. He asked the barmaid where Mr. Jackson was, and she replied that be was upstairs. The barmaid in charge of the premises was about 17 years of age, and she told him that the men said they were travellers from Farnworth. The men gave him their addresses as follows :—John Russell, 29, Church- street, Farnworth, Albert Cotton, 30, Church-street, Fern- worth, Owen Lennon, 29, Church-street, Farnworth, John Caldwell, 47, Church-street, Farnworth, James Grady, 47, Church-street, Farnworth. On inquiry the sergeant found thatall the men lived within the three mile limit, one of them I even residing just over the bridge.—P.C. Smith corroborated. —Albert Cotton said he was employed as a barman at Walker's Vaults, Waterloo-road, Widnes, and lived at 69, Irwell-street, Widnes. About four o'clock on Sunday after- , noon he was admitted into Wilson's Hotel with two com- panions named Russell and Lennan by a young woman. She never asked him whether be was a traveller or not.—By Mr. Rigby : Russell was the first that went in, and when asked where they came rrom he said Farnworth. He (witness) never spoke.—Br Mr. Fletcher: She asked, "Are you travellers?" Russell answered Yes." She said, "Where from? " and Russell replied, "Fern- worth." They were then admitted. When the officer ap- peared he gave Farnworth to make the best of a bad job.— Owen Lennart, of 52, Major Cross-street, Widnes. said he was a barman in the employ of Sir A. B. Walker. Be stated that the person who admitted them did not ask where he came from, bat she said something to Rnssell which he could not hear. He was never asked where he came from while inside the house.—John Russell, of 1, Major Cross- street, Widnes, bleaching powder maker, at Messrs. Sulli- van's works, Widnes, said he only answered for himself when questioned. When the officers came to the house the girl rushed into the room and said, "You are sure you are all from Farnworth?" No one replied.—By Mr. Fletcher: They said Farnworth because they thought Widnes was not far enough.—John Caldwell, of 22, Major Cross-street, Widnes, chemicil labourer, admitted that he said he was a traveller from Farnworth.---James Gray, 9, Elizabeth-street,, Newtown, Widnes, chemical labourer, stated that Caldwell said they both came from Farnwerth.—Mr. Fletcher asked the Bench in confidence whether there was any case for him i to answer. That there had been a fraud on Mr. Jackson was patent from the evidence, and he asked them whether a publican should be summoned under the circumstances detailed. On tbair own admission it was clear the witnesses were guilty of misleading Mr. Jackson through his servant by falsely representing themselves to be travellers in order to get served with liquor when they were not entitled to it, and they were subject to a penalty not exceeding £5. There was reasonable ground for supposing these men to be what they represented themselves to be, and there were two of the witnesses, barmen, who ought to have known better than to behave in this way to a person in Jackson's position. Their conduct was most reprehensible and he hoped their worships would take cognizance of it. Messrs. Greenall whom he represented, could not imagine why this dead set should be madeagainst the Wilson's Hotel. Those people who lodged in the house were prepared to say that there was no more repu- table and respectable house in Runcorn or anywhere else. Mr. Jackson tried his best to keep the place respectable, and he hoped their worships by con- victing in this case, would not deprive him of this means of getting his livelihood. Messrs. Greenall and Company still thought he was a fit person to be entrus- ted with the license, and they asked the bench to say whether, as the case stood, he ought to be prosecuted in this way by the police. He asked them to dismiss the case without hearing any further evidence.—lnspector Rolling- worth : Yon allege that we are persecuting Mr. Jackson.— Mr. Fletcher: I do.—lnspector Hollingwerth denied this The police simply said that people from Widnes ought not to he served.—Mr. Rigby thought it could hardly amount to persecution if there bad been a previous conviction.—ln- spector Hollingworth said the whole evidence bad been laid before the Bench in an unbiassed way.--Mr. Rigby said be was bound to say that the Bench were of Mr. Pletcheee opinion—that the case had failed. They were of opinion that Gray was a witness of truth, and be confirmed the Bench that Mr. Jackson had used I due precautions. They therefore considered it their duty to dismiss the case.—James Gray, John Caldwell, Owen Lennon, John Russell, and Albert Cotton were then charred by the police with having, on the 18th May, been found on the premises of Henry Jackson during prohibited hours, and also with giving false addresses to P.S. Walley. They were further charged, by a summons taken out by Mr. Jackson, with falsely representing themselves as travellers with the object of obtaining intoxicating lickuor,—The defendants

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL, BOARD,
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL, BOARD,

The monthly meeting was held at the Offices, Bridge- water-street, on Wednesday. The Rev. Canon Barclay pre- sided ; and there were present—the Rev. T. Fennelly, Messrs T. Norman, J. Pritchard, P. Briscoe, It. Lea, G. S. Hazlehurst, and F. Rigby (clerk.) THE SITE OF THE FROEOSSID NEW SCHOOL—The Clerk said he had seen Mr. W. H. Linaker, who had looked into the papers regarding the site the Board proposed to purchase for the proposed new school, off Greenway-road. He was of opinion that the Board would be fully justified in paying for half the street; and making the street. He had found that the land had not been dedicated to the public by Major Orred ; that it was paid (or; and had passed from hand to hand and had always been paid for—in fact not only half the street but the whole of it.—Mr. Norman : We cannot do anything more then until we hear from the Education De- partment 7—The Clerk: No. THE BOARD AND WATERLOO HOUSE—The Clerk read a letter from Mr. John Rigby, who, on behalf of his co- trustees, gave the Board p pwer to sub-let their offices to a suitable tenant. The Clerk added that he had laid the papers before Mr. Linaker, as solicitor to the Board, with respect to the resolutions and proposals of the Commis- sioners for the removal of the School Board to Waterloo House. Mr. Linaker had authorised him to say that his opinion was that any expense incurred ley the Board at Waterloo House until the expiration of the lease would be illegal, and would be disallowed by the auditor. All the expenses incidental to the maintenance of these present offices in case the Board removed to Waterloo House would also be illegal, and would be disallowed. In the event of the Board securing a suitable tenant for the present offices they would be relieved.—Mr. Norman moved that the present offices be put in proper repair according to the term of the lease.—Mr. Hazlehurst seconded.—Mr. Pritchard moved, and Father Fennelly seconded, that Messrs. Nor- man, Lea, and Briscoe be appointed a committee to deter- mine the work necessary and carry it out.—Both resolutions were carried. Ale INCREASE OF SALARY—SamueI In glesfiehl, the assistant visitor, applied for an increase of wages, placing before the Board a statement of his work for the past 14 inonths.—Mr. Norman moved, and Mr. Lea seconded, that the salary be increased from 108. to 15s. per week provided be would discontinue all night work.—Mr. Briscoe moved, and the Chairman seconded, an amendment that the salary be advanced to 12e. 6d.—Tne original motion was carried by four votes to three. APPOINTMENT OF TREASURER—Mr. J. R. Thompson, , the treasurer of the Board,,having been promoted from Run- -1 corn branch of Parr's Bank to Chester, it was resolved that [Mr. E. A. Chorlton be appointed treasurer. VISITOR'S REPORT.—Mr. Bowyer, the visitor, reported that during May there was an increase in the average atten- dance of 65.2, as compared with the corresponding period last year. The School Attendance Committee held a meet- ing on the 21st Miy, and inquired into 42 cises. There was no further business.

CADISHEAD. DRUNIKENNESS.—Jobn Taylor, cutter, of Cadishead, was charged on the 27th instant, before Sir John J. Mantell, with being drunk and disorderly. Police-constable Jones, 1178, proved the case. He was fined 7s 6d and costs. PARTINGTOIC—The new church here, which is a massive building with a beautiful tower, built free of cost, the gift of a clergyman of that neighbourhood, was consecrated for Divine worship by the Bishop of Chester, on Wednesday. The opening services were crowded, and were of a very- edifying character. This village is now well supplied with places of worship. There was a large gathering of Wesleyan Sunday scholars on Whit-Sunday afternoon at 2-30 in Wesley Chapel. The schools were well represented by the parents of the children and other friends. The meeting was conducted by the Rev.. R. Dillon, superintendent of the circuit. Special hymns were sung by the choir and children. Suitable addresses were delivered by the minister, Mr. Jackson, and Mr. Whal- ley, from Manchester. PRESENTATION.— Übe clergyman of Irlam Church was presented on Saturday evening by a committee of gentlemen representing the parishioners generally, with a beautiful illuminated address, a silver tea and coffee service, and a handsome clock with ornaments to match. The ground of the presentation to the Rev. Mr. Martin, M.A., and-Mrs. Martin. was their devotion to the welfare of the parish—as well as_ the recognition of Mr. Martm's disinterestedness in refusing the offer of the better living of the sew church at Partington. allerturau2„—A. very pretty wedding took place on Tues- day. Mr. Dyson of Manchester and Cadishead, and Miss Fryer, the daughter of one of our most respectable farmers, were married at Irlam a Kttle after eleven o'clock in the morning. The bridesmaids were Miss Dyson, sister of the bridegroom, and Miss Fryer, sister of the bride. There were three carriages in attendance. A select company sat down to breakfast which was given in the house of the bride's father. In the afternoon the young people left to spend their honeymoon at Blackpool.

A FLoattlza Per.acE —Sir A. B. Walker has just bad ' built Is his order a steam yacht, which has been described as the finest floating palace afloat. She has cost nearly £200,000, and is commanded by the late captain of the Sun- beam. The Cuhona, for that is her name, while on a pas- sage on Monday night from Amsterdam rendered her first service to humanity by rescuing a party of holiday leekera who bad been blown out to sea from Southsea.

i" As things are now," says the Irate correspondent,. a the man who attends a private view may be tolerably certain that be will be almost as much crushed and trodden on as if he were pushing into a pantomime pit on Boxing night," and, ~ hey will return home a sadder and a wiser man worn out, perhaps. with an ineffectual struggle to retain his catalogue in his hand and his hat on his head, bet im- pressed at the same time with ths drm conviction that those. hollow mockeries called private views shall know him no more until some much needed reform shall have changed their character altogether." Probably, from a feeling op the part of those invited that it would be ungracious to tell one's host that his guests are too many and his friends ill. chosen, the proverbial publicity of " private views" has- been hitherto little more than hinted at with gsntle irony. It is, nevertheless, a wonder that artists in their own interests, considering that the "private view" should he the great day for disposing of their works, do not unite in a dert-rinination to limit their generosity. It is possible to carry ceuitesy to an extent that spoils the order of things ; and tlac .:)urtesy that dispenses private-view tickets in wholesale- fashion is at the foundation of the many weaknesses in Burlington House arrangements to which so much attention is just BOIT being directed.

Mr. Moncurs Conway is about to return to the United States, thus removing a familiar figure from London Liter- ary Society. Mr. Conway has lived with us for twenty years. He began life in the States as a Methodist prPacher, continued it as a Unitarian clergyman, blossomed into at; anti-slavery ac:itator, came over to Londnn in search of better health, and settled down finally to journalistic life. He writes something for the English magazines, but chiefly for the American, being a correspondent of a leading daily paper in the States. He has also a church here where he preaches twice on Sunday, and draws a fashionable congre- gation. It was he who in the first year of the American Civil War declared from his pulpit in Cincinnati that Presi- dent Lincoln's daily prayer was "0 Lord God, I should like to have you on my side, but I must have Kentucky."

If the Maori King happened to be in the neighbourhood of Trafalgar-square yesterday and a few days age, he is likely to carry home strange ideas of the customs of the English people. On one occasion he would see a person with a crape hood over his head, dragging by a copper wire fastened at his wrist, a stout, chubby, and breathless divine. Yesterday be would have beheld another gentlercan blind- folded, towing by a silken cord a highly respectable gentle- man of more than middle age. To see this on two days within one week would, naturally enough, lead to the con- clusion that it Was a matter of everyday occurrence. For- tunately it is not, or it would become necessary for the police to interfere. This simultaneous outburst of thought-reading is due to the rivalry of the two chief practitioners. Mr. Cumberland, I believe, was originally in the service of Mr. Bishop, and is now running him very close in the matter of attracting tbe public. It is the fashion amongst the shrewde-t and cleverest of us to doubt the actuality of the accom- plishments that take place under our eyes. It is-impossible to deny that pins and other articles of portable property carefully and secretly disposed of are discovered in the most extraordinary manner. But the skill of the performer is depreciated by the invention of elaborate schemes of col- lusion. I admit myself to be an uncompromising convert to Mr. Stuart Cemberland's art. lam so for the best of all reasons, since I have been subject to it under circumstinces which, unless it be assumed that mai qui path was in col- lusion with him absolutely establish the reality of his art. It was one of the earlier of, his private parties that I at- tended, an earnest and interested inquirer after the truth with a strong disposition to believe that there was not a large supply at hand. Several successful experiments took place with gentlemen of well-known names, but I conine inv testimony to what happened to myself. A pin was given me and I was invited to hide it in some part of the room. It was a room with deeply recessed windows hung by thick red curtains. Going forth with the pin, Mr. Stuart Cum- berland meanwhile being in custody of • a committee in another room, I got tehind one of the thick curtains with the apparent intention of hiding the pin it. Instead of that I stuck it under the collar of my coat. When Mr. Cumberland ' was brought in he took my hand and almost immediately led me over to the curtained recess, where he failed to Ind the pin. The spectators were so certain the pin was there ' that they looked upon Mr. Cuinberland as having failed. He admitted that it was a hard case hut eventually he found the pin. I have talked the matter over with Mr. Labouchere, ,who has a very satisfactory explanation of the mystery. The curtains covered a window, behind the window was one of Mr. Cumberland's accomplices, who saw me put the pin in the collar of my coat ancicommunicated the fact to the arch imposter. Of course that is possible as most things are. But what an army of accomplices Mr. Stuart Cum- berland must maintain to meet such an utdooked for con- tingency. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The House of Commons resumed its work to-day without visible indication of overpowering enthusiasm. When the holidays end on a Thursday there is always a disposition.on the part of members to round off the week, and make Monday the day for actually oegin.ning work. On this occa- sion the tendency was increased by the announcement that the Premier would not be in his place till Monday. Ihere is a strong, and not ill-founded presumption that if Mr. Gladstone voluntarily absents himself from the House of Commons there is nothing particular going on there. What did go on to-night was Supply, the House being almost empty ani altogether languid. On Monday the tide of , political life will run fast and furious enough through both its channels. The Conservative peers having heroically de- cided not to take the extra week's holiday offered them are ; bound to Ise in their places, and being there must say and do ; something. Witn all kinds of rumours as to the conference, and, as Lord Randolph Churchill would add, "with rail. way stations flying up in the air all around us," Lord Salisbury must put Earl Granville to the question ; whilst in the Commons a multitude of questions are being already prepared for the peppering of the Premier.

Nothing is more remarkable about the dynamite explo- sions than the rapidity and completeness with which publis excitement has disappeared. It seems that as, according to common repute, eels grow accustomed to skinning, so does a great capital become placidly used to being blown up with dynamite. No arrests have yet taken place in connection with this latest outrage, and whether the police have or have not a clue is a Matter they wisely keep to themselves. There is the usual foolish outcry about the helplessness of the police, which must be particularly aggravating to a body of hardworking and intelligent men. The expectation ap- pears to exist in some quarters that either the police should intuitively put their hand upon the dynamitard as he pro- ceeds t 4 work, or should immediately after the explosion take a cab drive to his postal address and wait his return redbanded from the deed. As a matter of fact both these these things have happened within the past year. The pa- tient tracking of the dynaruitard whose headquarters were at Wolverhampton, his seizure with his pockets loaded with explosives, and the swift apprehension of his accomplices should not be forgotten because the police did not forestall the miscreants of Friday night and have not since arrested them. They are supposed to manage these things better in 1 France, and Russia is one vast police establishment. Rut in the palmy days of the French police Orsini bombs were plied, and in Russia the Nihilists are omnipresent.

It is certainly wrong to be amused at the misfortunes of others. But it is difficult to prevent a smile as one thinks of Ismail Pasha walking through the leafy gardens of the Palais Royale, probably thinking of his coining dinner, when suddenly there darts upon him an irate young man who soundly thrashes him, and, unrestrained, walks away. The last time I saw his Highness the little tub-like figure crowned by a stolid face and the inseparable fez., was waddling through the glittering throng in Lady Borthwick's famous white drawing-room. And to think of his imper- turbability being suddenly upset by an inexplicable young man with a stick is more funny than can Ise told to any not acquainted with his personal appearance. A year ago last October I had the honour of sitting next to the Ex-Khedive at dinner. tie told me he was about to leave Paris, where he Mad long been resident, and make his head quarters at London. "Egypt, since I left it," he said, "was ruled from Paris. it is now governed from London, and I go there." Tbe little incident in the Palais Royale will pro-. bably strengthen the impression in the mind of his High- miens favourable to residence in London.
