liton.wav Bonn.—An ordinary meeting of this Board was to be held on Tuesday, but owing to there not being a quorum present no business was transacted. The only members present were Messrs. Tyree and Lowe. CoNvanawriote.— On Friday a confirmation service was held in the Parish Church by the Right Rev. Dr. Hellnauth formerly Bishop of Huron (Canada), in the absence of the Lord Bishop of the Diocese, Dr. Ryle. One hundred and sixteen candidates were presented, a large number being from the different parishes in the neighbourhood. The church was well filled, the congregation joining in the ser- vice which was a hearty one. Mrs. Macnaghten ably pre- sided at the organ. ASSAULTING FOLICEMEN.—Edward Jones, a young man, was on Tuesday charged at Prescot Petty Sessions with having been drunk and disorderly on the Saturday previous, and also with assaulting P.C.5 Strong and Carlton. The prisoner, it was stated, at the time mentioned was fighting with another man, and on being taken into custody was very violent snd assaulted the officers.—Superintendent Barker said the prisoner was the most disorderly character in Woolton. For being drunk and disorderly prisoner was fined 10s and costs or 14 days, and for each case of as- sault he was also fined las and costs or 14 days.—Edward M'Quire and Thomas Jones, also belonging to Woolton, were similarly charged, and were each fined 5s and costs fer hav- ing been drunk and disorderly, and 103 and costs for the assault, or in default of payment 21 days' imprisonment. HEAVY FINES FOB POACHING.—Richard Wright was charged at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with haying trespassed in pursuit of game, and also with killing a hare on the land of Colonel Parkes, at Cronton, on the 15th nit.—A witness named Gilbert Blundell sthted that on the day in question he beard a gen fired on the land in question, and afterwards saw the defendant run across a field after a hare which he caught and took into his house. Defendant denied the charge, and said the witness had been drunk on the day in question and did not know what he was doing. —A fine of 20s and costs or one month's imprisonment was imposed for the trespass; and 40s and costs for killing the game or two month's imprisonment —Thomas Wright, a young man was also charged with having been in pursuit of game on land belonging to Captain Willis, at Whiston, en the 22nd May. It was stated that the de'endant had been seen with his arm in a rabbit hole. On being asked what he was doing there he replied that he was" fishing."—A fine of 20s and costs or one month's imprisonment was

CRUELTY TO hlousns.—Willi.am Lathom, a young man, was on Tuesday charged with cruelly illtreating A horse at Prescot on the 12th April. Sergeant Bull said that on the day in question the defendant was driving a horse along Derby-street. The animal was yoked to a cart filled with furniture, which it was utterly unable to draw up the bank in front of the police office, and consequently fell down. The horse was an aged one and in poor condition. Defen- dant said he was taking the furniture from Liverpool to War- rington, but Superintendent Barker would not let him pro- ceed further without first obtaining a chain horse. It was afterwards ascertained that the contents of the cart weighed 2 tons 41cwt5.—Defendant was fined 10s. and costs; and George Coleman, the owner of the horse, was fined 20s. and costs, or in default one month's imprisonment.—George Smith was also charged with having illused a horse at Pre- cot. Sergeant Bull said that on the night of the 23rd of last month he heard someone urging a horse outside the police station, and on going out saw that it was the deferslant who was in charge of a horse and cart. The cart, the defendant said, contained about three tons, and he also admitted that the horse had been working all day in Liverpool, whence he had set out about ten o'clock that night. The horse, Sergeant Bull added, was unable to draw its load up the bank, and he consequently stepped the defendant until he obtained a chain horse.—A fine of 15s and costs was imposed.

div.head: ILLEGAL PRACTICES BY CANVASSERS.-HEAVY
div.p: ILLEGAL PRACTICES BY CANVASSERS.-HEAVY
FINES.

At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Before Mr. H. Bright and Captain Willis, James Sergeant, beerhouse keeper, Kernble-street, Prescot, and Edward Crawley, watch- maker, Honghton-street, Prescot, were charged with having, on the 7th April, falsely assumed to act in the name of John Ford at an election of members of the Local Board of Free- cot; and further, with having fabricated part of a certain paper intended to be used as a voting paper, to wit the votingpaper of John Ford, a person entitled to vote at such election.—Mr. T. Swift (instructed by Messrs. J. 0. and W. Swift) proaecuted, and Mr. Segar (instructed by Mr. H. L. Riley) defended.—Mr. Swift, after having enumerated the preliminaries incidental to an election of members of a Local Board, said that in the present case the voting papers were issued on the 2nd April. They were delivered by police officers detailed for that purpose at the request of the local authority, and they were collected again before the 7th April, which was the day appointed by law for that purpose. Upon the Bth the voting papers were counted and the result declared, so that in that case the election seemed to have been properly initiated and carried through. A police officer who was delivering the voting papers upon the 2nd April in the course of his duty discovered that he was fol- lowed by men who were apparently canvassers, or were taking some part in the election. He spoke to them about what they were doing, as 'he felt that they were not doing what was right. With regard to the case of John Ford, an officer who was delivering voting papers went to the court in which Ford lives, and went into the house of a man named Ackers. Mrs. Ford was in Ackers's house at the time. As soon as ever the policeman had delivered the papers the two defendants and some other men appeared on the scene, and at once asked for the voting paper. He (Mr. Swift) did not make any complaint in Ackers's case about what was done to Ackers's voting paper. He believed that was done with the consent of Ackers himself. But when Ackers's paper had been dealt with Mrs. Ford was asked for her paper, although the defendants had not the slightest authority or pretence for demanding the voting paper or dealing with it in any way whatever. Mrs. Ford, when asked for whom she would vote, said she would vote as Ackers had voted, and the de- fendants then, behind the back of John Ford, without any communication with him, and without any authority from him, took upon themselves to fill up the voting paper that was designed for John Ford, whose name was upon it, they attested it, acting together, and, contrary to all proper rule and practice, put it into an envelope which was directed to the returning officer. It was quite obvious that those men, as far as lay in their power, did get this voting paper filled up in favour of such candidate or candidates as were their friends, and had done everything they possibly could to procure it against being further interfered with by being fastened up in an envelope and left directed to the re- turning officer. On the 7th, when the voting papers were collected, this paper was handed to the collector and counted the neat day without John Ford knowing anything about it. Ford had never authorised his wife to vote, and never found out that she had done so till the 12th April. He was then very angry about it. and went to the defendant Crawley and asked him what business he had to fill the voting paper up without his orders. Crawley replied " I don't know, you must go to Sergeant." Ford then went to Sergeant, who said that he thought Mrs. Ford was a widow. This pre- tence, Mr. Swift thought, was ridiculous, because the voting paper was in the name of John Ford. Mr. Swift also men- tioned that politics had not entered into this election at all. He thought he was entitled in saying that there was no political feeling whatever on either side. In prose- cuting these two men they were prosecutiog only the people they could get at. They should be very glad indeed if instead of prosecuting the mere agents they were able to get hold of and prosecute those who were the principals or prin- cipal in the matter. Of course men, if there be such, who employ others to go about and commit what was wrong, I were fully as culpable, or perhaps more culpable than those 'who actually commit it. However, they submitted that a great wrong had been done, and one that ought not to be winked at or allowed to pass by without any notice, and that justice should be meted out to the defendants, who were actually agents; and about anyone else they bad nothing to do with them that day. All be would say was that if they did escape the more was the pity.—Witnesses were then called in support of this statement.—Mr. Cross, clerk to the Prescot Local Board, one of the witnesses, 'aid that 144 voting papers had been returned in envelopes, which was an irregular way of returning them—John Ford said he never knew before Mr. Berry, one of the candidates for the Local Board, spoke to him that there was to be an election.—Mr. Segar, in defence, contended that no offence had been com- mitted within the meaning of the Act of Parliament. The something 7 intention of the Legislature was, he said, that no person done should be liable to a penalty URless he biiefhthheree mimudst been nve n knowny fa. to t be wrong. Us thgh all it was on the part of Mrs. Ford herself. Her husband had evidently cared nothing about the e ec i l ton before Mr Berry solicited his vote and persuade h• to cause that disturb- ! ance because his (Berry's) name had not been put the voting paper. Mr. Berry was a defeated candidate, n it was natural that he should have been piqued and aan- noyed, but it was another thing for him to cause a prosecu- tion in that manner in order that he might have something out of the election. If Mr. Berry wanted to urge anything

• he could have written to the papers and his views would then be attended to.—After a short absence the Bench re- turned and said they bad decided to convict, but would withhold the verdict till after the other cases had been dealt with.--The case in which the two above-named de- fendants and also John Makin, watchmaker, Warrington- road, Prescot, were charged with having falsely assumed to act in the name of Thomas Cray- mour, of Pemberton Court, yrescet, and also with fabricating his vote was then heard. The evidence in this case was in many respects similar to that given in the last,—lt was stated by Mrs. Craymour that the defendants put the initials opposite to the name of Mr. Hall in her husband's voting paner although she told them they had better leave it till her husband came home. She told them that her husband was going to vote, for Mr. Berry, and they left the envelope, in which they put the paper, open so that Craymour could place the initials opoos.te Berry's name. When her husband came home he rabbed out the marks made by the defendants and voted for those b.e desired to vote for.—Mr. Se'ar, in his defence in this case, said that there was a force behind Ford and Craymour, and he should very much like to know what that force was. His friend had said he should like to get to the actual perpetrators of those offences, but he (Mr. Segar) might be allowed to say that there were no princi- pals, because the defendants bad never been instructed to fabricate votes, and therefore there was no mysterious " bogy "in the background. What the defendants had done had been done in over-zeal. Mr. Segar also mentioned that he had been informed that Mr. Berry had nothing to do with these cases, and therefore be withdrew the remarks he made with regard to that gentleman.—The Bench said they would convict in this case also.—James Sergeant and Edward Crawley were neat charged with baying falsely assumed to act in the name of Terence Crap-Nom-, and also with fabricating his vote—The Bench decided also to con- vict in this case. After an absence of considerable length, the Bench decided that in the case of Thomas Craymour a fine of MO and costs would be imposed on each of the defen- dants; in the case of Terence Craymour a fine of L 1 and costs would be imposed on each defendant: and in the case of John Ford a fine of Ll and costs each. In default of payment the defendants were to go to gaol for two months.-The verdict caused considerable sensation amongst the large number of people assembled in the Court room.

I'HE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JUNE 7, 1884. THE LOST PURSE. We all know that the annals of the law courts during the past fifty years prove that not everyone committed to pri- son, or perchance penal servitude is guilty of the crime laid to his charge. Give a dog a teal name, and the whole city is up in arms against him, and he is hunted to desperation or death. Circumstantial evidence alone is a dangerous theory to convict upon in criminal cases, as the true sketch I am about to relate will clearly show. Some years ago, a pale-faced, emaciated, but intelligent- looking little boy, of fourteen years, was brought up before the stipendiary magistrate of —, and was charged with having stolen a sum of money from the shop of his em- ployer? The poor little fellow was in the deepest distress, and felt keenly the degradation of standing in the felon? dock. "What's your name ?" asked the magistrate. With a faltering tone he sobbed out his name, which, how- ever, was not caught by the bench. The officious police-officer roared out, in a tone which made the poor little fellow shake in his shoes— " Don't be snivelling, you young rascal, but hold up your head and answer when you're spoken to. Tell him what's your name." "Harry Blake," said the lad, humbly. "Where do you live?" "I' Brass Street, off Rochdale Road." "Now, Mr. Blinks, what is the case ?" said the worthy magistrate, with some interest. "The old story, your honour," replied the clerk, rather familiarly. "Thieving. He's stolen a purse containing over twenty pounds, and won't give any account of it." "Where are the witnesses ?" "Here, your honour. The gentleman who lost the money, and the boy's employer." "Go on with the case." The boy's master stepped forward, and, after swearing upon the book, proceeded to state the case. He was a keen-featured man, a love of gain stamping his manner and acts with a shrewdness and self-sufficiency. He grasped the rail of the witness-box with a firmness that showed his self-possession, and his determination to have the accused made an example of for the whole fraterutty of shop boys. With a pompous tone he thus stated the case : "This gentleman came into my shop, your honour, to pur- chase some goods. He paid me the sum of four eighteen-six, ordered the parcel to be sent home, and left the shop; but in the course of ten minutes returned for his pocket-book, which he missed, and was confident that he had left it on my counter. This boy, Harry, had been with me but a few weeks, and I remarked that he hurried away out of the shop immediately, and I did not lay eyes on him for three days afterwards. There was no one in the shop at the time but Harry and myself. The pocket-book was gone, and no one in the world would suppose I stole it. This lad must have stolen it, for he can't, or won't, give any account of it. I verily believe he's an incorrigible young thief and vagabond. He is one of those wretched street arabs whom I took out of charity and set to work, and this is the return he makes me. He was a poor naked little beggar, whom I clothed and fed, and he thus adds ingratitude to his villany." " Is that all, sir ?" "Yes, your honour. I hope you will give him at least five years in a reformatory, to teach other shop lads not to rob their employers." The owner of the purse, in his evidence, then stated that the shopkeeper's evidence was correct. He had lost over twenty pounds in the way described—and he saw no one in the shop but this boy and his master, and the lad had made his escape before he returned to tell his loss. He was quite positive he had not lifted the purse, for he remembered dis- tinctly where he laid it upon the counter, near where the boy was tying up the parcel of goods. He had not the least doubt in the world that he had stolen it, and made off with it during his short absence. His not turning up to his work for three days was dead proof against him. He hoped his honour would give him a sentence which he would not soon forget. These young rogues ought to be made an example of. It was no good trying to lift them out of the gutters. "What's bred in the bone is sure to come out in the flesh." "Now, my boy," said the magistrate, "have you any- thing to say ? You have heard the evidence of your master and this gentleman who lost his money, and the case looks very black against you. Do you wish to say anything, or to explain, eh ?" The poor little fellow was so much al'armed with the sur- roundings of the court and the apparent severity of his honour, though he was a kind and large-hearted man, who did not wish in any way to intimidate this almost infant culprit—that he sobbed out in a confused manner— "No, aur—pleeus stir. Aw didn't steyl it, aw didn't for sure!" "Do you know anything of this lad ?" said the magistrate to the police-officer. "No, air. But I believe him to be an ungrateful young thief." "Remand him for seven days for inquiry. Stubbs, call the chaplain's attention to this boy; possibly he may get him to tell what he has done with this money. If no new light is brought to bear upon the case we must commit him for five years to a reformatory school. Evil must be checked in the bud, and we must teach these street urchins that kind- ness must not be repaid by ingratitude." Poor Harry Blake was taken down to the bridewell cells, sobbing and sighing as if his poor heart would break. He sat down upon the wooden stool, and the cell rang again with his pitiful cries of— "Oh I what'll become of eaur Eddie ? Oh ! what'll he do ?" This was his little orphan brother, the only kith and kin he had in the world. Outcast and friendless as he was now left, he had a warm, affectionate heart, and a noble, gener- ous spirit. But three weeks ago he had promised his mother upon her deathbed that he would protect little Eddie. The destitute and helpless condition of his orphan brother made him weep and sob more than his own critical condition. It was a few days before Christmas, and the snow was falling, covering the ground with its dazzling mantle of white. Harry knew he was innocent, but poor Eddie was on the streets, homeless and friendless, without a single friend in the wide world. Where would he sleep, and who would now find him bread ? He was too little to work, and among the crowd of boys who "shined," or stood shivering at street corners, vainly endeavouring to sell their poor wares, he had no chance of picking up a single copper. This thought, and his own knowledge of the dangers and temptations of the streets, made him inconsolable. The following day a note was laid upon my desk, bearing the official blue stamp of the Central Police Court, calling my attention to this boy. I found him crying as if his heart was bursting, and sobbing out— " Oh ! Eddie! Eddie! who'll tak car on the neaw ? Nearly Kesmas Day, too, when aw thowt t' ha' sich a happy toime together!" The moment he saw who it WaS he rushed to the door, and seizing me by the arm, in the most piteous and entreating tones said— "Oh ! stir, will yo'—will yo' look after mi little brother Eddie, an' put him i'th' Boys' Refuge? Wi' ha' no fayther, an' mother, dee'd three weeks sin'. Do, sur, if yo' pleeas, tak care of Eddie. He's mi on'y brother, stir, an' o aw've getten t' love i' o this wide wo'ld !" Having heard his sad story, I promised at once to find Eddie, and place him in the Boys' Refuge. "But what about this purse and the twenty pounds, my boy ?" said I, patting the lad's curly head the while. With another burst of tears the lad sobbed out: "Aw didn't steyl it, sur. for aw never seed it, un wot's moor, knows nowt abeaut it." He was straightforward in his manner, with an open, genuine disposition' and I felt he was telling the truth. A lad at his age, who had been knocking about the streets of Manchester so long, and showing so much love and fore- thought for his little orphan brother, could not be a liar and thief. I determined to be present in court on the day fixed for his farther examination. When the case was called, the magistrate asked me if I had any report to make. To which I simply replied:— "This boy does not look like a thief, and from his dispo- sition, I am quite convinced that he did not steal the purse." "All very well, but the evidence is against him. Are the witnesses in court ?" "Yes," replied the clerk. The gentleman who lost the money was again in ,the wit- ness-box, and, having taken the oath, proceeded to detail, as before, the circumstances of the case. "Now sir, you hear yourself what the gentleman states. Do you any longer doubt that the boy stele the purse ?" admit all the circumstances are against him, still I believe him innocent. Permit me, though I know I've no right to ask such a privilege, to put a question or two to the witness. You have stated that you missed your purse, after leaving Mr. Brown's shop ?" " Yes ; with over twenty pounds in it." "You are quite positive that you didn't take it away with you when you left ?" "No, I did not." "You might have dose so." "But I sm as certain as that I am standing here that I did not." "Could you not have dropped it, then, in your hurry ?" "I tell you I hadn't it to drop. I placed it upon the counter, near to where the boy was making up a parcel. Look you, reverend sir, I am as certain that that young rascal took my purse as I am that you are sitting next to his worship." "You came back to the shop. How long after?" "Within five minutes or so." "And the boy was gone S" " Yes, and my purse, too," he added sharply. Thera was no doubt that the witness appeared to have the best of the case, and the Court believed that here was another proof that prison chaplains have more heart than head, and I hat they are tco apt to be "galled" by tbe tears of those whom adverse circumstances bring under their charge. my belief, ho vever, in the lad's innocence was still unshaken. "May I ask the prisoner a question or two, your worship." "Certainly, certainly." "Harry, did you steal that gentleman's purse ?" "No, ear, aw never touched it, for aw never see'd it." "Then why did you leave Mr. Brown's shop in such a dreadful hurry that night, as soon as this gentleman left,as he says you did?" "Whey, nut, mother wur sick an' deem," he said, the big tears rolling down his cheek,," an' me, an' eawr little Eddie war o hoo had t' take care on hur. Aw went straight whoam, for hoo towd mi i'th morning ut hoo wur a-deeM, an' nt afore mony days wur o'er we wud be orphans." "You went straight home, then, because your mother was ill? How long had she been ill. " A good lung time, ear." "But why did you not go back to your plitoe ? Why were you away three days ?" " Oh ! sir, mother dee'd that fleet, an' tiler war no one wi'

her theo, but poor Eddie an' me." The poor little fellow wept bitterly as he added, " Aye, stir, just as .hoo're a-deein hoo raised her honds an' blessed us booath, ac' prayed ut God ud raise a friend to puirtect her two helpless orphans. Her last words wur, 'Oh, Harry, mi lad, as them loves ml, look after Eddie; ml own darlin child, keep away fro o bad lads; raythur starve than tell a lie.' Aw'm a pnor orphan boy, bud aw never stole th' post, an' aw'at tellin no lie abeawt it." Here the boy, overcome with emotion, once more broke out into the most heartrending sobs. " Yopr worsh;p," I said, after a moment', silence, and gaining a mastery over my feelings, "there is no evidence to cmvict this boy. My firm conviction is that he knows nothing of the purse, and anything rgainst him rests on cir- cumstantial evidence alone. He has no friends in the world —no prospects now, with suspicion resting upon him, but to turn to his former occupation, shoe-1 lacking in the streets. This is, as you know, beset with many dangers. His little br, ,ther, Eddie, has now a home in the Boys' Range. Dis- Icharge him, and I promise to find a shelter for him too in the same establishment."
The worthy magistrate at once ordered the boy to be discharged.

Judging by the applause that greeted the magistrate's de- cision, the feeling of the people were evidently with the boy, who clung to my arm as I left the court. I made u 3 my mind to place Harry in a situation out of Manchester, where toe history of the purse was not known, fully aware that no matter how a lad may seek to retrieve himself, the shadow which rests on his character, by some strange fatality, stands in the way of his worldly advancement until, driven to desperation, he sinks lower and lower in the social scale, and becomes the associate of thieves and vagabonds, when, perchance, by the aid of a helping band, he might have be- come honoured amongst men. I procured Harry a place in the Boys' Refuge, and never shall I forget the meeting of the two brothers, as they fondly clang to each other, little Eddie weeping joyfully on Harry's breast.

A few days afterwards I received a note from Mr. Brown, saying that the purse, with its contents, hid been found by his customer. It turned out that Mr. Brown himself, in the hurry of making up the parcel, by some means or other, placed the purse inside, and, as the parcel was afterwards mislaid, Harry was blamed. Harry grew up a worthy, re- spectable member of society, eventually becoming a partner in a warehouse in which I was fortunate enough to procure him a situation.—From Ben Brierley's Journal.

div.head: LOCAL BOARD MEETING.
div.p: LOCAL BOARD MEETING.

A monthly meeting of the Local. Board was held in the Board-room on Wednesday evening, when there were pre- sent: Messrs. Preston (who was elected to preeide in the absence of the Chairman), Beesley, Hatton, Whitfield, FeJg, Goldsworth (surveyor), Cross (clerk), and Dickenson (nuisance inspector.) I THE INSANITARY CONDITION OF PRESCOT.—The Chairm on asked if Dr. Hall had forwarded any report, in accordance with the motion passed at the last meeting as to property in an insanitary state in the town.—The Clerk replied that Dr. Hall had written stating that he and Mr. Goldswortlo were making a house to house visitation of the property in Prescot, and Mr. Goldsworth would bring before the com- mittee all such places as were found to be in an insanitary state.

Flans .vEnscs Tmes.—Mr. Goldsworth, in accordance with a request of the Board, submitted a list of tenders for the supply of flags and kerbs.—ln the course of the discus sion which ensued, Mr. Whitfield maintained that tiles were cheaper than flags; to which Mr. Goldswoith replied that if his opinion as surveyor was asked he would say that flags were far better than tiles, and in the long run were cheaper. —Mr. Fogg afterwards moved that the following tenders be accepted :—James Walton, Manchester, for 3 inch flags; Butterworth aud Brooks, Manchester' for dressed edgings (kerksj, and dressed channels; R. Roskell, Billinge, fot best setts, and Marsh and Melling. St. Helens, for second setts.— Mr. Hatton seconded the motion, which was carried. OBSTRUCTION OF THE FOOTPATHS. —the Chairman in- quired if anything had been done with regard to the obstruc- tion of the footpaths in Prescol—The Surveyor replied that he had not gone fully into the matter but he had called upon pawnbrokers in Eccleston-street, and they not only promised to do away with the nuisance but at once com- menced to remove the obstruction.—The Chairman re- marked that it appeared to be as bad as ever.-Mr. Whitfield thought it was scarcely as bad as it formerly was.—The Chairman said as their warnings had been disregarded he thought it was time they took some action in the matter.— Mr. Fogg did not think they should deal harshly in the matter at first, but pressure should be put forth in order to put down the obstruction.—lt was ultimately decided to leave the matter in the hands of the Snrveyor. TRH OUTBREAK or FEVER.—Mr. Goldsworth reported that he and Mr. Dickinson had commenced making a house to house visitation all through the town, and were making progress with it, and they would present a proper report in a short time. It took a long time to go through the work, and they found it would be longer than they expected. When they pointed out any special part to Dr. Hall as re- quiring any attention that gentleman devoted his special attention to it.—Mr. F.)gg : I may take it after our hasty special meeting summoned a week ago, the epidemic has not extended P—Mr. Goldsworth : This report has no reference to the fever.—Mr. Fogg : Do you know whether it has extended or not P—Mr. Goldsworth replied that he did not.—Mr. Cross added that since the last meeting he had had no further communication from the medical officer in relation to the matter.—Mr. Goldsworth : Our present report has reference to the existing nuisances.—The matter then dropped. A SEWAGE QUESTION.—Mr. Fogg drew attention to an alleged case of sewage from certain property outside the Board's district in Knowsley-road being carried into the Board's sewage system, and expressed the opinion that such a thing ought not to be allowed without a certain sum be- ing contributed for the privilege. He subsequently moved that the surveyor be asked to report upon the drainage of the property in question, and Mr. Whitthld seconded the motion, which was passed.—Mr. Goldaworth asked for a committee to be appointed to consider the matter with him. —Messrs. Fogg, Preston, Beesley, Whitfield, and Hatton were therefore selected as a sub-committee for that pur- pose.

RE-ELECTION OF NUISANCE INSPECTOR.—On the motion of Mr. Fogg, secended by Mr. Beasley, Mr. Dickenson was unanimously re-elected nuisance inspector for the ensuing year at his previous salary. REGISTRAR'S MONTHLY REPORT.—The Chairman read the Registrar's monthly report, which showed that during the month of May there were 10 deaths, as follows : Prescot 9, Eccleston 1 ; and in the corresponding month last year the number was—Prescot 1, Eccleston 1; total, 2. The births in the same period were—Present 11, Eccleston 2, total 13 ; last year—Prescot 17, Eccleston 3, total 20. This was the only business of interest.

HAYD-OCK. TnEvr OF JongEres Toots. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, William Jones, of St. Helens, was charged with stealing a bass and a quantity of joiners' tools, together of the value of 203, the property of William Whitfield, foreman carpenter, employed by Messrs. H. Evans and Co. at the Lyme Pit, early on the 24th ult. The defendant was taken into custody while in the act of pledging the tools at Prescot. He was committed for trial at the bessions.

TRESPASSING ON Lawn.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Thomas Sweeney, of Haydock, was charge i with trespassing on land in the occupation of Thomas Hunt, on tbe 15th ult.—Mr. Moore, of Warrington, appeared for the prosecutor and stated that on the date named the defen- dant was observed on the land in question. The offance was aggravated by the defendant refusing to give his name. Many persons were in the habit cf trespassing on that land and he asked for a salutary punishment to be inflicted in that case.—A flee of Is and costs, and the damage, Is, was imposed.

The profit is over £l,lOO, which will enable the directors to pay a dividend of 17i per cent. The Congress of Ce-operators, concluded at Derby on Wednesday, is the best attended and is considered the most successful that has yet been held in connection with the co-operative societies of the United Kingdom. Next year's Congress is to be held at Oldham. CHESHIRE CHEESE FAlR.—There was a large attendance of buyers from all parts of the country at the monthly fair at Nantwich, on Thursday morning. All cheese on offer was of this season's make, and the quality was generally good. Prices were, however, down 35 per cwt. on those quoted at Chester fair a fortnight ago. Como-I,m eb.ese realised from 503 to 555; medium, 55s to 00s; and superior, Os to 704 per CIV/. FUNERAL OF SiR BARTLE FRERB AT ST. PAUL'S CATHEDRAL.—On Thursday with sad and solemn ceremonial the mortal remains of the Right Hon. Sir Bartle Frere were accorded an honoured resting-place in St. Paul's Cathedral. The Cathedral was thronged with mourners, amongst the first arrivals being Lord Wolsaley, the Duke of Cambridge, Sir Frederick Bramwell, and Lord Chelmsford. ' The service was a choral one. The London correspondent of the d'llanchester Guardian says :—There need be no doubt whatever as to the unshaken determination of the Conservative leaders to move the House of Lords to reject the Franchise Bill, and the shadow fd. this coming event, which may be looked for about the 17th of next month, will exercise an unquestion- able influence over the proceedings upon the bill in the House of Commons. div.head: EARL ESTOWN.
div.p: EARL ESTOWN.

A CAB PROPRIETOR FINED.—At the Petty Sessions held at Newton Town Hal Lon Satnrday last, Samuel Walton, of Cross-lane, Eirlestown, WAS summoned for keeping two car- riages without having a licence for one. He was fined 20s and costs.

THE SERIOUS STABBING CASE AT SURTONWOOW—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday. before It. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie, Esp., William Murray. a labourer, residing at Bold, was charged on remand with unlawfully cutting and wounding Martin Ford, a labourer. at Burton. wood, on the previous Tuesday.—Superintendent Jackson applied for a remand until the next sessions, stating that Ford was in bed, and would not be able to leave for some days—Mr. Swift, who appeared for the prisoner, said he had no objection to the remand, but asked that the prisoner should be allowed out on ball.—The Chairman intimated that as the case was a very serious one, the Bench would not be justified in granting bail. CHURCH AFFAIRS AT EARLF.STOWN.—There was no re- newel of the unseemly scenes ma Sunday at St. John's Church, Earlestown, the only incident Worthy of notice being the fact that at the forenoon service no offertories were taken, although the vicarannonnced that the offertories were in aid of the church expenses and the sick poor. There was not a very large attendance, and the fact that there are no wardens or sidesmen connected with the church (owlng to circumstances previously reported) will probably account for no collections being made. lathe evening, however, the offertories were taken by three or four members of the con- gregation. Owing to the absence of the Rev. H. E. Smith (curate) owing to a sudden indisposition, the preacher both morning and evening was the Rev. T. R. Matthews (vicar.) ILLNESS OF THE REV. H. E. SseiTa.-00 Sunday fore- noon a painful incident was noticed in the Church of St. John the Baptist, Earlestown. Before the service com- menced the curate (the Rev. H. E. Smith) intimated to one or two persons that he felt very unwell, but notwithstanding that, he, along with tha Rev. T. R.Matthews, proceeded with tee service. Before the sermon (which it was understood had to be preached by the curate) the latter gentleman was compelled to retire owing to his indisposition, and he pro- ceeded to his hume. A very general feeling of sympathy was manifested on all hands for Mr. Smith, who is much esteemed. The reverend gentleman was unable to take his accustomed part in the services in church in the evening, and we believe that he has since left for his home in Liver- pool. WHITSUNTIDE AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.—Whit Monday, which in other parts of the country is looked upon as a general holiday, and one of unfettered pleasure-seeking, is not observed as such in the Earlestown and Newton dis- trict. This is accounted for by the fact that the holiday season for Earlestown and Newton is the "Race week," when the annual races take place at Newton Common. Consequently Monday last passed over without any eoecial feature of interest. The Viaduct wagon works, the Vulcan foundry, McCorquodale's printing works at Newton, and the paper mills were all at work as usual and—with the ex- ception of one or two—none ef the shops or places of business were closed. The weather was somewhat dull and threatening, but notwithstanding a goodly number of persons from the surrounding country visited the attractive and beautiful Newton Lake, where the afternoon was plea- santly spent.

NEWT-ON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.—Monday was the day for the holding of the monthly meeting of the Board of Commissioners for the township of Newton, but owing to the day being bank holiday the meeting was post- poned until the aftemoosi of the following day (Tuesday) at the usual hour, four o'clock. At the latter hour the only persons who put in an appear- ance were Messrs W F Gooch (chairman), 13 B Glover, Thomas Hunt (members). .1 E Woreley (law clerk), R Brier- ley (surveyor), and Dr. Watkins (medical officer of health). As five members form a quorum and only three were pre- sent, no meeting could be held. Mr. Glover subsequently said: Mr. Chairman, it it now 20 minutes past four; is it any use waiting any longer I—The Chairman : is there any rule, or are we bound in any way 7—Mr. Brierley : I think not, sir.—The Chairman: What is the usual custom 7—Mr. Brierley : There is no obligation to wait —After a little fur- ther conversation Mr. Glover moved that the meeting be ad- journed until four o'clock next Monday afternoon, which was seconded by Mr. Hunt, and adopted.—Atter Mr. Gooch, Mr. Hunt, and Dr. Watkins had left the room, Mr. J E Pan- dey entered and was informed of the resolution which had been passed.,

KEEPING DOGS WITHOUT LICENSES.—Before R. Hough- ton and T. J.Gilleepio, Buis., at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, Dr. Arthur Handyside, of EarleStOWO, WAS summoned for ke-ping a dog without a license.—Mr. of Warrington, the supervisor of taxes, prosecuted.—lt was stated that the defendant ought to have taken out a license on the 12th March, but did not do so until the 20th.—Mr. Swift, of St. Helens, who appeared for the defendant, said that on the 12th March defendant had no license, but he got one on the 20th. He hal been in the habit of taking out a license for his carriage on the 20th, and it was only an oversight that he had left his dog license over until that date.—Patrick Flannagan7 Inland Revenue officer, stated that he did not think the defendant had any hatention of defrauding the Inland Revenue—Mr. Swift thereupon asked the Benet] to dismiss the case as the Inland Revenue officer did not think there was any intent to defraud—The Bench ordered defendant to pay the costs.---Wm. Alker. farmer, Ilaydock, was summoned with being the owner of four doge and not having a license for three.—The defendant main- tained that he was exempted from taking out a license in the case of two of the dogs, produced a license for one dog, and stated that the remaining dog was not his property, and that it had been sent to its owner.—A fine of 103 and cost was imposed.--Charles Shaw, undertaker, Legh- street, Earlestown, was summoned for keeping a dog with- out a license.—The de'endant asserted that he only got the dog on the Wednesday, and be took out alicense for it on the following Monday, but the inspector called between those days.—He was fined 5s and costs.

.BIIDD N DEATH OF MR. W. H. DAGNALL, of CROSS LANE —Earlestown has lost one of irs most respectsd and highly esteemed inhabitants by the death of M. William Hugh Dagnall, of Cross-lane, an event which occurred with painful suddenness on Tuesday afternoon. The news of that gentleman's death came as a surprise to his friends and acquaintances, and many were disinclined to believe the report, so strong, healthy, and hearty did he seem but a few day previous. Mr. Dagnall, as manager of the engineering works of Messrs. T. and T. Vicars, has had a close and in- timate connection with Earlestown for the past 18 years, and his loss will be felt in almost all circles of society. When a boy the deceased gentleman entered the works of Messrs. Vicars' at Liverpool, and by steady perseverance and attention to duty be gradually rose from one position to another, until 18 years ago, when the firm opened their extensive branch works at Narlestown, Mr. Dagnall was appointed manager, and the establishment virtually placed under his sole charge. Since that time Mr. Dagnall has grown in public favour and he was a leading man of the district. Sorne years age he was appointed one of the trustees Of the Druids lodge at Earlestown; he was a shareholder and a member of the committee of the Earles- town and District Liberal Club ; and also bad the honour of being appointed captain of the bowling de- partment of the Newton-le-Willows Cricket and Bow- ling Club. On Tuesday week Mr. .Dagnall complained of a slight chill or cold, but nothing serious was antici- pated. On the following day, however, he found himself unable to continue at his occupation, and he returned home. Dr. T. N. Patterson was called in on the Thursday, but not- withstanding the skill and attention of that gentleman Mr. Dagnall appeared to become worse. He was not confined to bed, however, and it was not until 4 o'clock on Monday aftei- noon that he took to his bed. On Tuesday morning it was noticed that he was much worse and was rapidly sinking, whereupon the additional services of Dr. Starkie Smith, of Warrington, were solicited, and Dr. Smith put in an appearance early in the afternoon. It was too late to be of any avail, however, for death put an end to the patient's illness at five o'clock. Mr. Dagnall was IStit in his 47th year, and his demise created a very sid feeling throughout the district. His wife died some eight or ten years ago, and, as Mr. Dagnall now leaves seven children—three sons and four daughters—compara- tively young, much sympathy is expressed for them in , their bereavement. The interment will take place at Wan- ; grave Church this (Saturday) afternoon.

ALTERATIONS AT Sr. PETER'S CHURCH, NEWTON.—For a considerable time past the belfry of St. Peter's Church Newton, has been in an unsafe condition, while its design has not given general satisfaction to the worshippers. Im- provements are consequently being carried out in order to render that part of the edifice more safe, and improve Its appearance. The old belfry has been pulled down, end a new one is being erected in its place, and the front Ef the church will be put in a thorough state of repair. The cost is expected to be about £l4O, which is the amount of the con- tract of Mr. Pennington of Earlestown. to whom the work has been let. The usual services in the church are not in- terrupted by the alterations. THE &anus-rows GOSPEL MISSION.—Mrs, Caroline John, of Bolton, the esteemed temperance worker, preached special sermons in the Co-operative Hall. Earlestown, on Sunday last, in aid of the funds of the Gospel Mission. There was a large attendance at each service. On Monday evening Mrs. John delivered a temperance lecture in the same hall, and there was a fair attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Clarke. Mrs. John referred to the work of the temperance reformers in the past, and impressed upon her hearers the necessity for continued exertions in the future as there was still a great work to be done. During the evening several melodies were sung by the choir, and at the close of the meeting about a dozen persons signed the pledge. ESSAY ON "OUR NEIGHBoIIR."—A meeting in connec- tion with the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the lodgeroom, Bridge-street, on Tuesday even- ing, when Brother George E Warburton, W C T, presided. One new member was initiated, after which arrangements were made for a series of meetings next week to be addressed by Mr. R. W. Duxbury, of Oldham. In constquence of these meetings it was decided that the lodge should meet next Thursday inetead of on Monday. Brother A. W. Kenyon then read an excellent paper on "Our neighbour," in which he pointed out that the duty of all was to help their neighbours and treat them in a way they would like to Ibe treated themselves. There were many ways in which they could help their neighbours; by a kind look, word, or action, or a little assistance in time of need, and in conclu- ding he asked them to be true to their professions. An in- teresting discussion afterwards took place, and a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the essayiet. THE ALLEGED KIDNAPPING OP CHILDREN: RECOVERY OF THE MISSING LAD.—After disappearing under circum- stances of a somewhat mysterious character about a week ago, the two children, Joseph Hilton, 61 years of age. and Richard Buckley, 31, the parents of both of whom reside in Rathbone-etreet, Earlestown, have now been recovered. I It will be remembered that a fortnight ago the two children were playing in the street and were suddenly missed. A vigilant search was instituted and enquiries were made at ' all likely places, without avail ; and the opinion gradually gained ground that they had been kidnapped by gipsies. The youngest of the two lads was handed over to his par- ents by the town-crier or St. Helens on the following Wed- nesday, an explanation being given that he had been picked up in the streets of St. Helens on the afternoon of the day (Saturday) on which he was missed. Ehe lad gave a rambling statement that some men who lived in a van or cart with baskets and "Sticks," had taken on his missing companion. Efforts were subsequently made to ascertain the whereabouts of the 'tribe of gipsies," whom it was supposed had conveyed the lad Hilton from his home and parents. Up to Thursday morning (this week) however nothing definite was ascertained about him, although many rumours were afloat as to the lad's treatment and the direction in which it was supposed his captors had travelled. On the morning of the day named, however, Mr. Hilton re- ceived a letter from the authorities of the Browlow Hill Workhouse, Liverpool, stating that his son was in that in- stitution, and asking for his removal. Mr. Hilten accord- ingly went there, and was happy indeed that the "lost one " had been found Mr. Hilton, we are informed, there ascer- tained that the lad had been in the workhouse since the night of the 24th ult. (upon which day he was missed), that he gave his right name and address, and whom his father was. It would therefore seem that there had been a censurable neglect on the part 'of some official in not ac- quainting the parents of the 6hild's presence in the " big house." The lad, it is stated, ±plains that when walking along the road he left the boy Buckley "looking at some birds," and he did not again se'e him. He says that he had a ride on a cart drawn by three horses, hut at present the adventure of the two lads is a little mysterious. It is need- less to add that it has formed a theme of conversation throughout the district.

ANTI-VACcINATION AT EARLESTOWN.—PROSE- -CU TIONS AT NEWTON. The prosecution of a number of persons for refusing to comply with the law relating to vaccination, at the Newton Town Hall, en Saturday last, created considerable interest throughout Earlestown. The summonses were issued by the Warrington Board of Guardians, and Mr. J. C. Sutton, their clerk, appeared to prosecute. The magistrates on the Bench were Rebett Houghton and Thomas J. Gillespie, Esqs. On the first case being called, Mr. B. Harrison (one of the defendants) asked to have all the cases adjourned, so that their representative could attend, but the magistrates refused to grant the application, and the cases were proceeded with. Alfred McWatt, of 111, Earle-street, Earlestown, was first called upon. He was charged that "being the father of a certain child named Joseph McWatt, born 6th January, 1884, unlawfully did neglect to take, or Cause to be taken, the said child to be vaccinated, according to the provisions of the Vaccination Act, 1817, and that you did not within three months after the birth of the said child take or cause to be taken to the public vaccinator or the vaccinationdistrict of Newton, in which it was then resident, hoe ctused it to he vaccinated by some registered medical practitioner, you not rendering a reasonable excuse for your said neglect, con- trary to the 29i1 sectiou of the said Act"— The defendant asked that the case should be adjeurned se that a Mr. Booth, of Leicester, could appear on his behalf.—The Clerk : Is be a solicitor 7—The defendant did not reply, and the Bench said they could not adj men the case.—Mr. Sutton thereupon proceeded to state that the summons was served before ten o'clock on the previous Thursday morn- ing, and no injustice could be done by the decieiohs of the Bench. The 16th section of the Vaccination Act, 1867, re- quired every patent to take a child before a public vac- cinator or before a private medical practitioner, in order that such child could be vaccinated, and the 29th section of the same statute read that every parent who should neglect to take such child, or cause it to be taken to be vaccinated ac- cording to the provisions of that Act should be guilty of an offence, and on conviction liable to a penalty not exceeding 203. It would be worse than useless to conceal the fact that there was an organised determination within the Earlestown portion of Newton to dispute the law, and it was suggested that a gentleman should represent the defendants, and who he (Mr. Sutton) believed was not a solicitor, not for the purpose of showing there were any special reasons why the law had not been complied with but upon some general grounds. Whether it was wise or unwise that children should be vaccinated the Legislature had in their wisdom determined it should be done. They required Beards of Guardians to see that the law was carried out, and they were all without discretion in the matter. He would require to bring a batch of cases at consecutive petty sessions before that objection to the law was thoroughly purged eat, but the Guardians were acting with moderation in the matter, and would not press for a penalty if the parents would consent to leave the children vaccinated within a given period.—Alfred Cooper, the vac- cination officer, was then called, and be stated that he had called upon the defendant to see why he had not had his child vaccinated. The defendant replied that be objected to vaccination.—The Bench asked if the defendant would consent to have the child vaccinated P—The defendant: I decline to answer.—A fine of 20s and costs was imposed. Samuel Stanley, of 109, Earl-st was summoned on a sim- ilar charge, in respect of his child Samuel,born 29th August, 1883.—Defendant pleaded not guilty, and said he had com- plied with the spirit of the law but not the lettet—The Clerk : We want the letter.—The defendant: You cannot have both—(a laugh)--The Chairman: You object to have , the child vaccinated P—Defeadant :1 decline to answer your question.—The Chairman: Very well, you will be fined 20s and costs.—Defendant: Thank von very much. John Clarke, ironmonger, 15, Bridge-street, was sum- moned for being "the father of a certain child called Alice Clarke, born April 7th, 1876, and that the above mentioned child, who is under 14 years, has not been duly vaccinated, that notice has, pursuant to sec. 31, Vaccination Act, 1867, been duly given to you to procure its being vac- cinated, and that the said notice has been disregarded." —The Clerk: Are you guilty or not guilty The defen- dant: I admit no offence.—Alfred Cooper, vaccination officer, stated that when he called to see why defendant's child had not been vaccinated the defendant said he ob- jected to vaccination.—Mr. Sutton: I ask for an order for the child to be vaccinated.—The defendant said he objected to vaccination on two grounds: first it was no protection against disease, and sEcondly it was injurious to health and life. He dare not trust it —The Chairman: That is only your opinion, I suppose 7—Defendant: Well, sir, it is from 30 years' experience and study.—The Bench said they would make an order for the defendant to have the child j vaccinated within three months—Defendant: Whatever I the consequences are I dare not trust it. Joseph Emmett, of 304, Earle-street, was summoned that he was "the father of a certain child called Minnie Priscilla i Emmett, born March 19th, 1878, and that the above men- tioned child, who is under the age of 14 years. has not been successfully vaccinated; that notice has, pursuant to sec. 31 of the Vaccination Act, 1867, been duly given to you to pro- , cure its being vaccinated, and that the said notice has been I disregarded."—The defendant objected to Mr. Sutton con- ducting the prosecution, and maintained that he had not been served with the proper legal notices before the proceed- I legs were commenced.—After some remarks from Mr. Sutton, the Bench over-ruled the objections.—The Chair- man: Do you still decline to have this child vaccinated ? Defendant: I decline to answer it—Au order wee made for the child to be vaccinated within 21 days. A similar summons against John Prescott, draper, Legh- street, was adjourned until the next sessions on account of his inability to attend. Alfred McWatt (already fined 203 and costs on one sum- mons) was further summoned on a charge similar to that against Joseph Emmett, and the Bench made an order for the I child to be vaccinated within 21 days. Charles Albert Owen, of Bridge-street, was summoned for a similar offence in respect to two children.—An order was made as in tee last case. William Gdmour, of 306, Earle-street, was called upon to answer a similar charge —He took objection to Mr. Sutton as the prosecutor, and asked for. the production of the minute book of the Board of Guardians showing his instruc- tion to conduct the prosecution.—Mr. Sutton pro- ceeded to read, a written extract from the minute '

book, and the Bench stated that that question had been previously decided.—The defendant added that he did not wish to place the magistrates and Mr. Sutton in a dilemma, but ho felt satisfied that Mr. Sutton was in the wrong,and he thought he (Mr. Sutton) would after- wards be made to appear foolish in the cyes of the publin. He (the defendant) had suffered very much from vaccina- tion, and he asked the Bench in. the name of common ilell9e and charity, if it was their child, aealthy and strong, would they have it vaccinated ? They did not want to bring disease or disorder into the country, but wanted to purify the children and make them healthy.—The Chairmen: The law says the children must be vaccinated whether we like it or not —An order was made for the child to be vaccinated within 21 days. James Barr, of 22, Legh-street, was summoned for a similar teff ,nce. and as he would not consent to have the child vaccinated, the Bench made an order for it to be vats- cinated within 21 days. Wm. Whitley Owen, butcher, Bridge-street : James Grim-, shaw..l77, Legh-street -, John Latham, 41, Sankey-street and Richard Higgins, Market-street, were summoned on similar charges, and all refused to consent to have their children vaccinated, and the Bench made orders similar tO those in the previous cases.—John Carlin (sweep) pleaded guilty to the charge against him, and said he would con- sent to have his childrea vaccinated. He would do any- thing for the sake of peace and quietness. (Laughter.) An tzder was made for the child to be vaccinated within 21 days.—Richard Parr, clogger, Oxford-street; Thomas Hy. Hipwood, 10, Chandbs-street ; Benjamin Harrison 2909 Earle-street; and Alexander Foster, of 19, Regent-street, were summoned for similar offences, and all refused to have their childreN vaccinated.—Mr. Harrison said he believed man was the noble work of God, and that God made hint impervious to disease if he obeyed physiological laws. The Clerk : You know what the law is I believe. —Mr. Itarrison : I don't believe the law has been rightly tried this morning. .He subsequently took objection to Mr. Sutton's appearance as prosecutor, and maintained that due I notices had not been served.—An order was made in each I case for the children to be vaccinated.

GOLD)RNE. THE EDUCATION ACT.—At the Newton Petty Sess'ons, on Saturday, Joseph Smith and Edward Young, of Golborne, were each fined 53 for neglecting to send their children to school as required by the Elementary Education Act. A CAUTION TO YoUTES.—On Saturday last at the New- ton Town Hall two youths named Peter McLoughlin and John Callaghan were summoned for running a race in nude state on the highway at Golborne on the 23rd May.— P.C. Ratcliffe deposed that about 2-30 on the afternoon of the date named he was en duty in Old Mill-lane, Golborne, and saw the defendants running a race naked along the highway. There were about a dozen boys and girls there, and two ladies who were coming along the lane turned back. There were a good many complaints about such conduct.— The Chairman: It is a most disgraceful thing for boys to run about naked. You will Is fined 5s and costs each: CrOLBORNE CASES AT NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.-00 Saturday at the Newton Town 13411 Mary Ann Malone was bound over to keep the peace for six months for lasing threatening language to Ann Houghton on the 13th May. Patrick Brogan, for being drunk and refusing to quit tbe Sir Charles Napier, Golborne, on the 13th May, and breaking two windows, was ordered to pay a fine of 7a GI and costs and 3s au as damages.—John Blake was fined lOs and costa for assaulting Margaret Hanbury, a widow, on the 13th ult.—Bridget Hansbury was summoned by Ann Noughton for doing damage to the amount of Is 81 to one of the win- dows of her dwelling-house, and she was ordered to pay the damage.

ATTEMPTED HIGHWAY ROBBERY AT LOWTON.-At the Leigh Petty Sesrions, on Monday, William Morris, a charged soldier, was charged with attempting to rob Ann Gill, of Lowton, on the highway, near Pennington Hall, about ten o'clock on Friday night—Complainant stated that she was accosted by the prisoner, who asked her if she had any money. She stated that she had not, and a: that moment a gentleman came round the corner, and prisoner left her. He afterwards seized her by the shoulder and frightened her very much.—ln answer to the Bench the prisoner said it was altogether a case of mistaken identity; but the woman positively swearing, that she was not mill- taken, the magistrates committed him to one month's Bo" prisonment with hard labour.

UPSETTING A DONKEY AND CARL—Befor e R. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie, Esq., at the Newton Town Hall, on Sat- tirday, George Bate, a young man, was summoned by Elizabeth Barlow for damaging a wooden stall, a quantity of glasses, and certain articles exposed for sale; and ale° injuring a donkey and cart to the amount of £2.—The com- plainant stated that she had a stall at the Crowning of the May Queen festivities, at Golborne, on the 10th May. The defendant, under the influence of drink, came out of a public-house, and without any warning got hold of the donkey and cart and " tippled" them over. He also upset the stall, and scattering the sweets and icetcream on the roadway.—The Bench imposed a fine of 5s and costs, and ordered the defendant to pay 20a as damages in addition. ACTION AGAINST A GOLEORNH MANUFACTURER —On Friday, at the Leigh County Court, Margaret Jane Scholes, a young married woman, sued Messrs. Brewis and Co.. COUOTI manufacturers, Golberne, for the SIDE of £2 2s. 9ela, wages alleged to have been earned by the plaintiff—Toe de- fendant set up a counter-claim of 7a, and paid the differ- ence into court.—lt was admitted that the money WAS drier but the plaintiff left her work on two occasions without per- mission. The understanding at the mills between the masters and the servants was that each side should give Or take 14 days' notice. On the 2od April she left her wora for three hours and the whole of the next day. Oa the 140 April she again absented herself the whole day, and likewise on the 16th and 17th, and she was told certain deductions would be made from her wages.—Plaintiff, in answer to HIS Honour, said all she wanted was what she had earned.—His Honour said he thought Mrs. Scholes was right in leaving when she was told to go unless she submitted to the deduc- tion, and gave judgment for ss. beyond the amount of £1 15e. Pd. paid into court by the defendants. ASSAULT ON A POLICEMAN.—James Mullighan. a respect- ably dressed man, was charged at the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednesday, with being drunk and disorderly in Golborne, on t'.e previous Saturday, and with assaulting P.C. Ratcliffe whilst in the execution of his dany.—Tlie. constable stated that at about six o'clock on the evening 0, Saturday he was in High-street, Goltorne, in plain clothes, when be saw the prisoner and another man very drunk and disorderly. The two men commenced quarrelling and light- ing together. Witness eeparated them and told them that he was a police officer, and they replied, "Yes, we know you M." Witness then asked them to go away qeietlY, but they commenced fighting again. Be once more interposed, and the prisoner struck him several times on the leg. seized. him by the throat, and tore his scarf off. Prisoner kicked and struggled all the way to the police station, :and if some of the pane had not assisted witness he should have bean badly assaulted, as the other man, who had effected his escape, also assaulted 11;ni with a stick—Prisoner, who said that he was drunk and did not know anything about what her had done, was flood 10a and costs, or fourteen days in default. WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES.—Whit-Monday passed cfr IC Frodsham much in the usual manner, and the pretty little village was largely patronised by those in search of pleasure and recreation though it was considered by many residents that the number of visitors showed a slight falling off when compared with the numbers of previous years. A consider- able number of Warrington people spent the holiday at Frodsham, but the visitors included many from a .consider able distance. The main street was for a time transformed into a fair ground, and whilst the juveniles contented theta: selves with aerial ascents in shaky looking swing boats, the adults indulged in the more manly amusement provided by . the various shooting galleries which did a brisk business. There were, however, a few adults whose dignity did not resent the swing boats, and a few juveniles who aspired to , shoulder the rifles. On the whole everything passed off merrily in the fair, and bands of music gave ,hoice speci- mens of their skill. The local members of the Blue Ribbon Army held a demonstration, and paraded the streets accom- panied by a band, and headed by a member on horseback, who looked as though a Whit-Monday procession were any- thing but an enjoyable thing to him. The quadruped ap- peared by far the most at ease. The procession was of a considerable size, and the members of it entered into the spirit of the demonstration with great entbusia,ra. In con- nection with the army a tea was held in the afternoon, and in the evening a public meeting was addressed by various temperance advocates. The meeting was conducted b 9 " Captain " Kerr, who had the arrangements of the day is hand. Numbers of people climbed the hill overlooking the village, whence a magnificent view is obtained.
Mr. W. H. Gladstone, M.P., the eldest son of the Premier, and now proprietor of the Hawarden estate, attained trig 44th birthday on Saturday.

The fine plantation of Orbliston, near FochabrF, Alor• deensbire, belonging to the Duke of Richmond and Liordon. was almost totally destroyed by fire on Monday. A very large number of Lancashire volunteers on Satur- day went under canvas for what is rapidly b-c•-,rnirn: cognized, if not already established, as their annual Whitsantide encampments.

MURDER AND SUICIDE BY A WIDNES WOMAN. A shocking tragedy occurred on Saturday last, when the wife of a Whines chemical labourer drowned herself and her infant, and attempted to drown an elder daughter, at a secluded part of the canal about two miles distance from Widnes, in the direction of Fidler's Ferry. The victims of the tragedy are Margery Gore, forty years old, wife of William Gore, 57, Davies-street, Widnes, and their child Sarah Ann Gore, who was three years of age. The elder daughter, as will be seen from the particulars given in evi- dence at the inquest that was subsequently held, had a miraculous escape, which was mainly attributable to the coolness and determination which she exercised when Placed in such a perilous position. It appears that on Saturday evening Mrs. Gore told her daughter Mary Ellen that she was going to visit a cousin at Penketh, as ehe felt in better health then than she had done for some time. The husband was not then at horn., and Mrs. Gore, with her two children, procseded to Penketh by railway. Arriving there she inquired for the house of her cousin, and then pro- ceeded to walk along the canal side for some distance until the party arrived near what is called Crosby Bridge, a part of the canal where a bridge has once be,n provided, and is now done away with. It was near this spot that the tragic occurrence took place. It is stated that whilst walking I on the canal bank Mrs. Gore engaged in perfectly rational conversation with her daughter Mary Ellen, who was carry- ing the baby, making several remarks expressive of admira- tion of the surrounding country. When near the bridge mentioned she asked her daughter to give her the baby. The daughter did so, and almost immediately the mother suddenly threw herself and two children into the water,l which is of a considerable depth at the spot indicated. When in the water the unfortunate woman said " It is better that we should all die together than be parted again." The eldest daughter courageously worked her way to the! side of the canal again, and succeeded by great exertion in getting out of the water, by which time her mother and sister had sunk. She then hastened to a house at Fidler's Ferry, where a man named Wright resides, and informed ' him of what had taken place. The alarm having thus been given, a search was made for the bodies which were dis- covered. soon afterwards, Had the daughter not been able to effect her escape, the affair would have been enshrouded in mystery, and probably the particulars of how they came by 1 their death would never have been known. As soon as the facts of the sad affair became known, much sympathy was expressed for the husband and other relatives of the deceased woman, and from the first—from the distressing circum- stances of the case—no doubt was entertained that the rash act vus committed whilst acting under the impulse of insanity. Mrs. Gore had always been in poor health, and Was at the time of her death approaching her confinement. I At her last confinement she suffered greatly, and her mind became so much deranged that she was sent to the Bainhiti Asylum, where she remained a patient for something like 18 Months. It is supposed that the anticipations of the suffer- ing that was probably in store for her, combined with the extremely delicate state of her health, had completely un- hinged the poor woman's mind. THE INQUEST, On Tuesday afternoon Mr. Husband, deputy county coroner, held an inquest at the Cuerdley Cross arms, Cuerd- ley, into the deaths of Mrs. Gore and her infant, when the subjoined evidence was adduced : William Gore, 57, Davies-street, Widnes, a labourer at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson, said that the bodies seen by the jury were those of his wife Marjory, and his daughter Sarah Ann Gore. His wife was forty years old last birthday and his daughter tbree years old last March. They both lived with him. When his wife was last confined she took it very seriously and went out of her mind, having to go to an asylum. She was for eighteen months in It dn- hill asylum, which she left on the 16th March, 1883. Since then she had occasionally been a little excited in her man- ner, but not so much so as to cause suspicion. She had never threatened to do away with herself, but last week she said that she wished someone would put her out of her misery. She had been very ill and was expecting her con- finement every day. When she said-that she wished some- one would put her out of her misery she was speaking to herself, but witness heard her. She had been delicate for years and had said that she did not think that she had had a day's good health in her life. About four o'clock on Saturday afternoon he left home and left his wife and family • in their usual health. When he was leaving his wife asked what time he would be back, and he replied about 8-30 or 9 o'clock. She said "we might be gone to bed then, you had better take the key with you." Witness did so, and that was the last he saw of his wife and the child alive. He heard of her death about mid- flight. He had given his wife his wages as usual and did not know of anything having occurred that afternoon to vex her. Witness thought that his wife had been unnerved by the suffering that she anticipated, as she was rapidly near- ing her confinement. She was always fond of her chil- dren. Sarah Ann Whitfield, wife of Thomas Whitfield, a carter, living at Penketh, deposed that at 7.45 on Saturday evening she was at the London and North-Western Station at Widnes, when she saw the deceased woman and spoke to her. Mrs. Gore had two children with her. Witness was waiting for the Penketh train and Mrs. Gore said that she was waiting to go to the Ferry, meaning the station for Penketh. Wit. fleas again saw her at Fidler's Ferry and left her on the platform. They bid each other "good night" and witness went home. The bodies of the woman and child that she had just viewed she could identify as those of the woman and child she had met as described. The elder girl she had seen waiting outside to give evidence. Mary Ellen Gore, living with her father, William Gore, said that of late her mother had not been in good health. About a quarter of an hour after her father went out her mother said that she was going to see her Cousin at Penketh. Mrs. Gore had never been to see her cousin, who had lived in Penketh seven years, before. Witness did not think it strange that her mother should wish to do so on Saturday evening, as she had said that she felt 'better then than she had done for some time and that she might not be so well another time. Witness, her mother, and the child then went to Fidler's Ferry where they crossed the railway and went down the canal side. Witness then thought her mother was going to her cousin's house. On the way Mrs. Gore spoke about the country, remarking how nice it looked. She ap- peared all right in her manner and was not at all strange. They walked about a mile distance from the station, and Mrs. Gore was talking all the time to witness, princi- pally about th 3 country. Witness was carrying her little sister, and her mother turned to take it from her, saying that she had better give it to her. Witness gave her mother the child. Her mother, with the child in her arms, then sud- denly put her arms round witness, and threw them all in. Witness was walking close to the water. When they were - in the water witness said "Oh mother," and the deceased woman said " It is better for us all to die together than to he parted. again." The water was deep. It was as they were coming up the first time that her mother used the words mentioned, which witness supposed were in reference to the asylum. The second time they rose her mother pulled her back again as she was struggling to get to the side, which witness succeeded in doing with great difficulty, after rising a third time. When she got to the side her mother and sister had sunk. It was then about 9-30 or 10 o'clock, and she at once made off for the nearest place that she could for assistance. When her mother wished to go anywhere either witness or her father had always accom- panied her. About five or six weeks ago witness heard her Mother say "I wish I were drowned." David Wright, living at Fidler's Ferry, said that on Saturday evening the previous witness same to his house with her clothing drenched, and from what she said he went with her on the canal side and got the bodies of her mother and sister out of the water. They were both dead. They were taken to the Cuerdley Cross Arms. The Coroner said that they had heard first of all the evi- dence of the husband, who himself was not present on the Vat when the affair happened. He (the husband) seemed to have hid no suspicion whatev3r that there was anything the matter with his wife, beyond what she usually suffered, and he had no suspicion at the time that she was excited or

in mental dread of her approaching confinement. In fact the daughter who was with her at the time did not seem to think that there was anything the matter with the mother mentally. She seemed as usual, and conducted herself rea- sonably, and although she was troubled in her mind the daughter did not appear to have had the slightest suspicion that there was anything seriously the matter with her mother. It was quite possible that the woman did not an- ticipate or did not intend anything of the sort until alndost when it occurred. There was no doubt that for some time the woman had been insane, because she had been in a lunatic asylum for eighteen months, and there was no doubt that the woman was of weak and delicate health, as the hus- band told them that she used to say that she thought she had never had a day's good health in her life. That was hard for any person to have to say. This woman appeared to be growing worse, and, above all things, she was suffering from a fearfully painful gathering. What was more, she was greatly excited at confinement, and the last time she was confined it rendered her so weak, he supposed physically as well as mentally, as to necessitate her removal to an asylum. That seemed to have played very much upon her mind, for when she suddenly took the whim of going into the the water with her children, she said, "It is better for us all to die together than be parted again." She appeared to have had a dread of confinement, and of having to go ta the asylum, and as she was with her children she took that opportunity of all going out of the world together. It was quite possible that as she walked along the bank a sudden whim seized her, and she jumped into the water. Of course they all knew how it was to stand upon a height and look down when they were seized with a desire to throw themselves down. As this woman looked down it might have made her weak head giddy, and thus caused her to commit the act. Mary Ann Gore told them very graphically the whole of the circumstances, still he thought she had rather stretched her imagination. That was about the only term he could use. People could not very well converse as they were in the water, and as a rule they cried out; but this girl seemed to have been wonderfully collected. She told them how she got back to the water's edge, and all that,be could say was that moat people would have lost all control under such cir- cumstances. People, as a rate, when they got into the. water, lost all control, but this girl came to the surface and managed with great struggling to get to the water's edge. For that she deserved great credit, and the only thing that struck him as strange was that the girl, so intelligent, sheuld net have had some suspicion of her mother's sanity winm they went to Penketh that night However, she was but a little girl, and might not have any thought about such a thing. He did not know of any other verdict open to them with respect to the child than that it came by its death through the act of its mother—that she was drowned in the canal by her mother, the mother then being in a state of unsound mind. With regard to the mother, the only ver- dict appeared to be that she committed suicide whilst in- sane. • The jury returned verdicts accordingly.

div.head: WARRINGTON IRONWORKERS' SPORTS.
div.p: WARRINGTON IRONWORKERS' SPORTS.

I The ironworkers of Warrington held their second annual amateur athletic festival on Saturday last, in a geld adjoin- ing St. James's Church, I atchford. The weather was every- thing that could be desired for such a festival, and this, I combined with an excellent programme, drew together a I very large gathering of spectators, it being estimated that , the number of persons present ranged between 2,000 and 3,000. Every arrangement had evidently been made for the cmvenience of the onlookers, and for the orderly carrying Oat of the programme and as a conseqeence everything passed off in the most satisfactory manner. The handi- capping of competitors appeared to have been judiciously' made, as there was a larger than usual proportion of closely ' I contested races. St. Paul's Brass Band was in attendance, and played selections during the afternoon. The surplus proceeds of the sportsOt may be mentioned, were to go in aid of the Infirmary and Dispensary. The following were the officials :-Committee: Messrs. B. Rudge (chairman), J. Griffiths, R. Mills, W. Bradbury, J. Ferry, M. Beswick, G. Perry, W. Lee, E. Atherton, J. L•mket, E. Gibson, W. Allen, J. Allen, J. PemlJerton, and J. Waring. Judges: Messrs. J. B. Yeomans, J. Griffiths, G. Legge, and F. Gib- son. Referee : Mr. T. Morris. Clerk of course: Mr. W. ; Allen. Starter: Mr. G. Perry. Handicapper for open events: Mr R. Andrews. Handicapper for closed events: The Committee. Treasurer: Mr. R. Mills. Hon. sec. : Mr. C. E. Bunch. Amongst those present on the grand sand were the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Harri- son), Mr. C. and Mrs. Broadbent, the Rev. R. Filcher, 8.A., and Mr. T. Paterson. ONE HUNDRED HORSES BURNED TO DEATH.—A fire , broke out about ten o'clock on Saturday night in the Glas- gow Western Tramway stables in North-street and Bishop- , street. Over a hundred horses were stabled in the upper floors, the cars being below, and only a few of the animals were rescued, the gangway communicating with their stalls having been destroyed by the filmes. At 11-30 the roof and walls fell in, and the fire raged till past midnight. The damage is estimated at £20,000, of which £6,000 represents the value of the horses. The loss is believed to be covered by insurance. A fire also occurred in Edinburgh in the City Tan Works on Saturday night, and left nothing standing but the bare wall. The loss is put at from £29,000 to £30,000. THE PIONEER OF THE CLEVELAND IRON TRADE.—On Monday, Sir J. W. Pease, M.P., unveiled opposite the Mid- dlesborough Exchange a bronze statue of the late Mr. John Vaughan, who, with Mr. Bolckow, was the pioneer of the Cleveland iron trade, and originated the firm bearing their name, the largest of the kind in the world, Mr. John Marley, who was with Mr. Vaughan when they discovered ironstone near Middlesborough thirty-four years since, de- tailed the incident. The member for the borough, the Mayor and Corporation, and the leading men connected with the iron trade were present, also a vast assemblage. The statue, by Lawson, cost £2,000, which was publicly subscribed. Ds.
