MB. BRADLAUGH AND PENsroNs.—The Chancellor e the Exchequer has informed Mr. Bradlaugh that he may if he wishes be formally heard against the commutatica of the Marlborough and Penn pensions. The bon. member for Northampton bas therefore applied to the Treasury to fix a date so that he may produce the evidence of his allega- tions.

OUR MAN-o'-WAR'S MEN.—How great a change has come about in the habits of our man-o'war's men since the old days when "leave ashore" was so commonly the signal for racket and license may be seen in Governor O'Brien's recent report, wherein details are furnished of the visit last year of the reserve squadron of eight Btitish ironclads under Rear- Admiral Sir A. Hoskins to the island of Heligoland. The vessels, says Mr. O'Brien, were visited by almost the entire population, and if their appearance and power were sources of admiration and wonder, the conduct-of the men who landed„to the number df nearly 2,0Q0, without the slightest irregularity or drunkennets, elicittsi equal praise on all sides. The good effect of each a visit, adds the Governor, cannot be overrated, especially seeing that, while our flag has heretofore hardly ever been shown here, there is rely a week that we have not foreign men-of-war in our roads. A few days later the German squadron, of four similar ships, paid, we are told, the island a visit; but though the officers landed, the men were not permitted to go ashore. Ateerilmet CLERICAL IMPOSTER.—At wandsworth Police Court, 014 Monday, John Henry Jenkins, a middle.aged man, was brought' up on a warrant, charged with stealing money from the missionary boxes belonging to-the Congre- gational Chapel, Park-creseut, Clapham, of which Mr. Samuel Morley, M.P. was one of the trustees.—Mr.Batelelor, from the offices of the Solicitor te the Treasury, prosecuted, and said the prisoner had pretended to be an ordained clergy- man.—James English, chapel keeper and deacon of the Con- gregational Chapel, Park-crescent, said at the endof 1882, the prisoner was there as an assistant preacher. they bad boxes in the Sunday echool for the collection of money from the children fer.the London Missionary Society, and when not in use they were kept in a locked cupboard, The prisoner came with- the key of the cupboard and counted the money in the boxes, amounting to upwards of £2. He took the money, saying he would take it to Miss Fulcher, the teacher. The prisoner remained two or three weeks afterwards, and then went away suddenly.—The prisoner, in reply to the magistrates, said he was guilty.—Mr. Shiel then committed , him for trial.—Mr. Batchelor said there was another case ' against the prisoner of stealing five watches and two clocke, but all the pawnbrokers were not present, and he could not complete it—A formal remand was granted. WARRINGTON V. CHRETHA.M.—This match was played on Arrney Ground,. Warrington, on Faturday, and resulted in a victory for the home team by a wicket and 85 ruts. Warring- ton had only a weak team to oppose the visitors, but Fair- clench eec'ded to send the Cheatham men In CO bat. Sinclair and Redferie first faced the bowling of W. Wallington and C. G. Lawton. The batsmen played very cautlously, for a time while 16 runs were put on. W. Wallington then got a ball to graze the off-stump of Sinclair. J. Tinker came next, and run- wetting proceeded more quickly. He hit four fours and two singles before C. G. Lawton clean bowled him. W TAcer gave little trouble, as did also Ogle The latter jumped out to drive one of C. G. Lawton's slows, and was cleverly stumped by Armstrong for his temerity. T. Dr. Mouritz was in favour of making an ar portant principle involved e matter.—Tke Chairman considered that there was an im- rangement with the medical practitioners in the town to 'in the matter. It was for the notify to the Board any cases coming under their observe- Board to say whetherthey would discass it that day or tion ; but it was pointed out by Mr. Bowyer that not one- adjourn it to some future meeting.—Mr. Pritchard : The question is have we had any grievance in the town with half the patients suffering from the disease were attended by respect to the Salvation Army ? lam not aware that there medical men, and the suggestion was, therefore, not adopted. is any grievance, and I propose that the letter lie on the The idea, too, of closing the schools for a certain period met table.—M'. P. Speakman seconded the motion. He did not with no favour, and it was eventually decided to address a see how they as a Board could take any action with regard letter to the school managers and teachers drawing their to the m atter, and when they considered the good that had attention to the outbreak, and asking them to inform the been done in the town by the Salvation Army—he was not School Board officials of any cases of scarlet fever that came speaking from hearsay, but from cases that had come under under their notice. The school attendance officers would his personal supervision—he thought it would be a great then at once visit the home or homes of the children, wrong for the Board to support the lettee that had been read and take steps for preventinn them attending school. at all. He therefore seconded the motion.—Mr. Shaw did nor think the matter required a resolution. If the Board did not intend to take any action in the matter, the Board should not commit itself to any definite course. Though the inhabitants of the town may not have complained hither- to, they did not know how soon they might begin to do so, and therefore they had better not hind themselves in any way. It all depended whether the Army conducted its ser- vices so as not to annoy the imhabitants or other worship- leers in the district. —The Law Clerk explained that the term lie upon the table meant that the letter could be con- sidered at any time.—The motion was then put to the vote and carried unanimously. SERIOUS OUTBREAK OF SCARLATINA.—Dr. Monritz's (medical officer's) report was read as follows :—The number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 36, representing a death rate of 28 per 1,000 per annum. Of the above deaths nine were due to scarla- tina, six to bronchitis, three heart disease, two dropsy. Croup, marasma, peritonitis, diarrhoea, premature birth, malignant disease, hepatic disease, erysipelas, debility, dis- ease of brain, and homoplysis account for one each. One inquest was held • total deaths 37. Seventeen deaths oc- curred among children five years and under, and eight under one year.—The Chairmau drew the attention of the members to the large number of deaths from scarlatina, observing that it way a very serious matter. Ha asked the medical officer if he could offer any explanation.—The Medical Officer said so far as he was concerned he could give no explanation oil the matter. The Board had not compulsory notification of the infectious diseases, and there- fore he received no intimation of them until he received the registrar's report. At the same time, he suggested whether it would not -be necessary t close the schools for a short period while the epidemic was in existence.—The Chair- man : Have you any information as to the cause of this attack of infectious disease apart from the number of deaths —are there a large number of people suffering from scares- tina?—The Medical Officer said he could not tell that at all. The disease cropped up at Weston in February er March, and since then it had spread to Runcorn.—Mr. Bris- coe: In any particular neighbourhood 2—The Medical Officer: It is spread over all the neighbourhood.—The Sur- veyor said the disease was not of a bad character, but there was a good deal of it.—The Medical Officer: There is too much in the town of Runcorn.-111r. Fisher: Have you any idea where it is more prevalent ?—The Medical Officer: It is all through the town. I don't think it would be fair for me to mention streets where it exists.—Mr. Pritchard observed that it would be a rather serious matter if the schools were to be closed at this particular month of the year, because within a month's time all the schools in the town would be examined by the Government inspector. At the same time, should the medical officer state to the Board that this epidemic was so prevalent that the closing of the schools was a precaution fleet wee absolutely necessary, it would be for the Commissioners and the School Beard, as well as other boards, to seriously consider the matter. If, however, the disease was not so generally prevalent that they could pass the matter over for three weeks, the holi- days would be on, and the schools would be closed for a month certain, and the holidays could be extended without injurious effects to the preparations for the examinations.— Mr. Shaw said he would suggest anoner course in dealing with this matter. Supposing they closed the echo el s they did not prevent the children mixing together, and that was what they wanted to do. He suggested that by some system or other they should get the medical men of the town when they attended a case to give information to the School Board officials, so that the children in the house where the infection existed could be prevented from attend- ing school. Even if the Board had to pay the medical men for the performance of thee extraordinary duties, he be- lieved it was the best way of dealing with the disease. It would be a far better way than closing the eohools and allowing the children to meet and play in the street, spread- the disease everywhere. It would be a great calamity to close the schools, and it would not achieve the object they Inc! in view. He suggested the appointment of a com- mittee.—Me. Pritchard remarked that the School Board had decided no, ffi been theii 6°l'4l.llSM-37 'pelers Very fleYetelY for the next three or four weeks in consequence of the scarlet fever.—Mr. Shaw: My point goes beyond it —The Medical Officer remarked OA a few years ago he wrote a letter making the exact suggestion Mr. Shaw had given utterance to—that no child should be allowed to attend school where one of the family was suffering from scarlet fever. (Hear, bear.) If that was carried out, he thought the disease would not be propagated in the way it was at present. He only suggested to them as Commissioners whether they considered it necasary to close the schools.— Mr. Speakman moved that Messrs. Fisher, Dobson, and the , Chairman of the Board be appointed a committee to confer ' with the School Board and make such arrangements and take such steps as they might deem necessary with the as- sistance of the medical officer to prevent the spread of infec- tious disease in the town.—Mr. Shaw seconded the motion. —The Medical Officer said it would be well if the water cart was impregnated with carbolic acid when watering the streets.—Mr. Speakman : The question is whether we get any water to put the carbolic acid in. That is more like the proposition we want. The streets are in a fearful condition. —The Chairman said it would be well that the committee and the School Board should meet as soon as possible. Scarletina was an insidious disease, spread rapidly, and was dangerous in its effects.—The motion was carried. HIGHWAY AND SANITARY SUBJECTS—The Highway and Sanitary Committee had received a letter from Major Orred's Agent with reference to the unsatisfactory state of the fence in Clifton-road ; and Messrs. Fisher, Norman, White, and Meadowcroft were appointed a sub-committee to consider and report thereon. The Medical Officer of health was re- quested to investigate the offensive smell arising from a sewer in Ellesmere-street, and report thereon. It was re- commended that Mr. Timmins be allowed to lay a telephone pipe across Heath-road, from Mill House to Bridgewater Foundry, on payment of an acknowledgment of Is per annum. The lodging-house and meat inspector reported that he had made several day and night inspections of the lodging-houses; all the registered houses with the exception of one in Mill-street have been cleaned and lime-washed ; that Mrs. Clarkson, of Wilson's row' had been fined 40s and Costs for keeping an unregistered lodging-house; that on the 26th instant he seized and destroyed a quantity of fish which had been left on the Market-ground ; that 224 ashpits have been emptied during the month. The Surveyor re- ported that nuisances bad been abated on beer-house pro- perty in Rutland-street; cottage property in Wellington- street ; Water-closet, Alexandra-buildings; that nothing has been done at the dilapidated cottage property in Back Cooper-street; that scarlatina was still hanging about, dis- infectants being freely used. It was resolved that the Sec- retary write to Mr. Lightburn, agent to Mr. J. A. Johnson, with reference to the insanitary condition of the cottage property in Back Cooper-street. It was recommended that a urinal be fixed near the steps leading from the bridge to the canal bank, and that the work be carried out under the direction and supervision of Mr. White and the surveyor; that the secretary write to Mr. Beswick, agent to the Marquis of Cholmondeley, with raterenc. to the dilapidated condition of the fence on Clif- ton-roed, and as to his promise to continue the road through, not yet carried out. Plans of alterations to cottages in Loch-street, for Me. J. R. E. Birkett ; of sixteen cottages in Speakman-street, for Mr. W. Farrell ; and of four cottages in Egerton-street for the same gentleman were approved. It was decided that the work in Moughlands-road, Princess- street, and Halton-road, as provided in the estimates, be Proceeded with. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Briscoe. GENERAL PI7RPOSES Commirrem—This committee re- commended that Mr. R. Hampson be asked to state the terms upon which he would continue to contract for repair. big the street lamps for a further period of three years from the first September next. They further recommended that the sum of £l5 be accepted in settlement of the Old Quay Fire account. It was resolved that a special meeting of the committee be convened by the chairman to consider the fire brigade charges and other matters connected therewith..._, The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Dobson seconded by Mr. P. Speakman. FINANCE.—The receipts for May were—Market rents and tolls £2O Si 21, slaughter-house rents £23s id, general dis- trict rate £92 18s, total 415 9a 3d. The following accounts were recommended for payment ;—General Purposes Com- mittee £2O 3s 46, Highway and Sanitary Committee £123 104 51, Finance Committee £l6 5s lid, total £219 193 86. It was recommended that the sum of £lO be transferred to the Library Com- mittee. A resolution that the Chairman confer with the Law Clerk and Secretary in the preparation of a detailed statement of the loan transactions of the Board, was passed. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. Fisher. Tem NRDITSOIL Coeirmecr.—Mr. Shaw moved, and Mr. Speakman seconded, the following resolution:—" That it be

WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES Al RUNCORN. Whit-Monday was observed with all the customary fes- tivities and gaieties at Runcorn, which were witnesEed by a greater concourse of people than has been previously kuown. The weather, upon which the success of the day's proceed. ings depends was highly favourable. The rays of the sun were tempered with a genial breeze, and altheugh occa- sionally the clouds gathered somewhat o.ninously there was no rain during the whole of the day, and the evening was as the morning, bright, warm, and genial. Under these cir- cumstances preparations for the day's carnival were early being made. By seven o'clock flags were fluttering on the roofs of many buildings, bands of music were discoursing sweet sounds as they arrived to take part in the festival, and hundreds of young men and youths were already parading the thoroughfares. By nine o'clock people were pouring into the busy little port from all directions. Across the bridge there was a constant stream of gaily dressed sightseers, boats from the Weaver valley discharged living freights, railway trains arrived closely packed, while vehicles of all aorta from the humble farmer's dray to the eight drag brought numbers of our " country cousins " to see the sights, and by ten o'clock so crowded were the streets that locomotion was a matter of considerable diffi- culty. It is estimated that up to about four o'clock about 14,000 people crossed Runcorn Bridge one way or the other, an 1 some idea may thus be gathered of the great influx of the multitude into the town. High-street, Church-street. and Bridge-street were Deed on either side with a compact mass of human beings gathered in anticipation of the pro- cession of the friendly societies, which was timed to start at ten o'clock from Devonshire-square. The arrangements had been admirably conceived, and were carried out without a hitch. Shortly after the hour fixed the Ebenezer Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, led by the Worsley Brass Band, filed out of the square in processional order, the number of members in the ranks being 51. Next in order was the Runcoru Pride Lodge of the G.U.O. of Oddfellows mustering 77 members, and headed by the Roughdale Fire Clay Shed Band. Following were 62 members of William IV. Lodge of 1.0. of Oddfel- lows, the Cadishead brass band leading them on. Then came the Shepherds Tent Lodge of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds, No. 777, Ashton Unity. The lodge was represented by 90 members, preceded by the Northwich Volunteer brass band, and it attracted the most attention from the spectators. A number of the most stalwart mem- bers were clad in huge skins, and in the centre of the pro- cession was a lurry decorated with a profusion of green branches and bright flowers to represent a garden. A raised platform supported the emblem of the Order, and standing near leaning upon crooks were the Shepherdess and Shep- herd (Miss Nickson and Mr. John Nickson), and at each corner of the garden sat a child of tender age tastefully adorned with flowers. The rear was brought up by a mem- ber who, clad in a sheepskin, looked of immense propor- tions, and held a dog in a leash. Following were 130 members of the Rose of Sharon Lodge G.U.0.0., preceded by the band of the 2nd Lancashire Engineer Volunteers (St. Helens); and then came the Star of Freedom Lodge I G.U.0.0.. represented by 66 members, and piloted by the Runcorn National School brass band. Next in order were 104 members of the Lily of the Valley Lodge of the G.U.0.0., each wearing a lily in his coat. They were attended by the Wincham brass band. The procession terminated with the Duke of Edinburgh Lodge of the G.U.0.0 , headed by the Runcorn Volunteer brass band. The members numbered 63. The total number of members in the procession was about 650. Each lodge was preceded by a large and gorgeous painted banner, and in the ranks were carried the charters of the various lodges, while each member was decorated with the regalia peculiar to the society to which he belonged. The procession pro- ceeded to Halton Castle, where they spent several hours in a pleasant manner. The Duke's Club held a separate de- monstration. To the number of 90 the members assembled at Bridgewater House, Bottom Locks, at half-past nine, and having formed into processional order walked through Duke's Field, Lord-street, Waterloo-road, to the Vicarage, where a selection of music was played by the Star of Tem- serence brass band (Widnes.) The pro Cession then wended its way down Greenway-red and High-street to Delph Bridge, then returning to the Parish Church. Occupying a position immediately behind the banner were the Rev. J. J. Bryant, M.A., alr..J. Meadowcroft (agent to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limited), Mr. Oldfield (secretary), Mr. T. Simister, and Mr. McWhannell. The service at the church was full choral. Mr. Meadowcroft read the lessons, the Rev. T. M. Armson the prayers, and the Rev. J. J. Bryant preached a suitable sermon, In the afternoon the I usual procession of scholars took plaee, and passed off with gratifying success. The Nonconformist schools, with one or two exceptions, held a united demonstration, the order of procession being as follows :—Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School (established 1800), 554 scholars ; St. John's Presby- terian School (established 1815), 236: Primitive Methodist School (establ Med 1839), 286 ; Mill Brow Wesleyan School (established 1845), 361; United Methodist Free Church School (established 1851), 256 ; Camden Wesleyan School (established 1862), 470- Nelson-street School (established 1878), 172. Total number of scholars, 2305. Each school was headed by its distinctive banner, and accompanied by the inmates of the chapel with which it was connected, and the superinten- dents. Leading the Brunswick School were the Revs. E. J. Robinson, and John Nowell; Messrs. John Simpson, It. Shaw, T. Norman, E. Sirnkin, W. Rushton. C. Littler, H. B. Toone, and B. Kniveton, while the Rey. E. Williams, Messrs. J. Humphreys, T. Pritchard, J. Kirkham, and J. Pritchard were with the scholars of St. John's Presbyterian School. The Primitive Methodist scholars marched to the strains of the band belonging to the denomination in War- rington, and they were accompanied by the Revs. J. Pick- well and L. Miles; Messrs. T. Stringfellow, J. Asbly, and Joseph Bate. The scholars of Mill-ttrow Wesleyan School were led by their own band, and attended by the Rev. G. Hack, Messrs. J. R. Frith, Joseph Williams, J. Withington, W. Shaw, T. Ince, S. Pope, ana W. Caygill. Accompany- ing the United Methodist Free Church School were the Rev. W. Vause, Messrs. M. Tirnperley, J. Holford, E. Gandy, and other officials of the school. With Camden Wesleyan School were Messrs. S. C. Beckett, G. R. Haalehurst, H. Randle, and A. Harrison. While with its prosperous branch, Nelson-street, were Messrs. S. Coventry and J. Bailey. The procession started from Church-street and proceeded up Bridge-street to Delph-bridge, then returning along High-street and Greenvvay-road t) a field kindly lent by Mr. Savage. A pleasant afternoon was spent in a variety of ways. In the evening entertainments were held at the various schools. The following schools held indepen- dent processions :—Parish Church, 450 scholars; Newtown Mission Church, 166; Holy Trinity Church, 300; Ragged School (Mill-brow) 100; Mersey Missions to Seamen, 270; Bethesda Congregational, 250; St. Luke's Congregational, 150; St. John the Evangelist, Weston, 130 ; Weston , Wesleyan School, 190; total, 1,900. The scholars of the National School were led by their own brass band, and marched in procession to the Vicarage, being accom- panied by the Rev. T. M. Armson, Messrs. W. Whittaker, A. Jordan, T. Bowyer, J. Johnson, W. Sutton, and S. H. Dawson. En routs they were joined by the scholars of Newtown Mission School, who were in charge of the Rev. R. Edwards, Messrs. G. Summerfield, C. Pownall, P. Moore, and J. Cropper. This school was headed by its own fife and drum band, conducted by Mr. Jones, the members wearing their new uniform. The scholars of Holy Trinity School were accompanied by the Rev. R. W. Preston, M.A., Messrs. W. Fisher, W. H Rogerson, and Mr. Bradshaw, in the procession from the school to the Old Parsonage, Halton-road. The scholars from the Ragged Scheel, in charge of Mr. W. J. Cunningham, joined the procession at Delph Bridge. The afternoon was spent in a field off Canal-street, kindly lent by Mr. R. Dutton. The children of the Mersey Mission, headed by their smart band, paraded the streets, and their bright looking appearance was gene- rally commented upon. Army brass band, the :-...-embers paraded the streets singing 1 in their usual manner. Subsequently a tea party was held in the " Mil-racks" followed by an entertainment which was held under the presidency of " Brickey " as the captain of the army is termed. Reinforced by large numbas of mem- bers from other corps, the Runcorn branch of the Salvation army bad quite an imposing array of forces, and paraded the streets both in the morning and afternoon with an enthu- siasm which frequently found vent in shouts of " hallelu- jah" and "volleys." In the afternoon what was described as a "ham, ja:n, and glory" tea was held, followed by a, "great rejoicing and hosanna meeting," which was largely attended. We may state that the most admirable order was kept in the town all day, the large concourse of people being managed with dexterity by the police. The arrangements were in the hands of Inspector Hollingworsh, and Sergeants Walley and McMichael. It is worthy of notice that no arrests for drunkenness were made.
A new writ was ordered on Thursday for Athlone, for which Mr. Parnell has a candidate ready in the son of Mr. Justin M'Carthv.
The sentence of death passed on William Smith, at the last Durktam AtNizes, for wife murder. has been ccmniuted to penal servitude for life.

- - - - WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB —The first annual amateur athletic sports in connection with this club ate announced to take place on the sth of July, under N.C.A.A. rules. Prizes to the value of £5O will be given. LIBERAL MEETlNG.—Arrangements are in progress for holding a large public meeting in Warrington which will be addressed by Mr. W. Crosfield, J.P, the newly-adopted Liberal candidate, and other gentlemen. The date has not yet been fixed, but it will probably be announced next week.

PROPOSFD BAND OF HOPE GALA—We u63eretand that arrangements are in progress for a demonstration of the various Bands of Hope in Warrington on Bank Holiday in August next, under the auspice.; of the recently organised Baud of Hope Union. Already a considerable number of the local societies have promised their support, and a gala of a most attractive character may be expected. BrITTERMARKET-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL.—It will be seen from our announcement columns that the anniversary sermons of the Buttermarket-street Wesleyan Sunday School, Warrington, will be preached to-morrow (Sunday), in Bold. Street Chapel, by the Rev. E. Lloyd Jones of Rhyl. A children's service will be conducted in the Jones, by the Rev. F. Luke Wiseman, 8.A., of Didsbury College. THEFT OF CLOTHING AT SANKEY.— A man named Michael Feeney was brought up at the Warrington Police Curt, yesterday morning, and remanded to the Newton Petty Sessions on a charge of stealing a suit of clothes, value £4. the property of Michael Maghan, a ,arm labourer, at Sat key, on Thursday. The prosecutor saw the prisoner is the act of carrying away the clothes, and gave him into custody. A THEATRICAL LICENSE FOR CAIRO-STREET SUNDAY Scappe.--At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yester- day morning, Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, attended before the magistrates, and said that as that was an adjourned session for the granting of theatrical licenses he wished to apply on behalf of Mr. Mallard, one of the trustees, for a license to perform stage plays at the Cairo- street Sunday and Day School. Mr. Brown explained that it was merely desired to have the license for performances to be given by amateurs belonging to the school and congrega- tion.—The Bench granted the app:ication.

HEALTH OF WARRINGTON- ANNUAL REPORT. Dr. Gornall, the Medical Officer of Health, has just issued his report of the health and sanitary condition of the borough of Warriugron, during the twelve months ended 31st Decem- ber, 1883. We give the principal portions of the report whicb has been prepared with great care. During the year 1883, the number of births registered in the borough amounted to 1,870, of which 957 were males and 913 females. This shows an increase of 95 upon the births recorded in the previous year, and 102 more than the average of the previous five years 6.878 to 1882). Of the 1,870 births 1,705 were registered in the Warrington Regis- tration District, and 165 in that of Latchford. Tne birth rate was 426 per 1.000 of the population, against 44, the average of the previous five years. The rate for the whole of England and Wales was 331 per 1,000. The total number of deaths recorded in the borough dur- ing the year 1883 amounted to 901, 890 being i•egistered in the Warrington, and 71 in the Latchford Registration Dis- trict. This number includes 12 that took place in the fever hospital, 10 in the infirmary, and 73 in the workhouse hos- pital. From the total of 961:deaths must be deducted 14 which occurred in the workhouse of persons admitted from several parts of the Warrington Union outside the municipal boundary. The remaining 947 represents the actual num- ber of deaths übe debited to the borough. This showsesu actual decline of 90 upon the year 1882, and is 31 below the average of the last 10 years. The rate of mortality for the year was tquivalent to 21.6 per 1,000 persons living, on an estimated population of 43,814 to the middle of the year, being 2.7 per 1,000 lower than 1882, and, excepting the unprecedentedly low death rates of 1880 and 1881, was lower than that recorded in any year since civil registration came into operation The excess ot births over deaths, representing the natural increase to the population was 923, this being 185 more than in 1882, and 73 more than the average of the previous seven years. Compared with tiSmean mortality of the preceding 10 years (1873-82), the death rate shosys a considerable reduc- tion, amounting to no less than 2 per 1,000, and compared with the previous 20 years, a saving of human life to the extent of 4 per 1,000, or 175 lives 'during the year under consideration. Zymotic mortality is equal to 12 per cent, of the deaths from all causes and to a rate of 27 per 1,000. The zymotic death rate in 1882 was 5.8 per 1,000, and the average rate for the ten preceding years was 4.1. The satisfactory decline in 1883 was due to the complete absence of any deaths from measles, the death rate alone from this disease in 1882 being 2.48 per 1,000, which is nearly equal to the whole zyrnotic death rate for the past year. NOt since the year 1867 has there been a similar immtinity from this dis- ease. As compared with 1882, when the total number of deaths was 253, there were only 120 in the year under review. The deaths from scarlet fever continue steadily to decrease. SMALL-PDX.—AS in the previous years 1881 and 1882, I am happy to state that the only case of small-pox notified was imported. Similarly in the year, as in both the preced- ing ones, there was no extension of the disease; and this is undoubtedly due to the immediate notification and removal to hospital, followed by disinfection of premises, and destruc- tion of infected bedding and clothing. The case—a malig- nant form of the disease—wae admitted to hospital on 28th April, and discharged cured on 16th July. SCARLET FEVER —The number of cases reported during the year was 127. 35 in the let quarter, 43 in the 2nd, 26 in the 3rd, and 23 in the 4th. Of this number 92 were removed to the Fever Hospital, the remaing 35 being treated at their own homes. During the year 27 deaths were regis- tered in the borough from this disease which included 14 in Warrington. 1 in Latchford, 11 at the Fever Hospital, and lat the Workhouse Hospital. The general rate of mor- tality from this disease was '5 per 1,000 against 1.22 in 1882, and against 108 the average of the seven years, 1875 to 1881. Daring the last three years, 1881-2-3, the number of cases isolated at the Fever Hospital has been equal to 74 per cent, of the total cases certified. FRVER.—Under this head are included typhus, enteric, and simple continued fever. The deaths recorded are-1 from typhus, 7 from enteric, and 1 from simple continued fever—a total of 9 against 1® in 1882, and 6in both 1880 and 1881, and a yearly average of 28 in the previous ten years, 1870 to 1879.

TYPHUS—Three cases were reported, 1 at Buckley's-yard, Haydock-street• The house had no through ventilation, was over-crowded and filthy. This case proved fatal. The other two admitted into the Workhouse Hospital were tramps.

ENTERIC FEVER—This disease has been somewhat more prevalent during the past year. 22 cases in all having been reported-4 in the Ist quarter, 2in the 2nd, 3in the 3rd, and 13 in the 4th. 'They were distributed as follows: North-West Ward : 8 cases-3, Buckley's-court, Winwick- street ; 40, Golborne-street; 42, Golborne-street; 43, Walker- street; 35, Walker-street; 33, Guardian-street; 10, Stamford- street; 9S, Hoyle-street. North-East Ward : 10 cases-132, School-brow; Chisnall's-yard, Winwck-street; 73, Winwick- street ; 6, Percival's-fold ; 21, Silver-street (two cases); 20, Chorley-street (three cases); 28, School-brow, South-East Ward: 2 csseS-1, Rose and Croca-streef ; 12. Musa, Howley. South-West Ward: Nil. Latchford: 2 cases-9, Barry-street; 197, Mersey-view. Total, 22 cases.— From the cases of this disease thus recorded you will not ice that many are associated with the usual accompaniments of fever, dirt, and improvidence, and in 1870 Dr. Ballard gave it as his opinion that the constant foul exhalations from badly-constructed and neglected middens was quite sufficient to account for the prevalence of enteric fever in the courts and narrow streets. But this disease you will also observe is shown to exist in houses of better construction, and healthier situation, and seems in no way capable of being referred to local filth, Jrc., for the pail system having been generally adopted all excremental matters are removed weekly. Nor can the water supply, which has been so much improved in quality of late, be credited with the pro- duction of enteric fever; and as far as I have been able to as- certain there is no connection between the fever and the milk supply. But there is one prevaleht source of danger which, though it canint in all cases bo designated the sore cause of enteric fever, is assuredly deleterious in its effects and offensive to a degree. I allude to the emanations from the sewers, a nuisance repeatedly referred to before, which lies more in the province of the Borough Engineer than that of the Medical Officer, but whose disastrous effects on the health of the community lam compelled to point out. In my intercourse with the medical men of the town I frequently receive information of other diseases, not in their province to notify, but troublesome and dangerous, all attributable to the Same cause, viz, the poisonous emana- tions from the sewers. The necessity then of frequent flushing, constant cleansing, and better ventilation of the sewers is self-evident, and I have the less reluctance in drawing attention to this—as from the natural comformation of the site of the site of the town there is every probability of its proving a chronic nuisance and danger unless special measures De taken to prevent its recurrence. COMPULSORY NOTIFICATION OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES A full four years has now elapsed since this Act came into force. Its effects have been now fairly tested, and its bene- ficial influence unquestionably established. The injury to the other members of the medical profession anticipated from its working has proved to be only fancied; the accom- modation provided for dealing effectively with epidemic outbreaks is now openly recognised as a great boon, and early notification is at last, generally acknowledged to exer- cise a salutary influence on the health of the town. A writer in a local medical journal, speaking of Warrington, quotes what he calls "The confession of a Town Coun- cillor," as follows:—" If the action had continued, the op- position must have utterly destroyed the operation of the Act." With this statement lam at direct issue. The action does continue ; the private practitioners notify apparently most willingly, without any existing good relations between them and their patients to my knowledge being in any way disturbed. Let me take the opportunity of again thanking them for working with me so cordially. Further, lam san- guine enough to believe that the inhabitants of the borough are so fully alive to the advantages of the present Fever Hospital, the necessary adjunct to all measures for the pre- vention of disease, that they would not have it done away with if they could. Once more, the educational advantages to the community of the working of the Act are very great; and in future years, when sanitary laws and their require- ments from enlarged experience shall be better and more generally known, they will be enormous. The public will be more sensitive to the danger of allowing disease centres to exist amongst them, they will recognise their own respon- sibilities under the visitation of epidemics, and they will know what steps to take to arrest their spread. The com- mittee have, then, every reason to be proud of their work, in carrying out with so little friction, and with such decided success, the clauses of an Act at first considered so objec- tionable. INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.—TotaI number admitted since the Hospital was opened, 28th May, 1877, 842. Number admitted since the Improvement Act received the Royal Assent, 765. Number of patients admitted during the year 1883, 106. 01 the 106 patients admitted during the year, 11 have been attended by private practitioners, and 95 by myself. During the year, 1,730 articles have been disinfected in Ransome's stove, including beds, mattresses, blankets, sheets, carpets, &c.. and various articles of cloth- ing. The following figures show the cost of maintenance during the year :—Salary--medical superintendent, £100; matron, £4O; wages—lodge-keeper and gardener, £121; nurses and skvants, £140; water rates and taxes, £23; coals. £144 12s Id ; gas, £97 2s 4d; provisions, groceries, milk, meat, Sic., £359 15a; alcholic stimulants (as medicine), £3 17s 6d; drugs, 8:c. (soda water), £2O 14s 4d repairs, £26 Ile 3d; painting the home £33; horse hire, £9 19s washing, £69 19s 6d ; total, £1,189 lie. The committee have every reason to be pleased with the efficiency of the working staff, everything being done willingly, quietly, and well, to the satisfaction of bath patients and medical officer. As regards economy. which I know, next to efficiency the committee have most a heart, I believe that our institution

will compare favourably with any other similar hospital in the kingdom; and though in times of freedom from epi- demics, it may appear a waste of strength and money te) keep so complete a staff, yet I think, in the end, it will prove the truest economy to be provided against all emergencies when outbreaks of disease vary so much in frequency and intensity. SANITARY WORK.-4 annex the report of the roiisance , inspector showing that a large amount of sanitary work has I been performed during the year. Ihe removal of pail closets is st stematically carried out, and I am of opinion that though it is done in the day time, so much more atren- tion is paid to general cleanliness at the Longford depot that there is not much occasion for even the sensitive to com- plain on the ground of offensiveness. The scavengering of the town, under Mr. Norman's supervision, has been well attended to. All the streets and common yards have been swept and gullies cleansed once A week, and the four prin- cipal streets (Bridge-street, Sankey-street, Buttermarttet, and Horsemarket-street) every day. The urinals have been washed and disinfected daily. The common lodging-houses, slaughter houses, milk-shops, bakehouses have all been regularly visited, the two latter by myself as well as the inspector. The report shows that, with few exceptions. their general condition was satisfactory. There are now only 99 closets on the old midden system, 109 haying been converted during the year. These have all been done on my certificate, and as the result of personal inspection. I must again direct your attention to the urgent necessity of your inspectors undertaking a minute and systematic house to house inspection of the district. lam of opinion that with your present staff this great desideratum could hardly be accomplished as the duties of your chief inspector are so numerous and important. The present time, however, is a fitting one for so valuable an inquiry being made as there is an absence of epidemic disease. I may note that similar inspections are now being carried out in most other towns. METEOROLOGY.— Temperature : Highest observed, 77 ; lowest observed, 11 ; mean temperature, 44.1 ; ditto in 1882, 76, 8,44 p respectively. Rainfall. Number of rainy days. 199; ditto, 1882, 224 ; total amount measured in 1883, 33 ; ditto in 1882, 3901.

LATEST NEWS _ „ A messenger who has arrived at Dongola from Shendy re- ports that General Gordon is still at Khartoum. Yesterday Mr. Hall, the Conservative candidate for Lin- coln, an Mr. Rushton, the Liberal candidate, each issued an address to the electors. In the Australian v. Lancashire, the Colonials in the second innings had recorded 202 for three wickets when the stumps were drawn yesterday. A Parliarnentary return issuedyesterdav, shows that there were 44 deaths from starvation in London last year, of which 39 were in central end eastern Middlesex. A number of workmen engaged on some excavations at Lincoin, yesterday, unearthed a Roman crmatory furnace and a sarcophagus. In the latter were ten cinerary urns containing dust and calcined bones. FOUND DEAD.—About five o'clock yesterday morning the dead body of a well-dressed man was found on the rocks to the south of the Sim at Scarborough. From documents on the body it is believed the deceased is Mr. Allanson Turner, farmer, of Cloughton, near Scarborough. Earl Granville arrived in London yesterday from Trent- ham, where he had been on a visit to the Duke and Duchess of Sutherland. In the afternoon his lordship had a somewhat prolonged interview at the Foreign Office with M. Waddington, the French ambassador. ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE.—At Sheffield, yes- terday, Ada Jenkinson, a young unmarried woman, was charged with attempting to drown herself and infant child. At midnight she went with the babe and jumped into the dam at Malin Bridge. Some young men passing heard the splash and rescued her, but it was not until after that they beard the child scream, and it was got out in a very ex- hausted state. The prisoner was remanded. THE INTERNATIONAL HEALTH EXHIBITION.—Cardinal Manning presided yesterday afternoon over the third of the ' series of conferences held in connection with the Inter- national Health Exhibition. His eminence in opening the proceedings said it was a shame and a blot on the British empire that in the imperial city of the greatest empire in the world there were to be found dwellings unfit for human habitation. Papers were read by Mr. Sherley Murphy, Mr. Whitelegge, M.D., and others. „. . LORD SALISBURY'S VISIT TO DEVONSHIRE The Juatepsis of Salisbury's visit te the West of England terminated yes- terday morning, when his lordship left Plymouth by the 10-35 Great Western train for London. He was accom- panied from the Winter Villa, Stonehouse, to the station by Lord Mount Edgcumbe, Sir Massey Lopes, M.P., and Mr. John Tremayne, and was greeted OB the platform by many other political admirers, who cheered his lordship heartily as the train steamed out of the station. Loss OF A STEAMER AND THREE LIVES.—IDIONTIatiOII was received at South Shields yesterday that the steamer Linhope, of Newcastle, while on a voyage from the Tyne to the Mediterranean, had foundered in the Bay of Biscay, through the shifting of her cargo and that three of toe crew, named Newham, Briazlin, and Muller, were drowned. Captain Ruthen and the remainder of the crew were picked up by a passing vessel, and landed at Bilbao. The Linhope was a vessel of fifteen hundred tons register, and built at West Hartlepool six years ago. THD RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR SALISBURY.—The inquest on the bodies of the four persona killed in the Downton railway accident, near Salisbury, was resumed at Breamore yesterday afternoon. The evidence of the passengers who escaped showed that, after leaving Downton, the train travelled at an unusual speed, and that there was in con- sequence a very noticeable oscillation. According to the medical testimony the death of Miss Chandler and Mrs. Corbin was due to drowning, wbilet the other two victims died from concussion and shock to the system. The inqairy was again adjourned.

div.head: Zetters to the editor.
div.p: Zetters to the editor.
WALKING DAY IN WARRINGTON.

Sr,—Seeing that Whit-week is now so generally recognised as a holiday, and that Newton Race Friday, as such, has ceased to exist, is it not high time that Walking Day should for the future be held, say on Friday in Whit- week ? There can be little doubt about it that the frequency of holidays of this character is a source of considerable pe- cuniary loss and inconvenience both to manufacturers and working -men. Far be it from me to suggest anything which would 'have the appearance of attempting to deprive the little ones of any portion of those holidays to which they look forward with such anxious delight. As a father, a Sun- day school teacher, and one who takes a deep interest in the welfare of working-people, I would do everything which is casistent with justice to increase rather than diminish the pleasures of My fellows, but I happen to know that many fathers and mothers are put to serious straits in their laudable desire to give their little ones the utmost pleasure on Walking Day, owing to the fact that Whit-week being a pay week has absorbed the greater part of the funds. Would it not, therefore, be better for all, Sunday schools, workmen and manufacturers, and also tend to restore the old harmonics feeling if steps were taken by those most in- terested, at an early period, to bring about this, in my opinion, desirable object. I shall be glad to co-operate with any friends who may agree with my views. lam aware that it is too late to make any change this year, but it seems to me this is the right time to discuss the matter.---Yours. A SUNDAY SCHOOLTEACHER.

div.head: NEW CANDIDATE.
div.p: THE NEW CANDIDATE.

Sir,—The Liberals of Warrington are deeply indebted to I Mr. McMinnies. As a practised politician, be has, the moment he found it necessary for his health's sake, given them timely notice of his intention to resign the seat. To swop horses while crosssng the stream is a hazardous task. To get firmly seated in the saddle before you reach the stream is a proof of wisdom. The step taken by oar res- pected member will enable the Liberal Association not only to get firmly seated, but to feel to a certainty that they will land their man at St. Stephen's. In Mr. McMinnies the borough has had a useful and a conscientious member; not a vote recorded, as yet, that Liberals can find fault with. We have no fear, that at some future day a vote will be un- earthed proving him wanting in one of the common in- stincts of humanity, viz., " mercy "; or that his enemies, if he has any, will be able to charge him with intimidating a poor working-man. In a Parliament that has been re- markable for talking obstructionists he has preferred to do silent work. At home he has given us annually an account of his political work in London. Not only this, Mr. Editor, but he has satisfied the people of this borough that he knows what politics are; and he, along with the Association were determined at the commencement of the winter season that they would teach the people, Liberal and Tory alike, all that could possibly be known of current politics. They have done their work well, but what has the other party done? Simply nothing. unless dragging a poor old octogenarian about the town be something. In looking about for a worthy successor of the represen- tative of "529," the Council of the Liberal Association have happily dropt on one whose name and associations are familiar to Warringtonians, one whose father served his aPprenticeshin in Warrington, and whose name is connected with one of the best gifts the town ever received. Mr. Wm. Crosdeld comes here not altogether a stranger; our business men know him. He has the reputation of being a hard worker, and I am sure all who heard him in Wycliffe Hall the other evening must allow that he knows something of politics. Just in the prime of life, he seems fitted to have a useful political career before hire. Sound.on all the burning ques- tions of the day, he will be a tough customer for any " heckler "to tackle. I was much pleased with the man- ner in which he dealt with the CALICIIS question. No doubt this is a tough morsel for the Tory magnates to swallow, but what would they have? Do they wish to have the power, as of old, to settle who shall and who shall not re- present the people? If so, they are mistaken, and the sooner they make a note of this the better. Di ay 29, 1884. CAPTAIN CUT rLE.

div.head: "FISHY" GREENALLITE.
div.p: A "FISHY" GREENALLITE.

Sir,—l read with considerable amusement, in your last issue, a letter signed "Fair Play." The writer evidently thought he had got a bite; but to your knowledge, Sir, as well as my own, be was simply bitten. He must guess again as to the writer of the letter to which he refers. Failing success in the effort, he may quietly retire amongst his fellow •• mugwurops." "Fair May," after the fashion of cowards, makes several charges, and then hides himself be- hind a nom de plume. If he cares to throw inuendo on one side, make his charges in plain English—l care not how strong they are—and then sign his name, I shall have great pleasure in noticing them. In the meantime, our friend may be dealt with as a would- be politician. We are told that Sir Gilbert is generous, though prudent." Well, this may be so, but Warrington, as a matter of fact, knows more of his prudence that his generosity, and the general impression is that when he gives more is meant than mectS the ear." Bnt iii hi paragraph there ie a deliberate stifling of principle, not at all an Un- common occurrerce in the Tory mind. Radicals do net select their representatives on account of their " generous and prudent" qualities with respect to local money matters, rather on account ot their strong adherence to national and progressive measures. We seek to benefit the whole com- munity, to render it impossible fora man to add acre to acre, or to make large tracts of country subject to his lordly will, to the utter exclusion of England's peasantry. Des "Fair Play" ever take a walk around the Walton estate? If so, he may have had short chats with some of those who are most likely to know something of the "generous though prudent ":Sir Gilbert. Certainly, the peasants are "few and far between," but when found and questioned they have but one tale to tell, and that is that cottage building is not encouraged, that Sir Gilbert wants as few resident labourers on his estate as possible; he prefers they should live in the town, walking to and fro night and morning. This means that the town must bear the burden that nature intended for Walton, and that town labourers should have competing with them those whom the Walton estate should find ample labour for.

With respect to the fishing business, "Fair Play" must • allow it is a " fishy " subject—that all the excuses and ex- planations put forth are so much trash, Sir Gilbert never • intended the people of Warrington to have one particle of pleasure out of that sacred neighbourhood—the water-works , district. Even mere students of botany have been ordered away, for the ground whereon they trod was holy. And since Sir Gilbert was ousted from Warrington by the his. torical "52P," school teachers have had to look elsewhere ' on walking days for a field in which their children might spend the day. But this has nothing to do with politics, and Fair Play" has only himself to thank for what is now said I disclaim any "political spite." I have no doubt Sir Gilbert is as " nice " a man as ever breathed ; I know he can "be true to you if you will be true to me," because he says so, hence it must be true. In the struggle that is now going on amongst us to make "life worth living," we natur- ally look around for those who are capable and willing to help us to the desired goal. And if we take any of the cur- rent political questions. we form opinions upon them, and we say this man or that represents the best of the current statecraft of the day, and is the man I prefer to trust to work out a satisfactory solution of the political problem. Is it the Merchant Shipping Bill, I say trust it to Mr. Glad. stone's Government, and the lives of our seamen will not be sacrificed on the altar of insurance policies. With the pre- sent Government "vested interests "is only another term for legalized murder. Is it a question of endearing the people to the land ? then I say help the present Govern- ment to pass the Franchise Bill, and you give the cottager at Walton the earns rights that are enjoyed by the cottager on Town Hill. Was it a question of passing a Bankruptcy Bill ? the Liberals did it, and already the country is feeling the benefit, and the lawyers are crying out. With Egynt and the Soudan question, not a Liberal but will allow that it is a difficult matter, made more difficult by self-seeking Tories, who, not content with unseemly squabbles amongst themselves for leadership, seek to make political capital out of England's difficulties. No subject too insignificant for their greedy. maw; from a wire drawers strike to a Kilmain- barn treaty is a wide stretch, but it includes the only mems the Tory mind is able to grapple with. When I think of the measures passed, and the measures promised, that are likely to benefit nw class, I am never even by accident reminded of Tory legislation. If the Tory working-man, one of nature's mad freaks, wants to judge how far he is likely to benefit by Tory legislation, let him study the victory gained by the landed interest on the Cattle Importation Bill. De- pend upon it twenty-two "Liberal "county members would not have voted for Protection on this question had the House been a representative one. How often has Ireland been pointed to as a sign of Mr. Gladstone's misgovernment, yet Ireland was never more tranquil or property more secure. The scene in Scotland-yard is only one of the results of past misgovernment ; the schoolmaster is abroad with political equality in his hand, and will soon alter all this. Jane 2nd, 1834. H. WHITHAM.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY C URT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY C URT.

Turasneer.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. CLAIM AGAINST A MASTER FUSTIAN CUTTER —ID this case Ruth Boskow, an apprentice to Michael Rogers, carry- ing on business as a fustian cutter in Warrington, claimed from her master the sum of Ss 3d, being the balance of wages due from him for work done.—Mr. Jenkins appeared for the plaintiff.—Defendant set up a counter claim of 13e 6d, being 123 6d for bad cutting of a piece of cloth which the plaintiff alleged that she had not heard of during the whole time she had been in the employof the defendant, and Is for two tears in the pieces, which plaintiff admitted to be right.—The defendant being only represented by his clerk, his Honour said that he shout" give a verd•ct for the plaintiff if the defendant did not appear in person. and prove certain facts.—The case was then allowed to stand over, and subsequently the defendant attended and was represented by Mr. A. Browne, in answer to whom he said that it was the custom of the trade to deduct certain amounts from the weekly wages of employe to make good damage done; he also produced the manufacturers' receipt showing the amount set down as having been caused by the damage. In answer to Mr. Jenkins defendant said that it would be over two years since the plaintiff cut the pieces in question. He did not deduct the money from the plaintiff's wages because her father was out of work.—His Honour said that it was no matter what WAS the custom of the trade he could not give judgment for the defendant, for a thing of that kind that had been condoned for so long. Plaintiff had continued working in the shop and he thought that the fact of the money not having been deducted from her wages was the strongest evidence in her favour. He should give judgment for the plaintiff. ADMINISTRATION ORDERS.—William Willett, veterinary surgeon, carrying on business at Stretten, who was repre- sented by Mr. Moore, made application for an administration order.—Mr. Fox appeared on behalf of Messrs. Hewlett and Sons, London. principal creditors and there were a number of the creditors in court—Mr. Moore said that in the latter end of September or October of last year the debtor met with a severe accident owing to the bursting of a paraffin lamp, and was unable to carry on his business for about four months, during which time he had to pay someone else to do his work. They did not ask for a reduction of the debts, but simply for an amount to be fixed, so that the debtor could discharge his liabilities in instalments. He suggested £1 a month as the amount to be fixed.—One of the creditors in court said that the case was a most disgraceful one. He had known the debtor for 20 years, had gone to school with him, and knew that with ordinary care the debtor, with his profession, might have made £5OO a year, but if he got ss. in his pockets he took it to the alehouse.—The Debtor; If you had been in the same mess that I have been in for four months you would not have been talking that way.—His Honour said that he very much doubted whether the debtor was a person who, under the circumsiences, was entitled to ask for an order of that kind. The law was to grant such orders to debtors who, hrough their circumstances, were unable to meet their debts, bet a person in the position of this debtor should be able to wipe out the claim, which was for £45 odd, without such assistance. It was not like the case of a poor man who was in indigent circumstances, for the debtor was a man with a good profession in his hands. His Honour having referred to comparatively small debts that had been wing sometime, said that there must have been something in the case, and that the debtor must have been guilty of intem- perance, or have spent his money in some other way instead• of doing as he should have done, and paid his debts.—Mr. Moore thought that His Honor's observations would refer to the question whether or not the liabilities of a debtor I should be reduced, and not particularly to the granting of I an order.—His Honour said that it referred to the whole question. He should refuse the order, and if Mr. Moore liked he could appeal and test the matter. If leave to ap- peal was required ha would give it.—Mr. Davies applied f r edminiseration order on behalf of Thomas Jones, Wright-street, Sankey Bridges. Mr. Davies said that the debtor had for some years been a puddler at Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co.'s works. He was a married man with a wife I and three children, and the reason be made this application was because he had five judgments against him in that court, which was brought about by his peculiar circum- stances, he having been suffering from a rupture in his back. The debtor asked for an order as to time, and • for a reduction of the . debts if His Honour thought they should be reduced. There were five judgments against him and his liabilities amounted to about £23.—The debtor was questioned at length by several creditors in court, as to his income and means.—His Honour said that the duty was imposed upon the court of taking , care that the benefits conferred by the act were not abused, ' and that it was not to be made an excuse for not paying debts or not making that effort to pey them which a debtor ought to make. The effect of an order was to suspend tho rights of creditors so long as the debtor kept up his pay- ments, but if he failed to de that, the creditors might at any moment come forward and throw him into gaol. On the other hand if a debtor had obtained an order he might for his life never get out of the court, for as long as his debts were accumulating they might be scheduled against him. His Honour then pointed out that in the case under notice it was shewn that some of the debts were of long standing, and that, although the debtor had sustained some injury he had not been entirely incapacitated for work, and was earning at present at least 303 a week. He could not there- fore think that it was a case deserving of any very great consideration on the part of the court. He should make an order for 25s a month.

APPLICATION FOR A NEW TEIAL.—Mr. Davies made an application for a new trial in the case of Samuel Fuiwood v. Ambrose Cotterill, which was heard before his Honour at a recent date.—Mr. Jenkins appeared for the defence.--Mr. Davies said that no doubt His Honour would recollect the circumstances ot the case. The plaintiff when the original action came on was not represented by a solicitor, and the defendant was represented by Mr. Jenkins. On that occasion plaintiff produced a small memorandum book which she said was a book of the accounts which she had notice from Mr. Jenkins to produce. She then was undeAthe impression that it was the only book that she ought to have brought, but if his Honour would grant a new trial she would be able to produce the proper shop book. He then explained the rea- son why the proper shop book bad not been produced on the first occasion, and proceeded to say that when the case was heard the defendant on his oath swore that the plaintiff did not keep a grocery shop at all, but a place with an off icense for beer, and that the account was for beer supplied to this wife. He (Mr. Davies) was prepared to bring witnesses who could prove the contrary. Mr. Davies then read the affidavit of Mrs. Fuliwood, wife of Samuel Full- wood, provision dealer, Winwick-road, Warrington, which set forth that the statements of the defendant that she did not keep a provision shop and that the amount claimed (£6 15s 4,1) was for beer supplied and not for provisions were absolutely untrue. It was also sworn that the defend- ant had himself purchased provisions at the shop—His Honour held that there was nothing to justify him in granting a new trial. Nothing mentioned in the affidavit was evidence that could not have been brought forward at i first. If people neglected such things t was a very unfor- nate thing for them, but he should be trying actions over and over again if he were to listen to applications simply based upon the ground that a person had evidence that might have been called and was not. He therefore declined to grant the application.—lt may be mentioned that Mr. Jenkins had an affidavit setting forth that bis clerk,Thes. Hy. Graner, visited the shop of the plaintiff on separate occasions, and did not see any goods that would properly 1 come under the category of provisions. or verify the con- tention that the shop was a provision shop. CLAIM AGAINST A FRIENDLY SOCIETY.—The adjourned action brought by John Chandley, labourer, Lymm, against "Court the Grove, No. 287 of the Ancient Order of Fores- ters (Lymm)," for the sum of £4 2s 6d, alleged to be due to him as sick pay, under circumstances already reported, came on for hearing.—ln the first instance plaintiff was represented by Mr Davies, who had now withdrawn from the case —Mr. Sparrow, barrister, represented the defen- dant lodge, and said that no doubt his Honour would re- member that the case was adjourned, as the 1 lodge in ques- tion was in suspension, in order to give the plaintiff an opportunity of so amending his claim as he might be ad- vised.—Plaintiff then gave evidence in support of his claim, and the rules of the Court were examined by the Judge. Plaintiff complained that he was placed at a dis- advantage because his solicitor had withdrawn from the case. His Honour: I have no doubt there there are good reasons why your solicitor has withdrawn

PERSONS DROWNED.—. Yesterday a sailing boat containing four excursionists, was capszed by the wash of a p losing steamer. One of the occupants was saved but the others, two women and a man. were drowned.
MR. GLADSTONE AND WELSH DISESTABLISH-

MENT. The Central News is informed that Mr. Gladstone has given Mr. Dillwyn, M.P., to understand that when the hon. member for Swansea brings forward his motion next month for the disestablishment of the English Church in Wales, he (the Premier) will not oppose it. This intimation has caused the greatest satistamion amongst the Welsh Noneon- formibts.

! THREATENING ATTITUDE OF ORANGEMEN. At a meeting held in Westminster yesterday, of a special committee of the Orangemen of London, a resolution was unanimously passed denouncing the action of the Govern- ment in permitting Nationalist meetings in Ulster. Another telegram says :—Numerously attended meetings of Orangemen were held in various districts in Londoz, yesterday, at each of which it was decided that if the Government do not proclaim the Nationalist meeting at Newry, on Sunday,,a large number of Orangemen will pro. coed to Ireland from England to assist their brethren at Newry. The secretary of the Special Committee of London Orangemen received the following telegram from the com- mittee at Newry :—" Have made all arrangements to prevent rebel meeting on Sunday; wire what you can do to assist us." It is stated that arrangements have been completed for sending the desired assistance. The Orangemen of Newry yesterday issued an ad- dress to the Orangemen of Ulster stating that they have de- termined at all hazards to hold a counter demonstration next Sunday, and calling upon them to assemble in their migist and assist their local brethren.

ADMIRAL HEWITT'S MISSION. CAIRO, FRIDAY ETENING.—Admiral Hewitt saw the King of Abyssinia on May 27th, and was well received by his Majesty. Admiral Hewitt intencted to start on his return journey on the let June.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The House met at 4 -07clrel.

- - • ZULULAND.—Mr. COURTNEY, replying to Mr. Ashmead- • Bartlett, said the report that Mr. Osborn, the British resident, had been defeated by Dabulamanze, and that Cap- tain Mansel was killed, was without foundation. GENERAL GORDON AND THE SOUDAN.—Lord FITZ- mt-criacm said the rumour that the Mandi had advanced on Khartoum had reached the Government, but they had no confirmation of it. Berber was still invested, but reports differed as to the extent. Satisfactory information had been received from Sir W. E. Hewett, and he had confident hope of the success of his mission.—Lord FITZMAURICE, reply- ing to Mr. Arnold, said the Government had no informa- tion that General Gordon had left Khartoum. Replying to other questions, the noble loqi said the latest telegram from General Gordon was April 9th. The last message sent to Gordon was May 21st. The Government had received in- formation of an attack on Suakim. It agreed with reports published; the rebels had been repulsed.—Lord HARTING- TON said there was a force of Marines at Suakim. NATIONAL DEBT BILL—The adjourned debate on the motion for the second reading of the National Debt Conver- sion of Stock Bill was resumed.—Mr. W. FOWLER thought the principle of both good, but he had doubts whether it, was wise or sound to increase the capital of the debt. He would vote for the second reading.—Mr. SALT had strong objection to the conversion of the three per cents, into new stock at two and a half and two and three quarters, as pro- posed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer.—Mr. MA.GRATC did not share the apprehensions of the last speaker as to the effect of the conversion of the debt. In this case the opera- tion was intended to be self acting. If it succeeded it would be well for the country, if it did not the country would be no worse off.—Mr. GOSCHEN contended it w.e the clear duty of the Government to pay off the debt when cheapness of money enabled it to do so.—The discussion was continued by Mr. Ashmead-Bartleft and others.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER defended the measure. The bill, be contended, was a symptom that the value of money had fallen, and they were bound to take advantage of circumstances —Sir S. NORTHCOTE considered the ex- planation satisfactory to a certain extent, but before the bill proceeded to committee the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer ought to say whether he intended to use commit- fiery claims.-1 be House divided—For second reading, 117; against, 34.—Toe bill was then read a second time, and tbe sitting suspended. A The Speaker resumed the chair at nine o'clock. Than House was counted, and forty members not being present,! it was adjourned at five minutes past nine.

FAsinoNA.LE WEDDING—On Wednesday morning a marriage was celebrated at the Parish Church, at Part bury, which caused an unusual amount of interest in 17. village, the contracting parties being Miss Charlotte Jones, second daughter of Mr. W. C. Jones, of The Daresburv, to Mr. J. F. Colebrlclge Boles, of glade. gend, Glamorgan. The ceremony was perfornvd Elc° !Rev. Mr. Whitley, and between the Church and The g_ three splendid arches of evergreens and flowers bearing ap propriate mottoes were erected over the road, while the church had been beautifully decorated for the occasion. The bride's dress was of white satin and Brussels lace.eb,ie , wore a diamond star in her veil and a pearl necklace 30' pendant. There were eight bridesmaids, namely. 1422. ! Jones, Miss Miller, Miss M'Laren, Miss Alice M`Larent Mi I Fannie Daglisb, Miss Weiss, Miss H. L. Jones, au," Ml'w D. Logan, each of whom wore a primrose sada dreg covered with white lace and bonnets of the same ColOnF with ostrich plumes. lace, carried in her hand a bouquet !of Marechal Neil roses, the gift of the bridegroom. The presents, which were very costly, numbered about 100. Among them were some beautiful jewellery, Plate, and china. The wedding guests numbered 67, and included a large number of Bold farmers. After the wedding party had returned from church they were photographed in a , group at The Elms on a large scale by Mr. BirtleS, tographer, of Sankey.etreet, Warrington. In the evening a supper was held in the Session Room, adjoining the Bang O'Bells, when about 50 persons sat down. Mr. Lowe neat' pied the chair. The repast was provided by. Mr. Philips, landlord of the Ring O'Bells. After the suppu the tablea were cleared and the usual loyal and patriotic tose:s were given from the chair. The toast of the evening, th.ft "The Bride and Bridegroom," was received with the greateet enthusiasm. Several songs were given during the tvening, and the proceedings terminated at a late hour with a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Host.

Sarah Ann. at Eocleston —This wife deposed that he came home very drunk and hit her with his fists about the face and body, and kicked her; bit he did not wish to press the case, as he had come to her house that morn- ing and asked her to forgive him, saying he would not.do so again.
